title: Second day of Russia-Ukraine-US talks concludes in Abu Dhabi
content:
Negotiations in the UAE could reshape European security as Kiev’s backers seek a seat at the table

Russia, Ukraine, and the US have concluded the second day of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. Wednesday’s meeting lasted just under two hours, compared to the nearly five hours of closed-door negotiations on Tuesday.

The Abu Dhabi November round marks the first formal trilateral negotiations since February, and were made possible only by Washington’s mediation efforts, which involved talks between US envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin last month.

Presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky is leading the Russian delegation. Also present were US envoy Steve Witkoff, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The Ukrainian team is headed by Foreign Intelligence Service chief Rustem Umerov, who has said Vladimir Zelensky has authorized the delegation to discuss all issues related to ending the conflict.

Read more

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov explained on Tuesday that the first priority for negotiators is establishing the parameters of security for Russia, Ukraine and the wider region before moving on to a settlement of the conflict.

Moscow has long insisted that a lasting agreement must address the root causes of the crisis.

Kushner has outlined Washington’s priorities as ending hostilities, establishing postwar security guarantees, supporting Ukraine’s economic recovery and addressing humanitarian issues.

Territory remains a major obstacle as Zelensky has once again ruled out Ukraine withdrawing its forces from Russia’s Donbass. Speaking at a press conference in Dublin on Tuesday, he argued that Washington should find “another way” to reach a deal with Moscow. 

Read more

The Telegraph also reported that Kiev has rejected a US proposal to redraw administrative boundaries as part of a territorial compromise. Russia has consistently demanded recognition of the territorial realities on the ground, including an end to Ukrainian control over the remaining parts of Donbass.

European representatives remain outside the trilateral talks, although they met separately with US and Ukrainian officials on Tuesday. Umerov said Wednesday’s trilateral session would also be followed by another separate meeting with Ukraine’s European backers.

Moscow has questioned their contribution and has accused European governments of undermining previous peace agreements and prolonging the fighting through continued weapons supplies.

title: Before We Declare Gender Bias Dead, Read the Footnotes
content:
By Stephanie Hodge
NEW YORK, Nov 11 2026 (IPS)

The United Nations knows how to announce a milestone. What interests me, after a career that has included working inside UNICEF and UNDP and evaluating institutions from outside them, is what happens between the announcement and the working day.

Thalif Deen’s IPS article of 3 November 2026 asks whether gender bias at the UN is approaching an “inglorious end.” It is a question, not a declaration, and the reporting gives considerable space to continuing inequalities. Alongside achievements in representation, staff representatives describe barriers to advancement, weaknesses in accountability and fears about reporting discrimination. The article itself supplies reasons to resist a premature obituary for institutional bias.[1]

I bring a perspective to this question, certainly. But the discipline of evaluation requires me to challenge my own expectations as carefully as an institution’s claims. If the evidence demonstrates progress, acknowledge it. If it supports a narrower conclusion than the public celebration, say so.

The UN’s published figures demonstrate substantial progress towards numerical gender parity. They do not, on their own, establish whether discrimination in recruitment, advancement, treatment or access to authority has diminished.

UN Women reports that women’s share of Professional and higher categories across the UN system rose from 47 per cent in 2021 to 48.8 per cent in 2023, reaching 50.4 per cent in 2025. It also reports that parity among the Senior Management Group and resident coordinators has been maintained since 2018. These are meaningful achievements, and dismissing them would weaken any serious critique.[2]

The dates matter. The Secretary-General’s 2025 report principally covers January 2022 to December 2023, with developments through mid-2025. Its figures should not be presented as a fresh assessment of the workforce in November 2026.[2]

But an institutional average is an exceptionally comfortable place to hide an uncomfortable distribution.

UN Women’s accompanying infographic presents the following figures for 2025, citing the system-wide dashboard in June of that year:[3]

These figures appear in the same published presentation. They show how an overall majority can coexist with women’s underrepresentation at director levels. Under the UN’s operational definition, parity falls within a range of 47 to 53 per cent; the D-1 and D-2 figures above remain below that range.[3] [5]

That distribution does not, by itself, prove discrimination in individual appointments. Nor does a snapshot establish that women progress more slowly than men. It establishes why an aggregate percentage cannot answer the question of equal advancement. For that, we need to follow careers: who applies, who is shortlisted, who is selected, who progresses, how long progression takes, and who leaves.

There is another question beneath the celebration: which UN are we measuring?

The Secretariat dashboard cited in the article explicitly covers a defined population of international staff. Its explanatory notes say General Service and national staff are not shown and are intended for a subsequent phase. It also specifies appointment types and excludes entities with ten or fewer people. These are legitimate statistical boundaries, but they are boundaries all the same.[4]

This does not mean the UN collects no information about those groups elsewhere. It means this particular dashboard cannot establish what is happening across the whole workforce.

The Secretariat and the wider UN system are not interchangeable reporting populations. Neither are international professionals, national personnel and consultants. Every claim should tell the reader whose working lives it describes.

The Secretariat’s own human resources strategy also identifies a measure that reaches beyond headcounts. In A/80/550, the gap between women and men in the employee-empowerment dimension of the staff engagement survey is recorded as eight percentage points in 2021 and nine in 2024. Closing that gap is an explicit objective.[5]

The table does not explain the causes, establish whether the change is statistically significant, or identify which group scored higher. It should not be used as proof that discrimination worsened. It does, however, identify a workplace-experience gap that representation figures alone cannot resolve.

Nor should scepticism escape scrutiny. Shihana Mohamed, quoted in the IPS article, argues that reductions in male-dominated parts of the workforce helped produce the improved percentages. That is an explanation requiring examination, rather than a demonstrated finding we can simply adopt. The article does not provide the underlying analysis needed to establish how much of the change resulted from workforce reductions.[1]

An illustrative example shows why the question matters. An organisation employing 400 women and 600 men has 40 per cent female representation. Remove 200 men, recruit nobody, and it reaches 50 per cent. The calculation is correct; the explanation determines what achievement can reasonably be claimed. This is a hypothetical example, not a description of what happened at the UN.

Conversely, that possibility cannot justify assuming that the UN’s gains are merely arithmetic. We need comparable data on recruitment, promotion, retirement, separation and post abolition, using consistent dates and staff populations. Scrutiny must work in both directions.

What would persuade me that institutional bias was diminishing? Evidence of fairer career progression across grades, nationalities and contract types; greater confidence in raising concerns; credible protection against retaliation; and demonstrable consequences for discriminatory management. These are proposed tests of institutional change, not findings that the representation statistics have already established.

I would also ask whose experience disappears inside the category “women.” An international director, a national officer and a consultant awaiting renewal may share a gender while having profoundly different access to security and influence. An assessment of equality should examine those differences, rather than assume that one aggregate can represent them all.

The UN deserves credit for its documented gains in women’s representation. It should welcome equally rigorous examination of what those gains mean for working lives.

Count the women, certainly. Then examine who advances, who has authority, who can challenge a decision safely, and whose expertise changes the decision. Numerical parity is a meaningful achievement. Establishing that institutional bias is diminishing requires further evidence.

References

1. Deen, Thalif. “Is Gender Bias at the UN Coming to an Inglorious End?” Inter Press Service, 3 November 2026. Syndicated version.
2. UN Women. “Improvement in the status of women in the United Nations system: Report of the Secretary-General (2025).” Publication summary accompanying report A/80/260, 25 July 2025.
3. UN Women. “Representation of Women in the UN System.” Infographic accompanying the 2025 Secretary-General’s report, p. 1; 2025 figures attributed to the UN System-wide Dashboard on Gender Parity, June 2025.
4. United Nations. “UN Secretariat Gender Parity Dashboard.” Coverage and methodological notes. Accessed 3 November 2026.
5. United Nations, Secretary-General. “Implementation of human resources management reforms: outlook for 2026–2029.” A/80/550, 28 November 2025, p. 13: gender-parity definition, employee-empowerment indicators and targets.

Stephanie Hodge, MPA Harvard (2006), is an international evaluator and former UN advisor who has worked across 140 countries. She is a former staffer of UNDP (1994-1996 & 1999- 2004) and UNICEF (2008-2014). She writes on governance, multilateral reform, and climate equity.

title: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt Biden with milk in Ireland (VIDEOS)
content:
Demonstrators at Trinity College Dublin accused the former US president of complicity in Israel’s military campaign in Gaza

Pro-Palestinian protesters threw cartons of milk at former US President Joe Biden during his visit to Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday.

According to the University Times (UT), a student newspaper, the protest broke out after Biden arrived at the university to watch his son, Hunter, receive the Gold Medal for Outstanding Contribution to Public Discourse from the College Historical Society.

Demonstrators chanted “shame on you” and “genocide Joe,” accusing Biden of complicity in Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, which has left more than 74,600 Palestinians dead since October 2023 and displaced much of the enclave’s population.

Protesters threw milk cartons as US Secret Service agents escorted the former president and his family from the venue. Security personnel used umbrellas to shield them, while other demonstrators were filmed scuffling with Irish police.

Objects were thrown as former US President Joe Biden and Jill Biden left Trinity College Dublin today. Pro-Palestinian protesters had gathered outside, and Gardaí arrested at least two people. https://t.co/GxS2NuHUlj

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 10, 2026

At least two people were arrested. UT reported that officers used batons and pepper spray against protesters.

NOW: Irish pro-Pals just tried to get at President Joe Biden as he arrived at a Trinity College in Dublin. The crowd is chanting “blood on your hands”. These ghouls will never be appeased. https://t.co/oCluflYoWo

— Heidi Bachram (@HeidiBachram) November 10, 2026

Trinity College Dublin Students’ Union (TCDSU/AMLCT) and Aontas na Mac Léinn in Éirinn (AMLÉ), Ireland’s national students’ union, condemned the police response. In a joint statement, they said Biden’s “role in the genocide of the Palestinian people is well-documented” and called on the university to revoke the honorary doctorate awarded to him in 2016.

Read more

Biden, who has Irish ancestry, faced widespread criticism during his presidency for continuing to provide military and diplomatic support to Israel. Some commentators have argued that his handling of the Gaza war contributed to Democratic candidate Kamala Harris’s defeat by Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

Ireland, one of Israel’s most outspoken critics within the EU, formally recognized Palestinian statehood in 2024. West Jerusalem has rejected accusations that its military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide.

title: El Salvador calls in ‘X killstreak’ on Haitian gang HQ (VIDEO)
content:
The platform’s users flagged the house of criminal warlord Wilson Joseph for destruction by Nayib Buklele’s forces

Salvadoran forces have destroyed the alleged headquarters of Haiti’s largest criminal gang, after a social media user shared its location with Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele. He has vowed to eradicate the gangs if they refuse to return four hostages.

In a post on Friday, a Haitian X user shared a picture of a palatial compound, which she alleged that the notorious ‘400 Mawozo’ (‘400 Simpletons’) gang had built on the eastern outskirts of Port-au-Prince. Led by Wilson ‘Lanmo San Jou’ Joseph, 400 Mawozo is the largest of Haiti’s criminal gangs.

“Give us the exact address, and we’ll destroy it,” Bukele responded in Haitian Creole. Multiple users shared GPS coordinates with Bukele, but the original post was deleted over the weekend. 

However, Bukele kept his word. A fleet of Salvadoran light attack helicopters blitzed the compound, firing rockets and partially destroying its main structure and outbuildings as its occupants fled the scene. Bukele posted a video of the attack on X on Tuesday, calling the gang members “cowards” for running away “without even trying to fight.”

“Some guy on X called in a killstreak on a gang’s HQ and Bukele went through with it. Insane timeline,” one X user responded, summing up the online reaction to the strike.

Haitian police and private security contractors stormed the compound after the rocket barrage, the Miami Herald reported. 

What is El Salvador doing in Haiti?

Read more

Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti late last month, after four Salvadoran military aircraft technicians were kidnapped while assisting the UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force (GSF) mission. The technicians were reportedly kidnapped by Chen Mechan, a smaller member of the broad confederation of gangs that has de facto ruled Haiti since 2021.

The hostages have not yet been returned, despite an attempt by a Chen Mechan-linked NGO to pass four unrelated corpses to Salvadoran forces last week. Bukele has claimed that El Salvador has “no interest in coming to dominate the Haitian people, nor in laying hands on Haiti’s wealth,” but has promised to wage war against the “Satanic” gangs until the captives are handed over. Bukele has also suggested that Salvadoran forces could remain longer in Haiti to assist the anti-gang mission.

Joseph initially vowed to drive the Salvadoran troops out of Haiti, but has since requested mediation from UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, according to AP. Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime will reportedly travel to El Salvador next week to meet with Bukele’s government, the news agency reported on Tuesday.

Crowdsourced airstrikes 

Bukele may be the first national leader to solicit targeting data from social media, but the concept of crowdsourced airstrikes is not a new one. During the height of the Syrian Civil War in 2016, a group of 4chan users geolocated videos posted by Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS) and other jihadist fighters and fed their locations to a Russian military blogger who went by the alias ‘Ivan Sidorenko’. 

4chan users find coordinates of terrorists in Syria and call in Russian airstrikes. 5-30-2016 https://t.co/wsfomyxONT

— Middle East Observer (@ME_Observer_) November 29, 2020

At least one jihadist training camp was subsequently destroyed by Russian airstrikes, although it remains unclear whether ‘Ivan Sidorenko’ supplied the coordinates to the Russian Defense Ministry, as he claimed.

Throughout the Russia-Ukraine conflict, both sides have used information gleaned from social media videos to locate and strike military deployment points, arms factories, and critical infrastructure.

title: Trump and Netanyahu in ‘shouting match from hell’ during Iran call – media
content:
The Israeli PM has reportedly been pressing Washington to resume strikes on Tehran despite the US president’s reluctance to escalate

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a heated phone call with US President Donald Trump over the possibility of renewed military strikes against Iran, Ynet reported on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the conversation.

Several media outlets, including Axios, the Associated Press and the Financial Times, previously reported that Netanyahu had been urging Trump to resume military operations against Iran shortly after the US midterm elections. Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in the November 3 vote, widely seen as a rebuke to Trump’s policies, including the unpopular war with Iran, which has driven up energy prices.

Ynet described the weekend conversation as unusually tense, with one source calling it a “shouting match from hell.” Netanyahu’s office dismissed the report as “fake news, absolute nonsense,” while a senior Israeli official confirmed that the call took place but denied that it had been confrontational.

Read more

Trump said on Sunday that he saw no reason to escalate the conflict with Iran, amid opposition to renewed strikes from Washington’s Arab allies in the region. He and US Vice President J.D. Vance have acknowledged that the Iran war contributed to the Republicans’ election defeat.

Nevertheless, Trump stood by his decision to launch the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran on February 28. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told the Wall Street Journal after the vote.

Netanyahu’s political future is also uncertain after his coalition failed to secure a parliamentary majority in Israel’s October 27 elections.

On Sunday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Netanyahu’s main rival, former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, with forming a new government after parties representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended him for the premiership, compared with 46 who backed Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days to assemble a governing coalition, with a possible two-week extension. 

The war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies that normally carries around a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil and liquefied natural gas trade. Trump has vowed to maintain the naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Iran has been attacking tankers using US-designated shipping routes, which Tehran considers illegal.

title: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies as the new parliament was sworn in.

The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israels longest-serving prime minister.

While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu's opponents now control a solid majority in parliament.

Eisenkot's bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies. They include launching an official government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead.

Israels president gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government

Competing calls for unity

The former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated on Tuesday that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions.

We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment, Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony.

Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties stole the elections.

In a speech following Tuesdays ceremony, Netanyahu reiterated his claim that Arab politicians, who represent a minority comprising 20% of Israels population, cannot be trusted. He attacked Jewish opposition leaders who have signaled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israels identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group.

I ask you: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state? Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot said Netanyahu's speech was divisive and hate-filled, adding: I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute. He later said he had canceled a meeting with Netanyahu's Likud party planned for Wednesday because of the speech.

RELATED STORY | Arab bloc signals willingness to back coalition seeking to oust Netanyahu

Netanyahu's opponents already have a legislative agenda

Eisenkot's bloc also triggered a process on Tuesday to install a new parliamentary speaker as they kicked off work on their legislative agenda.

A majority of members submitted signatures calling for the ousting of the current Netanyahu-backed speaker, Amir Ohana, the first step toward a vote on his replacement. The vote can take place even before a coalition government is in place.

The Knesset speaker is a powerful position. The speaker determines what bills the Knesset will take up, meaning one picked from among the Eisenkot-led opposition parties could propel their legislative agenda forward.

The opposition nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Eisenkots Yashar party, for the job. A vote to appoint him speaker could come as early as this week.

Netanyahu as caretaker

The swearing-in of the new Knesset ushered in an unusual transitional period in Israeli politics Netanyahu and his Cabinet remain in power, while the new lawmakers can introduce legislation.

Meanwhile, Eisenkot will meet with party leaders as he works to build a coalition that would likely make him prime minister. If he fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu the next opportunity to form a government.

As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu faces court-imposed limits on his powers. But he can still pursue appointments and could try to block new legislation. He retains full authority over national security, including the military.

Netanyahu has argued that Jewish-led parties should form a unity government to counter the threat of an Iranian attack. He renewed that call Tuesday, urging them to set aside all other considerations, and said Israel should work to topple the Iranian government.

A governing coalition without Netanyahu could leave him politically vulnerable as he faces an ongoing corruption trial and possible findings of security failures in the lead-up to the Oct. 7 attacks.

Spanish neo-Nazis trained in Ukraine for ‘armed uprising’ – media
content:
Members of the Nucleo Nacional group reportedly received weapons training from the Azov brigade to prepare militants back home

Members of a Spanish neo-Nazi organization have received military training from Ukraine’s notorious Azov brigade to prepare for an “armed uprising” back home, according to police findings reported by El Pais on Tuesday.

Militants from Nucleo Nacional (National Nucleus) traveled to Ukraine in August, where they established contact with the neo-Nazi-linked Azov unit, now part of Ukraine’s National Guard, the newspaper reported, citing investigative documents.

The Spaniards reportedly trained with AK-47 assault rifles and body armor, seeking to acquire combat skills they could pass on to recruits across Spain. In an intercepted conversation, one member warned that “without training, no uprising will work.”

Investigators traced the extremists to Kiev, a military training camp and an unidentified town roughly 20 kilometers from the Russian border. Photographs showed members wearing Nucleo Nacional clothing, including one carrying a rifle and displaying a Nazi flag patch. Others wore sweatshirts bearing the logo of Stormfront, a prominent white supremacist online forum.

Spanish police launched a crackdown on Nucleo Nacional last week over fears of violence at a planned November 7 march in Madrid. The authorities cited the group’s military training, international extremist connections and potential access to military-grade weapons.

Read more

Fourteen suspects were arrested across seven provinces. Ten were subsequently released under restrictions, including passport confiscation, travel bans, and mandatory weekly court appearances. The investigation involves suspected incitement to hatred, unlawful association, and possession of prohibited weapons.

Police also uncovered links between the group and extremist organizations in Germany, France, Hungary, Romania, and Croatia.

Moscow has repeatedly accused Western governments of turning a blind eye to Ukrainian neo-Nazi networks while continuing to arm and finance Kiev. Russia maintains that denazification remains a key condition for a lasting settlement of the Ukraine conflict.

Russian officials have also warned that Western support for Ukrainian neo-Nazi formations could backfire, allowing extremist networks, weapons, and violence to spread across Europe.

European law enforcement agencies have previously raised concerns about weapons supplied to Ukraine entering criminal markets. Ukrainian investigators have also uncovered arms trafficking from the front line.

In May, the Ukrainian authorities intercepted a shipment of grenades, anti-tank weapons, mines and ammunition allegedly destined for the black market. The seized weapons were subsequently handed over to the Azov unit.

title: Four EU states defy Merz’s Ukraine funding ultimatum
content:
Slovak PM Robert Fico has accused Berlin of “blackmail” over its demand to link the bloc’s next seven-year budget to continued spending on Kiev

Slovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic have rejected German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s demand to tie the EU’s next seven-year budget to additional funding for Ukraine. The three Central European countries have long opposed writing blank checks to Kiev, while Bulgaria elected a government more critical of such assistance in April.

The EU has pledged to cover around €45 billion of Ukraine’s projected €70 billion funding shortfall in 2027, as the conflict with Russia approaches its fifth year in February.

In a letter to European Council President Antonio Costa, widely cited by the media, Merz wrote that all member states “without exception” should commit to long-term funding of Ukraine beyond 2028. 

‘Unacceptable’

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico branded Berlin’s ultimatum a “textbook case of blackmail.”

Read more

“Today will not be business as usual – not by a long shot. Today, we must respond to blackmail,” he told journalists at a joint press conference with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis in Bratislava on Tuesday. “We have an equal say in this matter,” he said, adding that his country would not be a part of any loans to Ukraine. 

Babis also rejected Merz’s demand, saying Prague would not be “in any subordinate position.” He said that Ukraine has received €520 billion from the EU since 2022 and that the bloc’s budget already includes an additional €100 billion in funding for Kiev.

“I don’t understand why someone wants to block the budget when Ukraine has so much money. The question is whether it should be [in] the budget at all,” Babis said. 

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who traveled to Berlin for talks with Merz on Tuesday, said linking the EU budget with Ukraine aid was “unacceptable” and that Budapest was focusing on curbing its own budgetary deficit. He further argued that the bloc should prioritize helping its own citizens and businesses.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen the same day, also stressed the need to handle Bulgaria’s own deficit. He noted that Bulgaria was already supporting Ukraine through electricity exports, the restoration of energy and railway infrastructure, and the help it provides to refugees. 

Read more

‘Task for all of us’

Speaking at a joint press conference with Magyar in Berlin, Merz described long-term support for Ukraine as “a common European task” and said continued funding for Kiev must be reflected in the EU’s next budget to make it “fit for the future.” 

“This is a question of collective European security and thus a task for all of us,” Merz said. 

Germany has become Ukraine’s largest individual military donor as American assistance has fallen sharply since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. It has provided or earmarked €57.6 billion in military aid and €43.3 billion in civilian assistance since 2022.

However, only around 40% of the roughly €100 billion reported by Berlin qualifies as actual bilateral aid to Ukraine, according to an October report by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW). The institute found that more than 80% of the reported civilian assistance was spent in Germany, mostly on Ukrainian refugees. Another €1.3 billion consisted of export and investment guarantees for German companies operating in Ukraine.

The institute also found that the traceable total of German military aid was €56.3 billion, €1.3 billion less than Berlin’s reported figure. Of that amount, €22 billion consisted of future commitments, including approximately €12 billion in potential additional spending.

“Germany is clearly Europe’s biggest donor to Ukraine. But the German government’s communication about its aid is becoming increasingly confusing,” said Christoph Trebesch, head of the IfW Ukraine Support Tracker team.

Read more

According to the IfW, Berlin stopped providing detailed information on military aid to Kiev in June 2025, roughly a month after Merz took office. The assessment came two months after German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul criticized Kiev for not spending enough of Western-provided financial aid on weapons from Germany, arguing that Berlin’s massive support for Ukraine should benefit domestic arms manufacturers.

Germany amended the constitutional debt brake and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion for defense and €11.5 billion in military aid for Kiev, despite warnings from the German central bank about a looming record budget deficit.

Aiding Ukraine or… himself?

Merz has faced cratering public support, with an INSA poll showing last week that 82% of Germans were dissatisfied with his work. A similar number said they were dissatisfied with his cabinet, while 60% said their personal well-being had worsened during Merz’s time in office.

The chancellor, who came to power as a result of snap elections in February 2025, vowing to revive the struggling economy, has since argued that the welfare state “can no longer be financed” while announcing social spending cuts.

“This is actually about funding Germany, not Ukraine,” Rachel Marsden, a political columnist, told RT. 

“Ukraine is really just a convenient cover story for dropping billions on frontline defense… when 30 to 40% of that aid actually loops straight back into the German economy to prop up defense giants like Rheinmetall and Diehl,” she argued.

Marsden said Merz was “holding a metaphorical knife to Europe’s throat” by threatening to “single-handedly blow up” the EU budget unless other members get in line.

Fyodor Lukyanov: Abu Dhabi talks signal a major shift in the Ukraine peace process
content:
Moscow’s calls to rethink European security were rejected before the war. The Abu Dhabi talks suggest Washington is now prepared to discuss them.

The trilateral talks on Ukraine in Abu Dhabi have prompted mixed reactions, but most observers advise against expecting a breakthrough. The delegations may be senior, but their discussions are essentially technical, plus they can’t make political decisions, and the positions publicly maintained by Moscow and Kiev still offer little room for compromise.

Yet there’s a shared recognition that the talks are serious and more importantly, perhaps for the first time since the conflict began, the question of Europe’s wider security architecture, and the guarantees it would require, has moved to the center of negotiations, so that alone is a significant change.

To appreciate its importance, we should look back five years. In November 2021, President Vladimir Putin instructed the Russian Foreign Ministry to raise Europe’s security arrangements with NATO. Moscow had never regarded the post-Cold War, NATO-centred order as satisfactory and successive rounds of enlargement had gradually transformed Russian unease into a conviction that the bloc posed a direct threat.

The Foreign Ministry subsequently presented proposals for revising that order, but talks in January 2022 demonstrated how far apart the sides were. The Americans and Western Europeans were unwilling to entertain Moscow’s central proposition, which was that the existing security system needed fundamental change because, as far as they were concerned, there was no problem to solve.

What happened next is well known and at the time, Washington and the Western European capitals spoke with one voice, but five years later, something unexpected has happened in that a different American administration now acknowledges that security guarantees for all sides are indispensable to resolving the Ukraine crisis, and is prepared to discuss them in Abu Dhabi.

Read more

Western Europe hasn’t followed and its governments continue to insist that NATO must remain the organizing principle of continental security and that Russia can’t be allowed to dictate the rules. Nevertheless, the American shift matters because a subject once dismissed as inadmissible has entered the negotiating agenda.

Until recently, Washington’s diplomatic efforts had focused on territory and that appears to have been the principal issue at the Anchorage meeting in August 2025. Moscow, however, has never abandoned what it calls the root causes of the conflict, which are the wider arrangements governing European security and for the first time, those issues are being addressed by the other side as part of a possible settlement, but this doesn’t mean agreement is close because the obstacles remain formidable.

The first is Western Europe’s determination to resist any settlement that gives Moscow a role in reshaping the continent’s security order and the second is the changing political balance in Washington. The Republicans’ defeat in the midterm elections has weakened Donald Trump and strengthened those who oppose his approach to Russia.

Trump insists he will continue pursuing his foreign policy regardless and he may well do so, but domestic resistance will intensify, while Western European leaders, many of whom would like to see him reduced from a lame duck to a dead duck, will take encouragement. Together with Kiev, they have already shown that they can frustrate initiatives from the White House and they will now believe their leverage has increased.

And yet Abu Dhabi could still prove a turning point, not merely because the agenda has widened, but because the circumstances surrounding the negotiations are changing.

Read more

Ukraine’s financial and military requirements continue to grow as Kiev needs more money to sustain the state, more weapons and greater outside support for almost every aspect of the war effort and Western Europe is finding it increasingly difficult to meet these demands. The United States, meanwhile, is no longer willing to finance Ukraine on the previous scale and this reluctance may outlast Trump. Democrats will accuse him of appeasing the Kremlin and abandoning Kiev, but the pressure to prioritize domestic concerns is growing in their own ranks.

Ukraine’s internal position is also becoming more precarious with economic, social, and political strains accumulating, while Zelensky has little incentive to compromise given retreat would threaten the foundations of his authority. For now, he retains some room for maneuver, but what happens during and after the winter is much less certain, particularly if Western assistance does not increase.

There are signs, too, of unease within Western Europe’s establishment. The recent calls to Putin by the Norwegian prime minister and Finnish president, whatever explanation they offered, suggest a dawning recognition that the present policy has reached its limits and that it makes little sense to demand a place at the negotiating table while refusing to speak to one of the principal parties.

A common Western boycott of Russia was at least a coherent strategy while Washington participated in it but once the United States resumed direct engagement, Western Europe’s refusal to do likewise became an obstacle not only to diplomacy but to its own influence.

The prospect of a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the United States in Shenzhen remains open and should it take place, the symbolism will be unmistakable in that the major powers are increasingly discussing the future of international security without Europe.

That’s the deeper significance of Abu Dhabi. There may be no immediate agreement, and certainly no easy peace, but the debate is beginning to move beyond the Ukrainian front line towards the question Moscow raised before the fighting began, which is what kind of security order can Europe live with, and who gets to decide?

This article was first published by Rossiyskaya Gazeta, and was translated and edited by the RT team

title: US senator hails ‘beauty’ of paying Ukrainians to kill Russians
content:
An Arizona Democrat has argued that Moscow will eventually tire of the conflict if it suffers enough casualties

The “beauty” of US military support for Kiev is that Washington is paying Ukrainians to kill Russians, and the more the better, a sitting Democrat Senator has claimed.

Ruben Gallego of Arizona, a former US marine who has previously said he would “come after” Elon Musk, made the remarks in an exchange on X on Tuesday, after a commenter accused him of backing a lost cause. Gallego insisted that he supported Ukraine because he believed it could win.

“If Ukraine kills enough Russians they will quit,” the senator wrote.

In response to a suggestion that he should join Ukraine’s so-called “foreign legion” of mercenaries Gallego replied, “No that’s the beauty of this, we can pay the Ukrainians to kill the Russians.”

Asked how many dead Russians would be enough to satisfy him, Gallego responded, “There is always room for one more.”

Read more

Gallego, who took office in January 2025, has been a staunch advocate of US military assistance to Kiev. Last week, he accused SpaceX CEO Elon Musk of having “Ukrainian blood on his hands” and demanded that the billionaire testify before Congress over disruptions to the Starlink and Starshield satellite services used by Ukrainian forces.

Kiev claimed last month that a deliberate slowdown had disrupted its drone operations, initially suggesting Washington was responsible.

Musk countered that Ukraine had been exploiting a loophole in SpaceX’s civilian Starlink network to conduct offensive drone strikes, insisting that the vulnerability had been closed. He also stressed that Starshield was a separate, military-grade system controlled by the Pentagon.

Gallego also faced controversy in March for endorsing Graham Platner, then a Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, despite revelations involving Nazi imagery and inflammatory past statements.

Read more

Platner had a Totenkopf tattoo on his chest, a skull emblem used by Nazi SS units, including a division implicated in numerous war crimes. He denied knowing its historical significance and described himself as an anti-fascist.

The candidate also faced criticism over old online posts containing homophobic slurs and comments suggesting that military sexual assault victims should “act like an adult” and avoid getting “blacked out f*cked up.”

Gallego initially stood by Platner but withdrew his endorsement following allegations of sexual misconduct and rape, which prompted other Democratic supporters to distance themselves from the candidate and ultimately preceded the end of his campaign.

Moscow has repeatedly characterized the Ukraine conflict as a Western-led proxy war fought “to the last Ukrainian,” arguing that continued Western military assistance only prolongs the fighting and increases human suffering.

title: Russell Brand jailed while Epstein-linked UK elites walk free (VIDEO)
content:
The comedian has been sentenced to ten and a half years in prison, while former Prince Andrew and Peter Mandelson remain free amid separate investigations

British comedian and podcaster Russell Brand was sentenced on Monday to ten and a half years in prison after being convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others between 2004 and 2009. He denied wrongdoing, maintaining that all sexual encounters were consensual.

Brand has amassed 6.6 million subscribers on YouTube, where he has attacked what he describes as the UK’s corrupt ruling class and criticized Western governments over their handling of the Covid-19 pandemic and support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.

Some of his supporters have claimed that the prosecution was politically motivated. Billionaire Elon Musk and US commentator Megyn Kelly publicly defended Brand following his conviction, while former Fox News host Tucker Carlson had previously voiced support for him.

Read more

RT’s Marina Kosareva examines how other prominent British figures have faced allegations of sexual misconduct or scrutiny over their ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein without receiving comparable criminal sentences.

One of the most prominent cases involves Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the younger brother of King Charles III, who was stripped of his royal titles in 2025 following years of sexual abuse allegations and scrutiny of his ties to Epstein.

Andrew was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office over allegations that he shared sensitive government information with Epstein. He was subsequently released without charge but remains under investigation. Police have also examined allegations of potential sexual offences involving the former prince.

In 2022, Andrew settled a civil sexual assault lawsuit brought against him in the US by Virginia Giuffre, who alleged that he had sexually abused her on three occasions when she was 17. He has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a sexual offence.

Peter Mandelson, a veteran Labour Party politician, was dismissed as Britain’s ambassador to the US last year over his ties to Epstein. He subsequently left the Labour Party and resigned from the House of Lords.

In February, Mandelson was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office over allegations that he had passed sensitive government information to Epstein. He was subsequently released, with police lifting his bail conditions in March while continuing their investigation.

title: US moves aircraft from another UK military base amid potential threat for Iran, officials say
content:
The U.S. Air Force has moved a series of aircraft away from another U.K. military base this time from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, just east of London due to a potential threat from Iran, U.S. officials told The Associated Press.

About a dozen KC-135 refueling tankers, as well as some Osprey aircraft, have reportedly left the base, according to reporting from The Wall Street Journal. The aircraft appear to have relocated to other bases throughout Europe, including in Germany, Italy and Spain.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat

The U.K.'s Ministry of Defense said it does not normally comment on the military activity of other nations, adding that aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said aircraft also rotate for a variety of reasons, including training and real-world requirements, and did not offer any additional insight on matters of operational security.

The move follows an incident in September at another base in the U.K. that is used by the U.S. military. That incident led to a major security situation, with two British nationals accused of being involved in an Iranian-linked plot to target the base where U.S. long-range bombers were stationed something Iran has denied.

title: U.S. charges three with planning Iran-backed terror attacks, including on U.K. airbase
US charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK airbase
content:
Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat

"These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members," McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical it is very real."

Attorney General Todd Blanche said: "Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.

British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.

What to know about the suspected bomb plot against a UK air base

RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.

The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah.

In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. He called himself a "prisoner of war." He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.

Both Kata'ib Hizballah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata'ib Hizballah commander.

title: Russia-US-Ukraine trilateral talks: What are the experts saying?
content:
The commentators weigh in on Washington’s changing approach and Moscow’s vision for a new European security architecture

Russian experts are weighing in on the trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi, aimed at defining a new European security architecture. RT has asked top analysts for their take on developments and reviewed the best of Russian media to bring together their assessments.

Dmitry Trenin, president of the Russian International Affairs Council (RIAC): Peace, not just a ceasefire

The Abu Dhabi talks could pave the way for further high-level contacts between Moscow and Washington, Dmitry Trenin, the president of the Russian International Affairs Council (RIAC), has told RT.

”We can expect diplomatic efforts to intensify,” Trenin said, pointing to further consultations and a possible visit to Moscow by US President Donald Trump’s envoys.

However, he cautioned against assuming that a peace settlement was only a matter of time, stressing that “what is at stake is peace, not a ceasefire.”

The Ukraine conflict cannot be resolved without addressing broader European security concerns, the expert said, adding that “a peace settlement in Ukraine is part of Europe’s security architecture” and that “the two issues are closely intertwined.”

Trenin recalled that in 2021, Moscow presented the US and NATO with “separate but interconnected sets of proposals for a new security architecture.” The West rejected them, and Russia launched its military operation afterward, he said.

Read more

Any settlement would therefore have to include security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, he added.

The analyst said that he expects European governments to seek a “more active role” in the diplomatic process, although they will first need to clarify their positions on a number of issues. 

Read more

“We should not expect the EU to join the negotiations as a supranational institution. The European Union is not an international actor in the security sphere,” he said.

At the same time, Trenin considered the participation of European countries logical and necessary when it comes to addressing practical aspects of the continent’s security. The difficulty, according to him, lies in the positions currently held by many European leaders, whom he described as remaining “captive to unrealistic ideas.”

He suggested that dialogue could become possible once those positions, or the leaders themselves, change.

Sergey Poletaev, Russian foreign policy information analyst and publicist: Washington adopting Moscow’s perspective

A significant shift in Washington’s position on what the negotiations should achieve and what a peace agreement should look like marks the key difference between the current round and previous diplomatic efforts, information analyst and co-founder of the Vatfor project, Sergey Poletaev, has told RT.

”The US now appears to accept that such an agreement must include fundamental decisions on Europe’s security architecture,” he said.

According to Poletaev, this represents a move toward Moscow’s longstanding position, first set out in its security proposals to NATO in December 2021. “The Trump administration has, at least for now, adopted Moscow’s perspective,” he said.

Poletaev recalled that European security architecture was central to Russia’s demands at the time and that NATO’s outright rejection of those proposals helped trigger Moscow’s military operation. He said that the very phrase “security architecture” closely resembles the language used in Kremlin documents.

Poletaev contrasted Washington’s apparent shift with the position of Kiev’s European backers.

”European governments insist on the opposite sequence: a ceasefire first, negotiations afterward. Essentially, they are repeating the position they held before the war.”

Poletaev cautioned, however, that “Washington has changed course before and could do so again.”

The analyst said Washington’s current approach gives the negotiations a basis for discussing specific terms, even without European agreement on the broader security agenda. “Bargaining over the details can follow, while Europe may remain in its current state of denial.”

Poletaev stressed the significance of the renewed focus on European security, saying that “as the conflict approaches the end of its fifth year, the discussion is finally turning to the issue on which a settlement ultimately depends.”

Viktor Litovkin: Security guarantees must address the root causes

Direct talks between Moscow and Kiev, with US participation, provide an opportunity to exchange and compare positions on security after the fighting ends, Russian military journalist and analyst Viktor Litovkin has told RT.

The negotiations could help identify common ground and reach compromises aimed at addressing the “root causes of the conflict,” he said.

One major obstacle is the proposal by Kiev’s European backers to deploy troops to Ukraine under future security arrangements. Litovkin pointed to Moscow’s rejection of foreign military contingents, which Russia considers incompatible with a lasting peace.

Litovkin noted that European representatives were not part of the trilateral negotiations but could consult the Ukrainian delegation separately, including “in the hallway,” without joining the talks themselves.

He argued that if European countries considered themselves parties to the negotiations on the grounds that they were participants in the conflict, they would have to openly acknowledge that they were fighting Russia on Ukraine’s side. In that case, he warned, Russian strikes could extend beyond Ukraine to European territory. He noted, however, that European governments have made no such declaration, instead describing their role as helping Kiev.

Litovkin said Ukraine’s non-membership in NATO needs to be enshrined in its constitution. He also called for guarantees for the Russian language and the Russian Orthodox Church in Ukraine, along with an end to what he described as the persecution of Russians.

The analyst also criticized the idea of a Russia-NATO council, arguing that such a format would be unequal, with 32 NATO member states on one side and Russia alone on the other.

Evgeny Minchenko, political scientist: Russian delegation ready for substantive talks

Russia has sent a “strong” and “highly practical” delegation to Abu Dhabi, political analyst Evgeny Minchenko told Vzglyad ahead of Tuesday’s negotiations.

He pointed to the participation of senior diplomats, military officials, and representatives of the Federal Security Service (FSB). Deputy Foreign Ministers Mikhail Galuzin and Sergey Ryabkov, he said, could discuss in detail the system of checks and balances in a new European security architecture.

Minchenko also noted the presence of Igor Kostyukov, Russia’s military intelligence chief, and senior FSB official Aleksey Komkov, whose responsibilities include international relations and security matters.

The delegation’s composition, he concluded, showed that the talks were intended to address “concrete issues, not abstract discussions.”

Aleksey Martynov, political analyst: A wider European security dialogue

The Abu Dhabi talks are part of a broader process aimed at creating a new European security architecture, according to political analyst Aleksey Martynov.

Speaking to Vzglyad, Martynov said he expected discussions on the issue to continue at the APEC summit, with the Russian, US, and Chinese leaders taking part.

Martynov questioned the involvement of European leaders at the current stage, arguing that they were not prepared for constructive discussions on resolving the Ukraine conflict and were unable to defend their own countries’ national interests.

However, he did not rule out future contacts, saying that an exchange of views on key issues could take place “at the expert level.” Echoing earlier assessments, Martynov said EU leaders could join the broader dialogue at the final stages of implementing a new European security architecture.

Dmitry Solonnikov, Director of the Institute of Contemporary Development: Talks could yield practical steps

The Abu Dhabi negotiations could help bring an end to the Ukraine conflict by addressing its root causes, Dmitry Solonnikov, director of the Institute of Contemporary Development, told Moscow 24.

He argued that discussions on a new European security architecture marked a return to the issues raised by President Vladimir Putin in 2021, before the start of Moscow’s military operation.

According to Solonnikov, an agreement on the broader security arrangements would pave the way for resolving more specific questions, including how to end the fighting and establish new security boundaries. Those, he said, would become “technical questions” once the parties agreed on how to coexist in the future.

title: After the midterm bloodbath, what is Trump ready to concede?
content:
Washington DC may grind to a screeching halt as the president wields the ultimate power of the veto, while the Democrats have the vote on their side

On nearly all of the political fronts, the Republicans under Trump are in a steady retreat, backing away from core policies that have outraged their base and empowered the Democrats with an army of new supporters. The GOP suffered an extraordinary midterm repudiation – losing not just the House and Senate, but statewide offices in red states, from Texas to Kansas to South Carolina, that Democrats hadn’t won in decades.

Exactly how deep the humiliating loss was for the MAGA camp became clear in a sit-down interview with 60 Minutes on Sunday. The American leader conceded that his deportation policy “might be too tough” and that he would “love to do something on immigration” with the Democrats about to take over Congress, he told the news program in his first interview since the midterms.

Asked by CBS correspondent Ross Douthat whether the crackdown damaged Republicans in the midterms, Trump was ambivalent: “I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.” “But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation for breaking of the law. And that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Douthat then asked: “So you think your deportation policy went too far?” “It was too tough,” Trump said. “I think it might be too tough. Yeah.”

He said the deal he has in mind with Democrats is “something that’s actually doable”: “some kind of legal status for the landscapers,” and for people like a hotel maid or waitress who are suddenly “taken out of the country.” “It’s tough,” he said. “It’s a tough thing.”

Trump admitted that the hardcore far-right group inside of his administration would like everybody removed, while others are “more modified on that”: “get the killers out, get all the rough ones out, get the drug dealers out. But let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them.”

Read more

In a positive sign for dual party border cooperation, self-described “border security Democrat” James Talarico expressed his willingness to cross the aisle and work directly with Donald Trump to fix the border.

Talarico is the first Democrat to win a US Senate election in Texas since 1988 and will become the youngest US Senator; he has stated that he is eager to work with the Trump administration on immigration reform.

In February 2026, Talarico said he supported the Dignity Act, a proposed bipartisan immigration reform bill. In a January 2026 debate, he called for the increase in funding for ICE during the Trump administration to be diverted to other services. In a shocking move for a Democrat, Talarico has harshly criticized former US President Joe Biden’s border policy, saying it “created chaos in our border communities.”

However, there already appears to be a fly in the ointment as Trump, just one hour after his conversation with 60 Minutes, replaced his chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the aggressive architect of the controversial immigrant policy.

“We are being conquered,” border czar Miller told Fox News in 2023.

“So, a generation from now, I am telling you … people will not know the country that they are living in. These consequences are permanent. Unless there’s massive large-scale deportations by the millions, it will be irrevocable.” It will be very interesting to see if Miller is able to tame his strong sentiments in order to come to a meeting ground with the Democrats on the question of amnesty for immigrants.

Another political hotspot that will require a high degree of understanding and cooperation between the Democrats and the Republicans is the war in Iran, which continues to smolder in the background.

Read more

Israel, an allied friend of the Trump administration, has played no small part in this process. According to the Financial Times, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged Trump to carry out further strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections. Observers note that a continuation of the conflict could aid Netanyahu’s domestic political standing after his coalition lost its parliamentary majority.

Needless to say, Netanyahu has shown no concern whatsoever for the damage the war in Iran has caused for the Republicans in general and Trump in particular. Israel is attempting to restart the war during an open window of opportunity between now and when the Democrats assume power in January.

Just like their MAGA opponents, the Democrats are adamantly opposed to the war and will have ample ability to scuttle the US military once they take over both houses of Congress next year.

Democrats are looking to bring President Trump’s war with Iran to a halt once they retake the majority. Senate Democrats say they have some Republican support to end the conflict, which has dragged on for more than eight months, and have threatened to use the “power of the purse” to deprive the Pentagon of funds needed to wage the war.

Both the US leader and Vice President J.D. Vance singled out the Iran war as the main reason for why Republicans experienced an electoral blowout, with Democrats taking the majority in the House, Senate, governors’ mansions and statehouses.

“We are going to end the war. We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said at a press conference.

Read more

Meanwhile, Trump, aware of the damage that the military conflict did to his base with the 2028 presidential election fast approaching, has declared his hesitation in restarting a hot war with the Islamic state.

“The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.”

Finally, there is the question of inflation in food and gas prices. The war with Iran is a primary driver of the current affordability crisis, significantly inflating the cost of living for consumers through energy shocks, higher borrowing rates, and supply chain disruptions.

According to Moody’s Analytics, the conflict has cost US consumers hundreds of billions of dollars, translating to roughly $2,000 to $2,150 in added expenses for the average American household, which explains the Republican Party’s extraordinary losses on November 3.

The American people on both the right and left spoke loud and clear during the midterm elections, and it would be heedless and rash of the Trump administration to continue with war and anti-immigration business as usual. The political costs are simply too high.

1.5 Billion Women and Girls Live in Climate Hotspots, as UN Women Urges Stronger Action at COP31
content:
Communities in the Kavango West region of northern Namibia have firsthand experience of the severe impacts of climate change. The dry, cracked soil and emaciated livestock provide a constant reminder of the lack of access to water in this part of the country. Credit: UNFPA Namibia

By UN Women
ANTALYA, Türkiye , Nov 10 2026 (IPS)

More than one in three women and girls worldwide – at least 1.5 billion – live in climate hotspots, where high exposure to climate hazards, insecure jobs and deep gender inequality collide, according to a new UN Women fact sheet on “Gender Equality in the Age of Climate Crisis”. UN Women warns that while 73 per cent of countries recognize the climate risks facing women and girls, just over one in three address them comprehensively.

“Across the world, women are already leading the fight for a better future – in their communities, in laboratories, in parliaments and on the front lines of the climate crisis. We must give women and girls equal rights, resources and the power to lead, and they will help drive the change our world so urgently needs”, said Sima Bahous, Executive Director of UN Women.

On the current trajectory, the world is headed for a minimum of 1.8°C of heating, unleashing even more devastating droughts, floods, wildfires and cyclones, and creating irreversible loss and damage to communities and ecosystems. New data from UN Women shows that women and girls in the countries least responsible for climate crisis are hit hardest by it, from the food they go without to the violence they face, climate change is affecting every aspect of their lives.

    • Under a worst-case scenario, up to 141 million additional women and girls could be living in extreme poverty.
    • Based on data from 24 countries, a 1°C increase in average temperatures is associated with women losing 34 per cent more of their total income than men likely reflecting their more limited ability to shift to non-farm work or migrate when harvests fail.
    • Climate change is increasing unpaid care responsibilities, such as collection of water and fuel, and care for family members in the aftermath of disasters. Of the 1.8 billion people without water on their premises, women are primary water collectors in two-thirds of households. Under a high-emissions scenario, the time spent collecting water could increase by up to 30 per cent by 2050.
    • Climate-related livelihood losses, displacement and resource scarcity can magnify existing drivers of gender-based violence. Across 14 countries, exposure to prolonged extreme drought was associated with 21 per cent higher odds of sexual violence against adolescent girls and young women.
    • Over the past decade, progress in reducing child marriage has nearly doubled in pace. Climate change threatens to undo that progress. In 24 of 46 countries where data on child marriage can be disaggregated by exposure to slow-onset events, rates of child marriage were higher in more arid environments than in more humid ones.
    • AI technology drives up energy demand, while 326 million women and girls still lack access to electricity.
    • Women remain largely excluded from climate decision-making, holding just 12 per cent of energy portfolios globally, and women environmental defenders face harassment and even death for protecting their communities and the planet.
    • Developing countries receive less than a third of the climate finance they need, while just 4 per cent of climate-focused Official Development Assistance prioritises gender equality.

The fact sheet also shows that progress is possible. With the right investments, women could secure up to 66 per cent of net new green jobs, gaining 68 million additional jobs by 2035.

Governments are stepping up; 73 per cent of nationally determined contributions – governments’ self-defined climate action plans – now acknowledge gender-specific climate risks. However, just over one in three addresses them comprehensively.

At COP31, UN Women calls on world leaders to put gender equality and women’s rights at the heart of climate action, to move towards economies that put people and the planet before profits, build resilience for all and advance gender equality. That means guaranteeing the right of all women and girls to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, protecting the women environmental human rights defenders who risk their lives for their communities and the planet, and giving women and girls real power at the decision-making table.

It means delivering gender-responsive climate finance that reaches women and their organizations, advancing a just transition that redistributes care, and tackling the heightened risks of violence against women and girls as the climate crisis deepens. The new Belém Gender Action Plan must be fully implemented and fully financed, so that political commitments become real change for women and girls on the front line of climate crises.

IPS UN Bureau

EU to deploy military advisers to Ukraine
content:
Moscow has long warned that Western troops in the country would be legitimate targets

The European Council has decided to send EU military personnel directly to Ukraine, despite numerous warnings from Moscow that European soldiers would be fair game for Russian strikes.

European nations are scrambling to participate in the ongoing Russia-US-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, having been sidelined from several previous rounds.

On Monday, the Council extended the mandate of the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM) until November 15, 2028, with a budget of nearly €300 million ($334 million).

“The Council also decided to establish a presence in Ukraine to ensure direct and effective coordination with the Ukrainian military authorities,” according to a press release from Brussels.

The move marks a change for EUMAM, which had previously only trained Ukrainian soldiers exclusively on EU territory.

According to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, European leaders are increasingly demanding an unconditional ceasefire in Ukraine to pave the way for military intervention.

Read more

“Europe’s plan is quite simple, and they make no secret of it: as soon as a ceasefire is reached, they intend to move ‘stabilization forces’ into the territory controlled by the Kiev regime,” he said at a press conference on Tuesday, addressing the EU demands aimed at the talks in Adu Dhabi.

Brussels is seeking an immediate freeze in the conflict “to buy time” for Kiev to recover from its military losses, Lavrov said, adding that Moscow would “not agree to this.”

European nations “sending troops into Ukraine” would mean “war with Russia,” Russian President Vladimir Putin warned in September.

Russia has warned repeatedly that any foreign troops or military advisers in Ukraine would be considered legitimate targets. Moscow has roundly opposed British and French plans to deploy troops in Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire. Any NATO military presence in Ukraine is unacceptable to Russia as well, given that it considers the conflict a proxy war being waged by the US-led bloc.

Read more

Numerous serving and former military personnel from NATO member states have died during the Ukraine conflict. Serving British Army Major Paul Wilks was killed in Ukraine in September, London said earlier this year, stating that the intelligence officer died in a road accident.

Other deaths of senior military personnel from NATO countries have officially been attributed to non-combat causes, despite media reports describing them as caused by Russian strikes. One example was Polish Brigadier General Adam Marczak, who was reportedly killed by a Russian supersonic missile strike on a command bunker in Chasov Yar in Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic in 2024, which Russian troops liberated the following year. Warsaw insisted that he died of natural causes.

title: California rejects billionaire tax
content:
The proposed one-time 5% wealth tax on the state’s 240 billionaires was intended to fund healthcare, education, and food assistance

California voters have rejected a proposal to introduce the first wealth tax of its kind in the US, targeting billionaires’ fortunes, according to Decision Desk HQ projections released on Monday.

The measure, known as Proposition 40, proposed a one-time tax of 5% on most assets held by California residents with a net worth exceeding $1 billion. At least 90% of the proceeds would have gone toward state-funded healthcare programs, including expanded Medi-Cal coverage for low-income residents, people with disabilities, and the elderly.

The measure was proposed by the SEIU United Healthcare Workers West union, which hoped to raise around $100 billion over five years to offset cuts in federal funding for healthcare programs. Union President Dave Regan said the group will put the tax back on the ballot in 2028 if the Californian authorities fail to find another way to make up for the finance shortfall.

The proposition was put to a statewide vote on November 3, alongside federal and local elections. According to Decision Desk HQ, nearly 53% of voters opposed the measure, with 84% of ballots counted.

Read more

Opponents of the tax reportedly raised roughly ten times more money for their campaign than its supporters. Google co-founder Sergey Brin is said to have donated more than $100 million to a political action committee working to defeat the measure.

In October, those seeking to defeat the proposal launched an extensive television advertising campaign, while supporters, constrained by limited funding, relied primarily on social media and influencers, the New York Times reported earlier this week. The proposal was also opposed by teachers’ and firefighters’ unions, as well as the California chapter of Planned Parenthood.

According to a UC Berkeley-POLITICO poll, critics feared that the one-time levy could eventually become a recurring measure. They also warned that wealthy residents might leave California for states with more favorable tax policies, eroding the state’s tax base.

At least six billionaires announced plans to leave California before January 1, 2026, Fortune reported in March. Larry Page and Peter Thiel moved to Florida, Sergey Brin and Don Hankey to Nevada, Steven Spielberg to New York, and Travis Kalanick to Texas. At a 5% rate, the tax on their combined wealth could reportedly have amounted to around $27 billion.

title: Macrons hit Candace Owens with new transgender suit
content:
The French first couple have accused the US conservative podcaster of spreading “lies” about the first lady’s gender

French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte have filed a new lawsuit against Candace Owens, accusing the American podcaster of profiting off of “outlandish” and “far-fetched fictions” that Brigitte is actually a man.

The 409-page defamation lawsuit was filed in Owens’ home state of Tennessee last week, and picked up by the American media on Monday. In it, the presidential couple accuse Owens of using her podcast “to expand her lies about the Macrons, sell merchandise making fun of the Macrons, and collect donations based on her ‘reporting’ on the Macrons,” including “outlandish, defamatory, and far-fetched fictions” surrounding Brigitte Macron’s “gender identity, gender, and sexuality.” 

The suit expands on a case filed by the Macrons against Owens’ company in the state of Delaware last July.

Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron’s relationship has been the subject of gossip and scrutiny for years, largely owing to the fact that Brigitte is 24 years Emmanuel’s senior, and the pair met while Emmanuel was 15 years old and a student of his future wife. 

Read more

However, a new set of rumors took hold in 2021, after self-proclaimed ‘spiritual medium’ Amandine Roy interviewed independent journalist Natacha Rey, who claimed that Mrs. Macron was born a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux. The Macrons sued Roy and Rey, who were ordered to pay the first lady €8,000 in 2024.

Owens took up the cause that year, declaring in March 2024: “I would stake my entire professional reputation on the fact that Brigitte Macron is in fact a man.” Owens expanded on these claims in an eight-part investigative series – ‘Becoming Brigitte’ – in 2025. She presented family photographs, alleging that pictures of Brigitte’s brother, Jean-Michel, actually showed Brigitte before a sex-change operation.

“These lies have caused tremendous damage to the Macrons. Defendant has subjected the Macrons to a campaign of global humiliation,” the lawsuit states.

Among the humiliations cited in the lawsuit was Owens’ use of a crude “Brigitte doll” to poke fun at Mrs. Macron during her show. Owens claimed in one episode that the doll, consisting of a blonde wig on an ‘ET’ plushie, had suffered “an LGBTQ hate crime, because, you know, Jean-Michel Trogneaux is gay.”

I’m afraid to say this is accurate. The Macrons have indeed filed a NEW set of claims against me. 88 in total, and this time, they want justice over my Brigitte-Doll. Those of you who are fans of the show know that Brigitte-Doll has never pursued the limelight. For her to be called “grotesque” by the French couple is hurtful, to say to the least. The bleach incident referenced in the filing was a traumatizing incident, which occurred during a polar vortex in Tennessee. Brigitte-Doll will be making no further statements at this time.

— Candace Owens (@RealCandaceO) November 9, 2026

In a post on X on Monday, Owens ridiculed the lawsuit, announcing that “Brigitte-Doll will be making no further statements at this time.”
