Major Saudi oil pipeline hit in new attack
content:
The East-West Pipeline carries millions of barrels of crude daily and is an alternative to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz

A major pipeline carrying millions of barrels of oil from the Gulf region has come under renewed attack, the Saudi Energy Ministry has said, as cited by the Saudi Press Agency. Occurring during intense fighting with Yemen’s Houthi rebels, it puts a vital route for the kingdom’s crude exports at risk.

The East-West route was targeted in the Medina region on Monday, Riyadh said, causing a small fire. No casualties were reported, and operations were unaffected, according to the authorities. On Tuesday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree denied responsibility, calling allegations of the group’s involvement a “blatant lie” and saying its forces had instead targeted pumping stations along the same pipeline near Riyadh.

The 1,200 km pipeline runs across the Arabian Peninsula from Saudi Arabia’s oil-producing east to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The kingdom is the world’s largest crude oil exporter and has relied heavily on the route since the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, severely restricting exports from neighboring Gulf states. Riyadh has rerouted around four million barrels per day through the pipeline, or roughly 4% of global oil supply.

Saudi ARAMCO East/West Pipeline Pressure Breaking Station 12 (PBS-12), Al Torkiyah, Al-Madinah Province, Saudi Arabia. Copernicus & SOAR Sentinel-2 imagery on 09/11. Timelapse from 04/11 to 09/11. Google Earth recent imagery to compare. C: 23°54'17.02"N 39°12'38.71"E https://t.co/hokclpwI5s

— Hexagone Intel (@osinthexagone) November 10, 2026

The route was closed for several days in September following drone strikes blamed by Riyadh on Iraqi militias. The Houthis claimed a strike on a pumping station in October. 

Addressing the latest escalation, Saree said the group had carried out four operations involving ballistic missiles and drones. He described them as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen, including attacks on a market in Taiz and a village near Sanaa.

Read more

On Sunday, the Houthi’s claimed an attack on Saudi Aramco’s offices in Riyadh. Debris from intercepted missiles damaged the building in the King Abdullah Financial District. 

On Saturday, airstrikes blamed on the Saudi-led coalition reportedly killed 33 people, including 13 children and eight women, east of Sanaa, according to the Houthi-run Health Ministry. A market attack in Taiz province on Friday killed at least 30, with the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces blaming each other.

The Saudi-led coalition operating in Yemen said on Tuesday that its air defenses intercepted two Houthi missiles fired towards Riyadh, another towards the south, and a drone over the oil-rich Eastern Province.

Read more

The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi airstrikes hit a gas station and an oil facility in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. At least one person was killed and nine injured, according to the Houthi Health Ministry.

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis resumed in July after a truce dating back to 2022 collapsed. Tensions reignited when Saudi-backed government forces struck Sanaa Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The rebels subsequently declared an end to de-escalation and announced a naval blockade of the kingdom.

The Houthis have since repeatedly attacked Saudi airports and energy facilities. In October, the Saudi-led coalition said 20 strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over ten days killed at least 17 people and injured more than 300.

The group has also advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast towards Bab el-Mandeb, a major shipping route linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, adding to pressure on regional maritime trade.

title: British ‘national treasure’ accused of multiple grooming and sex abuse cases
content:
David Walliams had argued that revealing allegations against him could drive him to suicide

British comedian and bestselling children’s author David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct involving young women and teenage girls, according to British media.

He was identified on Tuesday as the celebrity who unsuccessfully sought to prevent the publication of sexual misconduct allegations, arguing that the revelations could drive him to suicide. His identity had been protected by a court order while he pursued legal action against two major news organizations.

Walliams, 55, best known for the comedy series Little Britain, his role as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent, and a string of bestselling children’s books, has been accused of using his celebrity status to pursue young women and teenage girls for sex. The allegations, uncovered in a three-year joint investigation by the Guardian and Independent Television News (ITN), include accounts from two women who claim he groomed them after first meeting them when they were 15.

In a personal letter to journalists investigating the allegations, published on Tuesday, Walliams denied wrongdoing while acknowledging that he had sometimes behaved thoughtlessly in past sexual relationships. “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law,” he wrote, adding that he regretted hurting women’s feelings but had never abused his celebrity status.

Read more

Walliams had sought a permanent injunction against The Guardian and ITN to prevent publication of the allegations. His lawyers argued that the revelations could have fatal consequences, telling the High Court in London that he had already attempted suicide twice after being confronted with the claims in May.

The court also heard that Walliams had been detained under the Mental Health Act and was receiving inpatient psychiatric treatment. His lawyers said he had no intention of returning to public life.

Justice Matthew Nicklin rejected the injunction on November 3, acknowledging the serious risk to Walliams’ mental health but ruling that preventing publication would constitute an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. The judge noted that psychiatric services were already taking measures to protect him and stressed that the court had not determined whether the allegations were true.

Read more

Walliams’ anonymity remained in place pending a possible appeal. His lawyers confirmed on Monday that he would not challenge the ruling, allowing the media to identify him.

The scandal has dealt another blow to one of Britain’s most recognizable entertainment figures, whose children’s books have sold more than 60 million copies worldwide.

His publisher, HarperCollins, dropped him in December 2025 following a separate investigation into allegations of inappropriate behavior toward young female employees, which he also denied. Earlier this month, Alton Towers, a major British theme park in Staffordshire, permanently closed its World of David Walliams attraction, which featured rides inspired by his books.

title: France’s ‘Cold War’: Paris blames Tehran for supermarket fridge hacks
content:
France now believes that Iran was behind a series of supermarket cyberattacks that were pinned on Russia less than a week ago

The French government has accused Iran of hacking refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets, claiming that the “cyber campaign” was the work of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The attack, which took place in October, affected fridges and freezers at nearly 700 distribution sites across France. Hackers reportedly targeted the fridges’ internet-connected control units and forced them to overheat, destroying tons of food and forcing several stores to temporarily close. A wave of similar attacks took place in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, and at least six other EU countries three weeks later.

“This was a cyber campaign of unprecedented scale and aggression,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Monday. “Today, thanks to the work of government agencies, we know who is responsible: the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Read more

Iran’s ambassador has been summoned, Barrot said, adding that France will “sanction those responsible and take all measures we deem necessary and proportionate to respond.”

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said that investigators discovered the hackers used Farsi and IP addresses linked to Iran, and that three IRGC members are suspected of carrying out the operation “to serve the interests of a foreign power – in this case, Iran.” 

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi rejected the allegations, accusing Paris of shifting blame for its own failures. “Unable to manage fridges let alone addressing grievances of its people, French government is shifting blame for its failures onto others,” he wrote on X on Tuesday.

“Yes, Iran is powerful. But unlike France, we do not exercise power via support for massacres in Gaza or bombings of schools and hospitals,” Araghchi added.

Although Beccuau’s accusation is stronger than that of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who stated “we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran” was behind a bungled “terror plot” at an RAF airbase in September, it is still not entirely watertight. WikiLeaks’ 2017 ‘Vault 7’ disclosures confirmed that the CIA had developed sophisticated hacking tools capable of leaving behind false digital ‘fingerprints’ in foreign languages, including Russian, Chinese, and Farsi, to implicate other countries in cyberattacks.

The accusations mark a dramatic turnaround from the climate of mid-October. Then, despite it taking place at a time of daily riots and anti-government demonstrations, almost every commentator speaking to European media outlets accused Russia of committing the attack. “We strongly believe this activity could be attributed to a Russian state-sponsored threat actor,” cybersecurity executive Xavier Bellekens told Politico last week, in an article that portrayed the hack as something straight from the pages of “the Kremlin’s hybrid playbook.”

Read more

“When we pull on the thread it does look like it could well be Russia. So, that is basically where we’re at,” Bellekens told Euronews – which, like Politico, is funded by the EU – two days later. Russia is “looking into where the weaknesses in the systems lie,” former Dutch intelligence officer Tim Bosch told NU.nl. “Right now it concerns refrigeration, but next time it might be a hospital.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the claims as “baseless,” “absurd,” and “backed up by no reasoning.”

Neither Iran’s Foreign Ministry nor the IRGC has commented on Tuesday’s accusation. However, Iran’s state Mehr News agency has dismissed it as “baseless and unsupported by evidence.”

German World Cup winner placed on Ukrainian ‘kill list’
content:
Former Germany football star Mesut Ozil had criticized FIFA and UEFA for banning Russian teams while allowing Israelis to compete

Former German football star and 2014 World Cup winner Mesut Ozil has been added to a Ukrainian “kill list” after accusing FIFA and UEFA of double standards over their treatment of Russia and Israel, media have reported.

The notorious Mirotvorets website, which maintains the list, publishes personal information on people it considers “enemies” of Ukraine. The database, which claims to be a private research project but enjoys tacit backing from Kiev, has published data on over 180,000 people and marks the profiles of deceased individuals with a “liquidated” stamp.

Ozil came under fire after publicly criticizing FIFA and UEFA for suspending Russian teams from international competitions while allowing Israeli teams to continue participating. The website has accused him of supporting Russia’s military operation in Ukraine.

Read more

Ozil made the remarks during a veterans’ football match in Istanbul between his former Turkish club Istanbul Basaksehir and Russia’s Zenit St. Petersburg.

“Football has always brought people together,” Ozil said, arguing that sporting organizations should not discriminate on the basis of nationality or religion.

“As you know, FIFA has not imposed any sanctions on Israeli teams, but it has done so against Russian teams,” he said, urging football authorities to abandon double standards and treat all countries equally.

Russian national teams and clubs have been barred from FIFA and UEFA competitions since February 2022, following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Israeli teams, meanwhile, have continued to participate in international tournaments despite growing calls for their suspension over Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

Ozil, 38, retired from professional football in 2023 after a career that included spells at Real Madrid, Arsenal, Fenerbahce and several German clubs. He made 92 appearances for Germany, scoring 23 goals, and helped the national team win the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

Launched in August 2014 following the Western-backed change of government in Kiev, Mirotvorets claims to identify individuals it considers threats to Ukraine’s national security. Its database includes Western journalists who reported from Donbass and Crimea and Ukrainian writer Oles Buzina, who was murdered in 2015 after his personal details appeared on the website. His killing remains unsolved.

Read more

The list has also included prominent foreign politicians and athletes. In August, former Soviet and Russian footballer Akhrik Tsveiba, who won the 1990 Soviet championship with Dynamo Kiev, was added to the database.

More recently, Polish MEP Ewa Zajaczkowska-Hernik and Poland’s presidential chief of staff were reportedly added after criticizing Kiev’s commemoration of Ukrainian nationalist figures who collaborated with Nazi Germany.

The website has repeatedly faced international criticism for publishing personal information without consent. In 2016, the OSCE warned that the disclosure of journalists’ details could endanger their safety, while human rights organizations raised concerns about threats against those named on the platform.

title: Orban accuses Hungarian authorities of ‘witch hunt’ after brother’s arrest
content:
The government of Peter Magyar is trying to establish a one-party system, the former prime minister has said

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban has claimed the detention of his younger brother is part of a campaign by the government of Peter Magyar to eliminate political opposition in the country.

Aron Orban and three other people were arrested on Monday in a human trafficking case. The 49-year-old businessman, who owns the firearms company Multi Shot, was photographed arriving at a detention center in Budapest on the same day.

In September, reports emerged that the former prime minister’s sibling was part of a separate investigation into alleged falsification of paperwork to help Vietnamese workers enter Hungary.

In a post on X later on Monday, Viktor Orban, who left office after 16 years in power this May, accused Magyar’s government of going on a “witch hunt.”

“I am the real target. My younger brother is simply being used to get to me,” he insisted.

Read more

According to the former prime minister, the aim of the “dirty political game” played by the authorities is “to eliminate opponents and establish a one-party state.”

Orban also suggested that his brother’s detention was an attempt “to divert attention” from the scandal that erupted after Magyar’s government released the records from Hungary’s communist-era secret police last week.

Critics warned that the move could lead to public shaming, reputational damage, and painful family revelations. The historians stressed that the files, containing 50,000 to 60,000 names, were incomplete and unreliable, adding that being mentioned in them doesn’t necessarily serve as proof of collaboration with the agency.

After the pro-EU Tisza party’s election win, Magyar promised accountability for Orban-era politicians over alleged corruption and abuse of power.

Orban’s Fidesz party hosts “a list of political prisoners” on its website, which includes the names of its members who have been arrested since the change of leadership. On Tuesday, Aron Orban’s name became the sixth to be added to the list.

READ MORE: US wants Orban to be next UN chief – WSJ

Magyar’s cabinet has been actively dismantling the legal, media, and financial structures set up by the previous government. It also changed the constitution to impose a 12-year term limit on MPs, effectively banning Orban from running for office again. Fidesz has repeatedly labeled the conduct by its Tisza rivals as “authoritarian.”

High-stakes Ukraine talks resume as Europe pushes to be included
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of Seven developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia.

As three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States got underway in the United Arab Emirates, top G7 diplomats were meeting Tuesday with Ukraines foreign minister in France.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha started his day in Paris in talks with Rubio before heading to the French foreign ministry for a larger group meeting with the entire G7. Neither man spoke as they posed for photos ahead of their discussion.

The State Department said afterwards in a brief statement that the pair had discussed negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war, energy resilience, and defense cooperation.

The larger meeting was expected to cover defense and security assistance to Ukraine, which the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has reduced, causing consternation not only in Kyiv but in capitals across Europe, the largest of which Paris, Berlin, Rome and London are G7 members.

RELATED STORY | Trilateral talks between US, Ukraine and Russia to resume this week

It was not immediately clear if the U.S. or any of its G7 partners would announce any new assistance for Ukraine.

Meanwhile in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, Trumps envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner began talks with Russian and Ukrainian officials in part to persuade Moscow to agree to broader negotiations that would include key European officials on how to end nearly five years of war.

In Paris, Europeans have been clamoring for a seat at the table in Abu Dhabi, but two U.S. officials said Monday that representatives from Britain, Germany, France, NATO and the European Union would not join the main talks but rather discuss potential security guarantees and the long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe beforehand.

Russia has resisted European participation in negotiations and insisted the talks should proceed strictly as a trilateral format involving Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. The three last held talks in February.

But on Monday in Paris, German Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul, who met separately with Rubio on the sidelines of the G7, was emphatic that Europe must be included.

RELATED STORY | Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US

I am still very grateful to the United States of America for making every effort to get the parties to the conflict to the table, he said. But I made clear again here that Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe, only with Europe.

Rubio said the U.S. has no objection to eventual European involvement in the direct talks, but that it wasnt yet time.

Ultimately, it would be a positive, but weve got a ways to go, he told reporters after a full day of group and bilateral meetings with G7 counterparts. But, no, its good that theyre talking, its good that the trilateral talks are on again. Its better than not having talks.

On the eve of the talks, Russia battered Ukraines power grid again on Monday and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russias biggest oil refineries.

The two countries remain locked in battle with no sign that either side is ready to budge from their demands. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

title: AFP builds a new funding model for investigative journalism
content:
By Maria Lisicka

With 1,700 journalists in 151 countries, Agence France-Presse documents events around the clock. But Karl Malakunas, its Head of Philanthropic Partnerships, described a different kind of experiment they have under way: “a completely new editorial and funding model for AFP” for in-depth and investigative journalism.

Malakunas, an Emmy-nominated and Walkley Award-winning journalist, joined AFP in Hong Kong 25 years ago. “Breaking news is in my veins,” he said. Yet, like a lot of journalists, he always wanted “to scratch that itch” of going deeper.

He did so in the Philippines, turning a 700-word article on environmental defenders in Palawan into a 90-minute feature documentary. The film took 10 years and was largely funded by foundations.

In March 2025, AFP’s global news director asked him to bring that approach inside the agency.

AFP gets about a third of its funding from the French state and two-thirds from its 4,000-plus clients. Philanthropy adds a third stream, focused on the “Future of the planet” and the “Future of societies.” Above all, editorial independence must remain “sacrosanct,” Malakunas said.

A global desk for environmental justice

The first project is AFP’s Environment and Climate Legal Desk, billed as the world’s first global newsroom unit dedicated to environmental and climate justice. Its specialist reporters will support AFP’s bureaus on cases too complex for busy news teams, such as SLAPP suits (lawsuits designed to silence critics) in the Philippines.

Raising the money proved to be the more difficult part.

“It’s definitely harder, the fundraising element than the editorial element,” Malakunas said. “We’re not going to sugarcoat that.” AFP bypassed traditional journalism funders to approach environmental foundations, “a long, slow process.”

The desk now has a founding editor to build and lead it, and is hiring reporters in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Impact you can document

Working with The Gecko Project, which brought the story idea, AFP put its boots on the ground to reveal that an Indonesian mill supplying Asia Symbol, a Chinese maker of “so-called carbon-neutral packaging,” had processed wood from plantations where orangutan habitat had been cleared. Haleon, the British maker of Panadol, then dropped Asia Symbol as a packaging supplier for its China operations.

AFP now documents such outcomes.

Asked how impact is measured for funders, Malakunas said AFP is building its first impact tracker. Beyond distribution reach, it asks: “Is it cited by civil society? Is it cited by lawmakers? And did it lead to anything?” The results go back to funders. As AFP reaches audiences through its media clients, journalists will log impact themselves.

“It’s boots-on-the-ground journalism. That’s the differentiator … And it’s expensive and it’s hard to do.”
– Karl Malakunas, Head of Philanthropic Partnerships, AFP

Protecting independence

AFP published a code of ethics on day one. Once the desk is running, there is a firewall: “Foundations can speak to me,” Malakunas explained, but they “don’t have direct access to our journalists.” AFP is also not “foundation-led”: “We did spend a lot of time determining what we wanted to do, what our value was […] and not chasing what foundations wanted.”

Funding, he said on the panel, is “fickle” and the sector “opaque”, especially after last year’s USAID cuts sent many organisations to philanthropies. AFP’s answer: no more than 25 or 30% from any one funder.

Lessons for Asian newsrooms

In Southeast Asia, investigative journalists face harassment, rising costs, SLAPP suits and barriers to US and European foundations.

“It’s extremely difficult, but it is possible,” Malakunas noted. “There is big money in the US and Europe. It’s extremely hard to access, but it’s there.”

Established outlets have an edge, he argued: “Foundations do take confidence in the fact that you’re an established media organisation; you’re already doing good journalism.”

His advice for the next 12 months: commitment and training. “You’re going to have in your newsrooms people who are raring to go,” he said. “Even without the extra funding, if you are committed to this, allocate some space for one or two or whoever those people are.”

 About the author: Maria Lisicka is a young professional in PR and strategic communication, currently pursuing her studies at the University of Amsterdam and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.

title: Without Action, Climate Change Could Push Women Further Behind by 2050, CGIAR Warns
content:
A CGIAR report warns that climate change will further reduce the availability of water and increase the amount of time women spend collecting water by 30%. Credit: Busani Bafana/IPS

By Busani Bafana
BULAWAYO, Zimbabwe &, Nov 10 2026 (IPS)

Fetching water was once a back-breaking daily reality – one that Nomuhle SibandaMpofu will never forget.

Mpofu, from Inyathi village in Bubi District in Matabeleland North Province, is a horticulture farmer and livestock farmer. Water is everything to her livelihood. She has had to overcome the challenge of travelling many kilometres to fetch water for her family and for irrigating her crop and livestock farming enterprise.

For millions of women in the rural areas, increasing droughts, worsened by climate change, are not just an environmental crisis but mean a labourious and time-consuming daily water collection marathon.

Water scarcity could increase women’s water-collection time by 30%, while the shift of rural women into off-farm jobs could either create more resilient livelihoods or entrench inequality, finds a CGIAR GENDER Accelerator report, Advancing equality, transforming futures.

The CGIAR gender report warns that without deliberate policy action, climate change and economic disruption could leave women further behind in food, land and water systems by 2050. The report was released ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) underway in Antalya, Türkiye, until 20 November 2026.

Farmers like Mpofu have insulated themselves against the risks of water insecurity by drilling boreholes and adopting water-saving methods.

“Before I drilled a borehole I used to fetch water from a community borehole and from a seasonal dam nearby,” Mpofu tells IPS. “I used a wheelbarrow to collect water from the dam, which dried up mid-year, and the community borehole more than a kilometre away was the closest source of water.”

Mpofu grows spinach, tomatoes, kale, onions, and occasionally potatoes on her two-hectare fenced plot.

“I used to wheel three 20-litre containers of water from the borehole before I bought a scotchart and donkey and was able to carry 24 containers of water for my vegetable garden. I would skip two days before I made another water run because of the labour of the task,” Mpofu recalled.

Long Walk to Water Freedom

Then three years ago she saved enough money and drilled a borehole in her homestead and  erected a 5000 litre water tank, enabling her to  easily water her garden and her goats, sheep, pigs and cattle.

“Before I had a borehole it was difficult collecting water, a tough task which I had to balance with other chores in the homestead, but now that difficulty is past, I now turn on the tap, and water flows.”

Drilling a borehole within her homestead helped Mpofu end at least five hours a day she spent collecting water, a chore that challenges millions of women in rural areas in Africa.

In April this year, ICRISAT helped and installed the Chameleon water-saving tool in Mpofu’s field. The Chameleon Tool  is an  easy-to-use tool that helps farmers apply the right amount of water to their crops. It consists of  three sensors permanently installed at different depths in the soil. A hand-held reader shows blue light for wet soil, green light for moist soil or red light for dry soil.

“Before I used to water my crops almost every two days, but now I water after four days when it is hot and after five days when it’s cloudy, saving a lot of water that way,” said Mpofu.

The International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) has helped  smallholder farmers in Southern Africa manage irrigation water more efficiently using the Chameleon soil moisture sensor.

With the El Niño phenomenon – a natural climate pattern characterised by the unusual warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean – now underway, there are growing fears of widespread drought in Southern Africa. The 2026–2027 El Niño is projected to cause water shortages and severely disrupt  agriculture production across Southern Africa.

The CGIAR GENDER Accelerator report notes that the global food crisis — fuel, fertiliser, climate extremes, trade disruptions — has disproportionately impacted women over the past year. At the same time, women are central to building resilient food systems needed to guard against emerging threats.

Els Lecoutere, senior officer at the CGIAR Gender Impact Platform and one of the report’s authors, highlights that the report was motivated by the need to predict and prepare for an uncertain future, as negative impacts of climate change are seen in increasing droughts and water scarcity, which affected women differently.

“We do know that climate change is widening gender gaps, so what should we do now so that we avoid a future that could be more unequal in food systems rather than more unequal if all these crises happen?” Lecoutere said. “We sought to look into the future and learn from what we know now, as we have a lot of evidence of what works to increase gender equality.”

Projections based on the current trends show that by 2050 in a business-as-usual scenario, the Middle East and North Africa region will still have a female unemployment gap and a female earnings gap, and in South Asia the female earnings gap will improve, but a big female earnings gap will remain. While in Sub-Saharan Africa employment will go up in the most optimistic scenario, the female earnings gap remain stagnant.

“Water will be scarcer in some regions, and we already know that the task of collecting water falls on the shoulders of women and girls, and they spend so much time on that task, meaning the education of girls is affected, and women, for instance, cannot open their shops or attend to other activities,” Lecoutere said.

“Given the norm that women and girls are in charge, given the lack of infrastructure, the implications for women and girls are clear: that without a change of customs, the choices and options they have are reduced.”

Closing the Gender Gap

Opportunities to reduce gender inequality include institutional, legal and social reform, inclusive infrastructure, social protection, improved data-gathering and the responsible use of emerging technology, the CGIAR GENDER Accelerator report recommends.

Ismahane Elouafi, Executive Managing Director of CGIAR, notes that we cannot feed our future without including women in our food systems.

“The choices we make over the coming years will determine whether food, land, and water systems become more equitable or more unequal, more resilient or more fragile,” said Elouafi.

The Rome Declaration on Water Scarcity in Agriculture, adopted during the High-level Rome Water Dialogue in Italy in 2024, acknowledged that drought responses are contributing to crop failures in parts of the world and an acute food insecurity crisis in vulnerable countries. The Declaration noted changing rainfall patterns are resulting in increased droughts.

“I am aware that with any drought women are in a difficult situation where they have to collect water over a long distance. I encourage women to invest in boreholes; they are one solution to surviving the drought by bringing water closer to home and relieving them from the task of collecting water from afar,” Mpofu says.

The report also finds that digital technologies hold significant potential to bridge gender inequities across food systems, despite the current digital divide between men and women. It cites research showing that in Kenya, for example, women are up to 25% less likely than men to access digital climate advisory services due to structural gender barriers. The report calls on technology developers to involve women in the development of breakthrough technologies like AI before scaling their use.

“Investing in women, not as labourers, but as leaders, is the path towards unlocking the full potential of our food, land and water systems,” said Nicoline de Haan, Director of the CGIAR GENDER Accelerator.

IPS UN Bureau Report

title: Trump backs ‘honeypot-hit’ Nvidia boss
content:
Jensen Huang is “an amazing guy,” who is “suffering greatly” due to the scandal, the US president said

US President Donald Trump has said that the FBI has launched a probe into Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman accused of working for Chinese intelligence, but stressed that he believes in the Nvidia chief’s innocence. Beijing has vigorously denied the spying claims.

On Monday, Nvidia, a US company which dominates the market for chips used to power AI, said that it started its own investigation into allegations that its founder and CEO was targeted in a Chinese intelligence ‘honeypot’ operation. Earlier in the day, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife, but didn’t name the woman he had been dating.

The New York Times and Financial Times reported previously that the 63-year-old tech entrepreneur had developed a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive formerly associated with the Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed International, who had allegedly been gathering data on Nvidia for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Read more

When asked about the scandal around Jensen Huang during a media briefing at the White House later on Monday, Trump said that “we’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else. I think he will be in good shape.”

“I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem,” he added.

The US president said that he had already discussed the situation with the Nvidia CEO, whom he described as “an amazing guy” and “a high-quality person.”

“He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” he stressed.

Trump noted that he believes that Huang is “suffering greatly” due to the whole ordeal after reading the tech entrepreneur’s statement, in which he said that he was “deeply sorry” for hurting his wife and children.

Huang is seen as one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley as the president insists on the US winning the AI race against China. The Nvidia CEO accompanied Trump on a state visit to Beijing in May and was awarded the National Medal of Science last month.

Read more

Trump contradicted claims by NYT that he had been briefed on Huang’s affair and the security risks posed by it before the Chinese trip, but decided not to take any action on the information.

“Well, I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago,” he said.

The US president was also asked if he’ll raise the issue with Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping at an APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next week. “No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it,” he replied.

On Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun denied claims of Beijing collecting intelligence on Nvidia. “The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” he insisted.

Nvidia lost nearly $200 billion of market value after Huang acknowledged the affair and the company launched a probe against him.

title: Taiwan’s CommonWealth Magazine doubles down on data-driven investigative journalism
content:
By Maria Lisicka

Despite the challenges and costs of investigative journalism, pursuing it is paramount for news publishers: “The externality is much bigger than its cost,” Chen told participants at WAN-IFRA’s Asian Media Leaders Summit recently in Singapore.

Chen cited Reuters Institute research ranking original investigations and on-the-ground reporting as top priorities for news executives in the AI era.

“The reality is very simple,” Chen noted. “AI and video have already completely changed how people consume news.”

Breakthrough investigative reports, she argued, “send a powerful wake-up call to both society and our subscribers. They remind people the media are here and that we create value that AI can never replace.”

No investigative unit, but an investigative culture

Chen’s first takeaway was counterintuitive: CommonWealth’s most popular investigations did not come from a dedicated investigative unit.

“Every single beat has the potential for deep investigative work,” she pointed out. The key is “an open editorial culture where all journalists can pitch early leads [and] hold honest discussions.”

Once committed, the newsroom backs the work with proper, not excessive, resources, ensuring that “when we bet our resources, we deliver something significant.”

Reading China through unconventional data

As examples, Chen showed two projects built on “unconventional data from China.”

First, CommonWealth worked with scholars from Taiwan’s Academia Sinica, using AI to analyse more than 10 years of CCTV footage of Xi Jinping’s face, speech and gait. The finding: Xi looked noticeably thinner at the 2025 military parade, but his health was “actually quite stable for his age.”

The second project was personal. “I come from the most dangerous place on earth,” Chen noted. “It’s related to our life.” It began in 2020, when a CommonWealth reporter on holiday in Tainan kept hearing fighter jets scrambling overhead and asked herself: are we going to have a war?

The available data was terrible, Chen said: two static PDF images a day from Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense. A team of just three logged every flight path and aircraft type by hand, for a full year.

What emerged was striking. The sorties were not aimed at Taiwan at all.

Coordinated with the Chinese navy, they pushed southwest towards the South China Sea, a sign, Chen explained, that Beijing’s real goal was to break through the “first island chain” from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines.

“It’s not only a Taiwan story,” she concluded. “It’s actually an Asia story.”

From three reporters to a live dashboard

In 2023, AI took over the mapping and data entry. By 2025, the project had become a fully automatic dashboard tracking Chinese military activity every day, later expanded with Japanese and Philippine data.

Then Beijing’s playbook shifted to “grey zone” warfare.

The team began tracing China Coast Guard ships day by day, using AI to scale up to more than 1.8 billion lines of ship-tracking data. Cross-matched with data from US think tank CSIS, Japan and the Philippines, the conclusion was stark: these operations target not only Taiwan, but Japan and the Philippines too.

Long-term projects, Chen observed, “give us historical depth” and keep the newsroom from “very sensational panic reporting.”

“With AI, we can process data at a scale we never could before. But the true secret sauce, I will not say it’s AI. I will say it’s still the editorial vision and the research methodology.”

– Yi-Shan Chen, Editor-in-Chief, CommonWealth Magazine

Asking the right questions and staying curious

During a panel discussion, Chen said that the hardest part is not the tools but “asking the right questions and keeping curiosity to discover the right topics.”

She also urged newsrooms to look beyond their walls, as data companies, white-hat hackers and NGOs are often willing to help. “We just need to spend some time to look around,” she added.

Her advice for smaller newsrooms: since covering every topic is rarely possible, choose one or two fields worth investing in and find the right people for them.

About the author: Maria Lisicka is a young professional in PR and strategic communication, currently pursuing her studies at the University of Amsterdam and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.

title: U.S. House derails attempt to impeach Hegseth
Regime Change Blowback
content:
By Jomo Kwame Sundaram
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia, Nov 10 2026 (IPS)

Trump and Netanyahu went all out for regime change in Tehran. This month, their electorates gave them regime changes, albeit not quite what they wanted. The wars continue, but the politics have changed.

Trump’s military spending
In Trump’s second term, the US president and the outgoing Republican-controlled Congress have shown even less respect for the Constitution.

Jomo Kwame Sundaram

With his new chief of staff, Trump may not even seek approval for additional war spending from Congress, which alone has the authority to tax and spend under the US Constitution.

Trump wanted a $1.5 trillion military budget for fiscal 2027, starting in October, up from $860 billion in Biden’s last budget, an increase of over $600 billion, or nearly 2.0% of GDP!

Financing the massive increase in US military spending would require substantial tax increases. Without them, Trump would have to increase the budget deficit, risking even higher interest rates.

Greater military spending and higher interest rates have diverted economic and human resources from more socially useful purposes. Besides exhausting the economy, it is also economically and socially wasteful.

War raises interest rates
Before Trump and Netanyahu attacked Iran on 28 February, the interest rate on 10-year US Treasury bonds was around 4.0%. It subsequently rose to around 4.7% by late August.

Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for individuals and governments. Having to pay more, corporate borrowers will surely pass the costs on.

Higher expected inflation alone cannot explain the higher interest rates. Unexpectedly, after more than six months of war, expectations of future inflation were slightly lower than in February!

Higher interest rates probably reflect broader changes in expectations, as investors now expect much larger US budget deficits than early this year.

The US Federal Reserve now projects that the Fed funds rate, widely seen as reflecting investor attitudes, will be higher in 2027 and 2028 than before the war.

Likewise, long-term interest rates on other countries’ debt have risen, indicating Trump’s war has raised interest rates worldwide.

Raising interest rates ineffective
Raising interest rates does little to address inflation caused by deliberate supply-side disruptions. Trump appointed Kevin Warsh as Fed Chair to bring down interest rates, but the Chairman has not obliged so far.

Inflation has been above the Fed’s 2.0% target for over half a decade. With US unemployment rising in 2024, it lowered interest rates. After Trump’s re-election, inflation rose due to stockpiling in anticipation of his tariffs, and then the tariffs themselves.

Inflation would probably have declined again if not for the second attack on Iran, which pushed oil and other prices up. Relief from inflation now hinges on the very uncertain prospects of ending the war.

As higher inflation has been the pretext for the Fed to raise interest rates, it should lower rates if prices fell. Likewise, when the AI bubble bursts, interest rates would likely decline too.

Macroeconomist Dean Baker suggests that the Fed has kept interest rates up to appear to be doing something. With wage growth barely over 3.0% and falling, income has been shifting from wages to profits.

If wage-profit shares stabilise, even the usual productivity growth rate of 1.5% should keep inflation under 2.0%, as higher productivity more than offsets rising wage costs.

If the productivity boom that AI proponents are promising were to materialise, inflation would be well under target, even with wages rising at current rates. Clearly, wage inflation is not accelerating.

Meanwhile, Trump may raise tariffs again or start another war, raising prices further. But again, raising Fed interest rates cannot help.

Affordability
The popular consensus is that the Iran war was largely responsible for the Republican Party setback in last week’s US mid-term elections.

The war and its consequences are widely seen as primarily responsible for the current US affordability crisis. Trump has raised inflation, not only by waging war, but also by imposing tariffs on most trading partners and sanctions on some.

As higher inflation has been the pretext for the Fed to raise interest rates, it should lower rates if prices fall. And when the AI bubble bursts, interest rates should decline.

Fuel prices jumped by $1.50 per US gallon after the war started and remain over a dollar higher than before. Diesel prices rose by almost $3 per gallon at their peak and remain over $2.50 above their pre-war level.

Food prices are also expected to rise further in the new year due to fertiliser shortages, as much of the world’s supply has come from the Persian Gulf region.

Ironically, Trump’s war has accelerated the green energy transition worldwide, with electric vehicle and solar panel sales soaring, thereby reducing demand for oil and gas in the longer term.

Ending the April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs did not return prices to earlier levels. Similarly, ending the war will only partially reverse the economic disruption and damage caused.

IPS UN Bureau

Merz threatens EU budget veto over Ukraine aid – media
content:
The German chancellor is reportedly demanding that every member state contribute to Kiev’s financing before Berlin approves the bloc’s next seven-year budget

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to block the EU’s next seven-year budget unless all member states commit to providing more financial aid to Ukraine, several media outlets reported on Monday.

The EU has pledged to cover around €45 billion ($52 billion) of Ukraine’s projected €70 billion funding shortfall in 2027, as the conflict with Russia approaches its fifth year in February. However, Hungary, Slovakia, and the Czech Republic have signaled opposition to contributing to additional financial assistance for Kiev, while Bulgaria is expected to follow suit.

“Bilateral assistance to Ukraine is distributed unevenly and carried mostly by only a few member states,” Merz wrote in a letter to European Council President Antonio Costa, according to Bloomberg. The chancellor reportedly argued that supporting Ukraine was “a matter of our indivisible European security.”

“A collective commitment that all of us, without exception, will contribute fairly to closing this gap is an essential prerequisite for resolving this issue and for discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications,” Merz wrote, as cited by Euronews.

Read more

He also called for “a sound and multiannual financing perspective for Ukraine from 2028 onwards, including the interest liabilities that have already accrued.”

Hungary, Slovakia, and the Czech Republic had previously secured exemptions from financial obligations, including interest payments, on the EU’s €90 billion ‘loan’ to Ukraine agreed in December 2025.

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico warned last month that linking Ukraine’s financing to negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget would be dangerous. He has also argued that financing the war would prolong the fighting rather than bring peace.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis similarly argued that funds for Kiev “should not be part of the multiannual financial framework, where member states do not have enough money.”

Merz is also facing mounting political pressure at home amid widespread dissatisfaction with his government. According to an ARD-DeutschlandTrend poll published on November 5, only 12% of Germans were satisfied with his performance, while 85% were dissatisfied. 

The chancellor’s declining popularity has coincided with major electoral setbacks for his CDU. In September, the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) won state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the left-wing Die Linke came first in Berlin, defeating the CDU. Merz described his party’s performance in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania as a “disaster.”

title: Republican lawmaker moves to impeach Trump’s war secretary
content:
Thomas Massie has accused Pete Hegseth of attacking Iran illegally and carrying out extrajudicial killings

Outgoing US Representative Thomas Massie has reintroduced eight articles of impeachment against US President Donald Trump’s War Secretary Pete Hegseth after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

Massie, a self-described libertarian Republican from Kentucky, alleges that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and failed to minimize civilian casualties during US strikes. The conflict, triggered by a joint US-Israeli attack on Iran on February 28, has been “unlawful from its inception,” Massie said on Monday.

The congressman also argued that the 2025 strikes in Yemen and the January commando raid in Caracas, during which US forces abducted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, were illegal. He described US strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean, which have reportedly killed at least 243 people, as extrajudicial killings.

“My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what’s coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year,” Massie said.

Hegseth has condemned impeachment efforts against him as “sabotage.” “It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt,” he said during a press conference on Tuesday, calling criticism of him and the war on Iran “policy disagreements.”

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer echoed Massie’s call in a speech on the Senate floor. “America needs a serious Secretary of Defense right now – not a wannabe warlord. Hegseth must stand trial before the Senate,” he said.

Read more

Massie first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September, but the effort stalled after Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson canceled the chamber’s remaining votes ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. The House could vote on the renewed impeachment resolution as early as Wednesday.

Democrats subsequently dealt Republicans a major electoral blow, winning control of both the House and Senate. The results were widely interpreted as a rebuke to Trump’s policies, including the unpopular Iran war, which has driven up energy prices by disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and LNG trade.

On Truth Social, Trump dismissed Massie as a “total loser” and hailed Hegseth as “perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the country.” The secretary of war remained defiant, vowing over the weekend to “finish what we have started” despite the Republicans’ election losses.

On Monday, Trump said an escalation with Iran “seems to be quite unlikely” and expressed hope for a negotiated settlement. “We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected,” he wrote on Truth Social.

title: Trilateral talks between US, Ukraine and Russia to resume this week
content:
U.S. officials are cautiously optimistic as peace talks between Ukraine and Russia restart in Abu Dhabi Tuesday, noting each side is showing flexibility on territory.

The working level discussions with the U.S., Ukraine and Russia mark the first trilateral talks since February. The goal is to start defining how were going to end this war, according to a U.S. official.

The talks come as Russia has continued to carry out missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian energy targets, and Ukraine calls for more aid for air defense, while striking Russian military targets.

Kyiv's power now travels 200 miles, and Russia knows the weak point

President Trump said the administration is seeing a very strong inclination to end Russia and Ukraine.

The public positions remain the same, which is Russia said they want to they want all Donetsk, and Ukraine is saying let's do the contact line. But both sides have shown a little bit of have shown a little bit of flexibility privately, and so we're going to start the discussion about what that can be, said a U.S. official.

RELATED STORY | Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US

The session of talks will include territorial issues, according to a U.S. official, and another will include ceasefire monitoring and post war security.

This is the first time I feel like we see real desire on the Russian side to finish, said the official. They believe to solve the Donetsk issue post war security architecture must also be worked on.

We can only welcome the negotiators on U.S. President Donald Trumps request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on Ukrainian settlement on, said Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

While Europeans have pushed for a seat at the table for efforts to end the war, a U.S. official said they are proposing bringing Europe to the table after the trilateral meeting to run a parallel track of discussions on the security architecture, and will seek to get Russia to agree to a multilateral meeting.

We do believe very strongly that at this point, in order to end the war, you really need to have Europe at the table, the official said.

Ahead of the trilateral meetings, the U.S. is holding talks with Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, NATO, the EU and Ukraine to address security guarantees and long term security plans between Russia and Europe.

In terms of the U.S. role, again, you know, we'll see what President Trump decides. But we've asked the Russians for us to be able to give an Article Four and an Article Five-like security guarantee to Ukraine, along with NATO providing the same, said the U.S. official.

RELATED STORY | Crisis deepens in Ukraine as Russian official's White House visit draws scrutiny

However, past talks have failed to yield an end to the war. Zelenskyy has suggested freezing the contact line and called for a ceasefire, while Russia has publicly not changed its position.

So what Russia is showing is they're showing positive signs towards wanting to create an end, the official said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said they will propose de-escalatory steps and that there must be an understanding of how to arrange a trilateral meeting at the leaders level to bring this war to an end fairly and for real.

The Ukrainians have conceded a recent humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky shows that Russian President Vladimir Putin can stop the fighting when he wants.

Ukrainian officials believe the effort in Oleshky showed value in piloting de-escalation efforts.

Besides Oleshky, and besides besides its humanitarian human value, there is another big value: is that we started to kind of train or pilot de-escalation efforts in case the big, you know, ceasefire will come. How to execute the ceasefire, said Arakhamia.

Trump met with the Russian delegation, but not Ukrainians, after each side commemorated the effort at the White House with First Lady Melania Trump last week.

Unfortunately we do have a choice, said Davyd Arakhamia, a majority leader of the Ukrainian parliament, on copying Oleshky operations to other regions.

title: Russia, Ukraine to meet for U.S.-backed peace talks on Tuesday
Russia, US and Ukraine outline priorities ahead of peace talks (VIDEO)
content:
Donald Trump’s envoy Jared Kushner has said Washington will discuss broader European security arrangements during the Abu Dhabi meeting

The United States plans to discuss new security arrangements for Europe during peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week, US President Donald Trump’s envoy Jared Kushner has said.

Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, will travel to the UAE with fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff to mediate the talks on Tuesday and Wednesday, marking the first trilateral negotiations since February.

“We are working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment,” Kushner wrote on X on Monday.

The envoy said the US was focusing on four key issues: ending hostilities, providing “credible postwar security guarantees,” developing an economic recovery plan for Ukraine, and addressing humanitarian concerns. Kushner said Washington was also seeking to improve existing European security arrangements and “identify where existing mechanisms have fallen short.”

Speaking at a press conference in Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov welcomed the US negotiators’ decision to prioritize collective security. Russia has repeatedly called for a comprehensive peace agreement with Ukraine that would include security guarantees for both countries.

Lavrov said the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi would include Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov, who has extensive experience in arms control and negotiations involving NATO and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).

In a speech in Vienna on Monday, Ryabkov said that Europe’s security architecture “has been destroyed and cannot be restored,” adding that long-term stability would be impossible without taking into account the interests of Russia and its allies.

Kirill Budanov, head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, said negotiators would “devote significant attention to the humanitarian track,” including efforts to accelerate prisoner exchanges.

Read more

Ukraine’s European partners have scrambled in recent weeks to find ways to influence the US-mediated peace talks. The leaders of Finland and Norway broke with Europe’s policy of maintaining minimal contact with Moscow by speaking with Russian President Vladimir Putin by phone late last month, sparking debate over Europe’s role in the negotiations. Some questioned the need for talks, with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas saying the bloc would first “like to see a sign of goodwill from Russia.”

Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, said the Ukrainian delegation would hold separate meetings in Abu Dhabi with representatives of the UK, France, Germany, Italy, the EU and NATO.

“We are doing everything possible to ensure Europe is part of the diplomatic process,” he wrote on X.

Kushner, meanwhile, expressed hope that the talks would pave the way for eventual “direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.”

Russia has accused the EU and UK of sabotaging previous peace efforts, including the 2022 Istanbul talks, and remains skeptical of Europe’s potential contribution to future negotiations. “What matters is not what the Europeans want, but what added value they can actually bring to the table,” Lavrov said late last month.

The negotiators will meet following a rare weeklong local truce around the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region, which allowed more than 750 civilians to be evacuated. The agreement was reached with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump.

RT’s Igor Zhdanov breaks down what’s at stake.

Iran vows to ‘rain down hell’ if US escalates war
content:
Tehran’s proposal remains on the table, but Washington must meet its conditions, the Iranian foreign minister has warned

The US risks “dire consequences” if it escalates the war, Iran’s Foreign Ministry has warned, urging Washington to accept its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and pave the way for further negotiations.

The warning followed American strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island near the strait on Sunday night, according to local officials. Air defense and radar installations on Qeshm were also targeted last week.

Tehran’s proposal remains on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday, urging the White House to choose diplomacy.

”Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell,” he wrote on X.

Tehran’s conditions include lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, easing sanctions, releasing frozen assets, and ending hostilities on all fronts. Under the proposal, Washington would implement the initial measures on the first day, followed by the reopening of the waterway on the second. Before the war, about a fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait.

Read more

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed some of those demands as “outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.” Tehran’s spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei described the offer as “the most logical plan on the table,” saying it could restore security in the strait and the Persian Gulf.

Iran insists on retaining what it describes as sovereignty over the strait, including requiring vessels to coordinate passage with its authorities, a demand Washington opposes.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Tehran’s lead negotiator, accused Israel on Monday of drawing the US into an endless war. “Unless Washington drops the ‘Israel First’ mindset, America and its allies are headed straight for a dark age,” he said.

Israel has left open the prospect of further military action, with Defense Minister Israel Katz saying on Sunday that the mission against Iran was “still not complete” and accusing Tehran of renewing efforts to obtain nuclear weapons. The Islamic Republic maintains its nuclear program is peaceful.

Read more

US President Donald Trump met Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday for talks on Doha’s mediation between Washington and Tehran.

Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin reportedly said US Vice President J.D. Vance would meet Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Doha next week. However, Tasnim news agency cited a senior Iranian security official as denying any such plans until Washington meets Tehran’s conditions.

Russia has also backed a diplomatic settlement. President Vladimir Putin met Rezaei in Moscow on Thursday to discuss the conflict and regional security.

The US and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran on February 28, triggering months of fighting that have disrupted global energy supplies and shipping.

title: Iran removes limit on ballistic missile range (VIDEO)
content:
Tehran has warned it will target US bases in Europe in case of a new attack

Iran no longer considers itself bound by a self-imposed 2,000-km (1,200-mile) limit on the range of its ballistic missiles, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said. Iranian officials recently warned that Tehran would target military installations in Europe used by American forces, should the US and Israel attack the country again.

Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi said during a press conference on Saturday that “this restriction [on the range of ballistic missiles] has been lifted for us.” He stopped short of providing further details, noting that the Iranian military is currently focused on “demonstrating these capabilities in practice.”

While the Islamic Republic is not known to have in its arsenal missiles capable of reaching targets beyond the 2,000-km range, US officials believe the country possesses the technologies needed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles, as reported by the Associated Press.

Read more

However, even that range means that parts of Greece, Bulgaria, Romania, and the entire Middle East are already within reach of Iranian missiles.
Mohebbi also said on Saturday that the

The Iranian military is preparing to unveil “surprises… on the battlefield” if a new round of military confrontation erupts with the US and Israel.

“They should know that Iran’s next blows will be even harder,” the IRGC representative warned.

Speaking to RT on Monday, Ezzatollah Zarghami, a member of the Iranian government’s Council on Cyberspace, explained that given the changing nature and scope of the threats potentially facing the Islamic Republic, “we will naturally redefine our defense capabilities and policies accordingly.”

“It is natural that we will no longer impose geographical limitations… or our defense capabilities,” he said.

Last week, Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of the Iranian parliament’s security committee, told Euronews that “if America uses its bases in Europe, including in Italy and Germany, Iran’s missiles will be fired towards Europe.”

Around the same time, the IRGC issued a statement that quoted Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei as pledging an “effective response without geographical limits to every level and type of threat.” He also reportedly ordered military commanders to update Iran’s “target bank” to include the “enemy’s material and non-material assets within range.”

US President Donald Trump on Sunday told CNN that renewed strikes on Iran are “highly unlikely,” provided that Tehran signs a “very strong agreement” with Washington.

Trump, however, indicated that US forces in the region are ready to resume hostilities if deemed necessary, with a list of targets prepared.

title: Macrons take Candace Owens to court in her home state
content:
The Macrons are not about to let their case against the far-right media figure Candace Owens go and have now taken their lawsuit to her home turf.

In her home state of Tennessee, French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte have filed a defamation suit against the far-right conspiracy theorist.

The couple filed the complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. Their lawyers argue the state is the right venue because Owens lives in Nashville and allegedly put out the material from there.

It is the newest turn in a long legal battle the couple has mounted after Owens made false claims that Brigitte is a transgender man. Last year, Owens released an 11-part series, Becoming Brigitte, which garnered millions of views, accusing the First Lady of France of secretly transitioning from a man to a woman.

The Macrons had initially brought a defamation suit in Delaware in July 2025 against Owens and her two media companies where they are registered. However, a court in that state last month limited the scope of the complaint to just the corporations under its jurisdiction.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon K. Rennie dismissed Owens herself from that case on Oct. 27, finding the court had no jurisdiction over her since she lives in Tennessee. Claims against Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc. are still pending there.

Owens said at the time she was “in the absolute best mood” about the ruling. The Macrons’ lawyers at Clare Locke said they would look into other ways to hold her personally accountable.

On Monday, once the new filing from Nov. 4 showed up in the legal databases, a representative for the Macrons’ lawyers confirmed it is real, per Politico. In this 409-page document, the team has gone into what it calls the “outlandish, defamatory, and far-fetched fictions” of Owens and put forward financial and ideological reasons for her work. “She has continued to use her podcast to expand her lies about the Macrons, sell merchandise making fun of the Macrons, and collect donations based on her ‘reporting’ on the Macrons,” the complaint reads.

The Macrons are seeking actual, presumed, and punitive damages, along with an order barring Owens from republishing any statements a court finds defamatory.

Owens is also facing two other defamation suits, filed in Tennessee and Utah, over her commentary on the killing of Charlie Kirk.

title: Trump confesses: forgiving enemies to enter heaven is beyond him (VIDEO)
content:
Some persecuted him and also did great harm to America, the US president told 60 minutes

US President Donald Trump has said he cannot forgive enemies he accuses of persecuting him and harming the country, even if forgiveness were the condition for entering heaven.

During a ‘60 Minutes’ interview which aired on Sunday, correspondent Ross Douthat recalled Trump’s speech at the memorial for conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was shot dead in Utah in September 2025. Trump said at the time that he hated his opponents and did not want the best for them.

Douthat asked whether, standing before God’s judgment throne, Trump could forgive opponents such as former FBI Director James Comey and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi if it would allow him to enter paradise.

Trump described the figures named as “extremely dishonest people, very bad people, very bad for our country.” When asked whether his answer was therefore no, he replied: “The answer is no. I want to be honest.”

“I do hate some of my enemies. I think they’ve been terrible. Look what they’ve put me through, the weaponization. I got indicted. I got impeached,” Trump said.

READ MORE: Trump faces impeachment push over Iran conflict

The president remained unmoved when Douthat questioned how someone with such a fortunate life could refuse forgiveness. “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will,” Trump replied.

Trump was impeached twice during his first presidency and subsequently faced several criminal prosecutions, which he has portrayed as politically motivated efforts to stop him from returning to power. 

Pelosi led the House during both impeachment proceedings and has remained one of his fiercest critics. Trump has repeatedly branded Democratic opponents, including Pelosi, an “enemy from within.”

Read more

Comey, meanwhile, was a central figure in the debunked Russiagate hoax that claimed that Trump’s campaign had supposedly colluded with Moscow. He has also been charged with publicly calling for Trump’s assassination in a coded social media post.

Trump has accused the former FBI chief of trying to undermine his presidency and has branded him a “dirty cop.” 

In the ‘60 minutes’ interview, Trump was also asked whether he expected to reach heaven. “I hope so. I don’t want to go to hell,” the president replied.

He expressed similar doubts last year, when a reporter aboard Air Force One asked whether brokering the Gaza ceasefire would help him get there.

“I think I’m not, maybe, heaven-bound,” Trump said with a chuckle, adding that “I don’t think there’s anything gonna get me in heaven. I really don’t.” He noted, however, that he had “made life a lot better for a lot of people.”

title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10 1/2 years in prison for rape and sexual assault
content:
Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 1/2 years in a British prison for rape and sexual assault.

Russell Brand sentenced to 10 1/2 years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand that he showed a casual and arrogant disregard for any woman who said no to him.

About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous, Bennathan said. You were clever and in many peoples eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.

Brand showed little emotion during the hearing and turned to mouth the words we'll be OK to his wife after he stood up and was led away by court officers.

The 51-year-old actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and behavior on television and radio broadcasts, along with drug and alcohol battles, had maintained his innocence and said all his encounters were consensual.

But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers on allegations dating back to 2004. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame.

He used it to facilitate access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity," Karmy-Jones said.

Brand supported by wife, father and fans outside court

Brand wore a gray suit and an open collar shirt with a loose white tie. His long, graying hair was pulled back and knotted in a man bun atop his head. He clenched a crucifix in his right hand.

Defense lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to consider Brand's good character, saying his only previous conviction was for marijuana possession in 1995 and that had performed charitable work and helped others overcome drug and alcohol abuse.

Brand was supported in Southwark Crown Court by his wife, Laura, who entered the courthouse without him, and his father, Ron Brand. Russell Brand had been free during the trial but was jailed following Thursday's verdict.

A couple of Brand's supporters who reflected his recent conversion to Christianity held a banner bearing crosses with the words: Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth.

Victims tell court it was difficult to see Brand celebrated in public

The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accounts from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand.

One of the women he was convicted of abusing spoke in court about the impact of the crime and the others provided statements read by the prosecutor.

A woman Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004 said that the assault left her in shock and turmoil and made her feel like damaged goods.

For many years as his star was rising it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke," she said. There were many times I felt visibly sick at the sight of him parading around thinking he can get away with anything."

Brand stared straight ahead as she spoke out of view, hidden from the public behind a curtain to preserve her identity.

Rape victim felt powerless

A former fan he was convicted of anally raping at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009 said that she was left feeling anxious and humiliated and had difficulty eating and sleeping, and went through periods of heavy drinking.

She said it took years for her to speak up and that she only came forward after police opened an investigation following the documentary.

I felt that if I reported him, I would not be believed, she said in the statement read by Karmy-Jones. His fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless.

Winter, the defense lawyer, tried to minimize the significance of the rape, saying Brand should be regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given following consensual sex.

A woman he was convicted of kissing and groping at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 said it had a lasting impact on her life.

Since the sexual assault ... Russell Brand has managed to move on and even forget, she said. Over the years, hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump.

Culture at the time silenced woman

The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who said the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.

Immediately after the incident I spoke up, and sadly it was brushed under the carpet by senior management," she said. There was a culture at the time which meant I felt I had to just carry on and not talk about it anymore, which meant I did not give myself time to lament on it, boxed it up and pushed it aside.

Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Partys annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the mens bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.

The Associated Press doesnt name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

Brand, who was known for edgy stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, rose to prominence in the early 2000s hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
