title: The general seeking to end Netanyahu’s rule: Who is Gadi Eisenkot?
content:
The former military chief trying to unseat Israel’s embattled leader has promised political change but shares key positions on Gaza and Palestinian statehood

Israeli General Gadi Eisenkot, Former Chief of the General Staff,  has been tasked with forming the country’s next government, dealing a major setback to Benjamin Netanyahu after an election overshadowed by years of war, political scandals and deep divisions within society.

The struggle for power comes as Netanyahu faces genocide accusations over Gaza, mounting condemnation of military operations and state-backed settler violence in the occupied West Bank, and criticism of expanding regional wars, including the unprovoked campaign against Iran.

Eisenkot has promised to remove Netanyahu and restore an accountable government, but his military record and policies have raised questions about how exactly he would govern and whether Palestinians would actually see a change for the better.

Who is Netanyahu’s challenger?

Eisenkot, 66, was born in Tiberias to Moroccan Jewish immigrant parents and grew up in Eilat, far from Israel’s main political centers.

He joined the Israel Defense Forces’ (IDF) Golani infantry brigade in 1978 and spent 41 years in the military, rising through senior commands in the occupied West Bank and northern Israel before serving as chief of staff from 2015 to 2019.

As a senior commander, he advocated the so-called Dahiya doctrine, stating in 2008 that Israel would use “disproportionate force” and inflict “huge damage and destruction” on the Lebanese villages from which it was attacked.

Eisenkot entered parliament in 2022 and joined Netanyahu’s emergency government after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, attending the war cabinet’s discussions on the Gaza campaign as an observer.

Read more

The war brought Eisenkot personal losses. His son Gal was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023 and his two nephews were also killed during the conflict.

Eisenkot resigned from the government in June 2024, criticizing Netanyahu’s handling of the war and the lack of a clear postwar plan for Gaza. He has nevertheless continued to support military action against Hamas.

What does he promise?

Eisenkot founded the centrist Yashar, or “Straight,” party in 2025, appealing to centrists and center-right voters seeking a security-focused alternative to Netanyahu, including secular and traditional Israelis united by their desire to remove him.

His military experience, personal losses and demands for accountability over October 7 have been central to his campaign. He has also sought to distinguish himself from Israel’s traditional political establishment through his Moroccan-Jewish upbringing.

Read more

Eisenkot has promised an independent state commission of inquiry into the 2023 Hamas attack and the failures that preceded it – demands that have been resisted by Netanyahu, who has backed a government-appointed investigation instead.

The former military chief has also promised to protect judicial independence, tackle living costs and broaden compulsory military or civilian service.

The service issue has become a particular source of resentment among Israelis repeatedly called up for duty while many ultra-Orthodox men receive exemptions. Netanyahu’s religious partners have fought to preserve those arrangements.

What’s his stance on Palestinians and foreign policy?

Eisenkot shares Netanyahu’s opposition to an independent Palestinian state and has advocated for Israel to retain overriding security control between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.

In Gaza, Eisenkot wants Hamas disarmed and removed from power. He has pledged to replace its administration within 18 months of taking office, either through a US-backed arrangement or military force.

He has also supported allowing reconstruction to proceed alongside partial disarmament and said the Palestinian Authority would be preferable to continued Hamas rule if those were the alternatives.

Read more

In the West Bank, he supports settlements in principle but opposes unauthorized outposts and settler violence. He has also criticized the E1 settlement expansion east of Jerusalem, which would further fragment Palestinian territory and obstruct its connection with East Jerusalem.

On Iran, Eisenkot has questioned the need for another campaign and has accused the government of failing to achieve its previous war objectives. Netanyahu, meanwhile, has campaigned on promises to resume the offensive against Tehran and overthrow its government.

Can he actually remove Netanyahu?

Israeli President Isaac Herzog formally gave Eisenkot the mandate on Sunday, following recommendations from parties representing 67 lawmakers. His core opposition bloc, however, controls just 48 seats in Israel’s 120-member parliament, the Knesset, short of the 61 needed for a majority.

Read more

The additional backing has come from Arab-led parties willing to help remove Netanyahu, including through support from outside the government. But Eisenkot’s conditions, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and dismantling Hamas’s military and governing power, have complicated potential cooperation. Some of his allies have rejected relying on Arab support altogether.

Eisenkot could also seek support from ultra-Orthodox parties traditionally allied with Netanyahu, but is expected to face demands to compromise on conscription. His ally Avigdor Lieberman has signaled a willingness to negotiate despite years of opposing those parties.

RT correspondent Charlotte Dubenskij reports from Israel on the compromises that could determine whether he succeeds.

Netanyahu remains in office while Eisenkot negotiates, and his Likud party holds more seats than any other single party. He has urged Eisenkot to join a broad unity government that includes his existing partners, while claiming that a government dependent on Arab parties would endanger Israel’s survival.

Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, potentially extended by two weeks. If he fails, Herzog could ask Netanyahu or another candidate to try. A prolonged stalemate could trigger another election.

The new Knesset is due to be sworn in on Tuesday.

title: Reforming the UN Must Begin with Reforming Staff Representation
content:
A group of UN Staffers outside the Secretariat. Credit: United Nations

By Naïma Abdellaoui
GENEVA, Nov 9 2026 (IPS)

Stronger staff representation means a stronger United Nations. This is not simply about protecting jobs or preserving acquired benefits, important as those objectives are. This is about protecting the institutional capacity, integrity and independence of the United Nations itself.

Every abolished post can represent lost expertise, institutional memory and operational capacity. Every deterioration in employment conditions can affect the Organization’s ability to attract and retain professionals of the highest caliber. Every restructuring undertaken without meaningful staff participation risks undermining trust, morale and the quality of mandate delivery.

At a time when financial pressures, political interference and technological transformation are reshaping the international civil service, staff representatives should be contributing to the design of sustainable institutional solutions, not merely managing the consequences of decisions taken elsewhere.

Staff representatives should be capable of challenging flawed policies, identifying alternatives, defending institutional independence and bringing the practical knowledge of the workforce into strategic decisions.

A strong, independent staff representative system is not an obstacle to reform.
It is an essential condition for reform that is legitimate, sustainable and faithful to the UN’s mission.

Returning to the spirit of the Charter

Articles 100 and 101 of the UN Charter establish the foundations of an independent international civil service whose members serve the Organization rather than individual governments and whose employment is guided by the highest standards of efficiency, competence and integrity.

Those principles cannot be reduced to administrative slogans. They require institutions that protect professional independence, uphold fairness and enable staff to speak and act collectively in defense of the Organization they serve.

The UN cannot advocate democratic governance, fundamental labor rights and institutional accountability throughout the world while leaving serious shortcomings in its own representative arrangements unaddressed.

Naïma Abdellaoui is Staff Representative UN Office at Geneva (UNOG) and member of the Executive Bureau of UNOG Staff Union.

IPS UN Bureau

title: A-lehdet speeds up AI adoption with an in-house short video script creator
content:
About the publisher: A-lehdet is a Finnish publisher best known for its portfolio of magazines that cover current affairs, living, design, health, culture and lifestyle. Beyond print, the group has diversified into digital media, influencer marketing, and e-commerce. Founded in 1933 with the launch of its flagship periodical Apu, the company remains family-owned to this day.

Streamlining social video production

As news publishers increasingly use social media for video distribution, many newsrooms face new challenges that are upending traditional workflows. From writing to editing, the process of creating video content can add pressure on an already busy newsroom, particularly if the publisher has little background or few resources dedicated to video production.

This was the issue that Milla Kukkonen decided to work on during her participation in NextGen AI Leaders, a WAN-IFRA programme in partnership with the Google News Initiative. The programme is designed to help young media leaders reach the next stage in their careers through responsible AI deployment and strategic leadership.

In her job as Executive Producer at A-lehdet, Kukkonen has seen how much work transforming an article into a short-form video represents. A particular challenge she had identified was coming up with a strong “hook” that distils the article into an interesting question and captures the viewer’s attention from the start.

Using Google AI Studio, she began working on a video scripting assistant, also involving her colleagues in the editorial department for their feedback. A working prototype was already finished before the NextGen AI Leaders programme ended. “It was energising to see how quickly you can create things,” she said.

Finding the right opening

Kukkonen’s solution allows users to upload their source material (an article or an interview) and generates suggestions on how a video script based on it could be structured, including an attention-grabbing opening.

More broadly, mobile video is playing an increasingly important role in A-lehdet’s content strategy, and the new tool supports this by simplifying the process of journalists producing their own videos. The publisher also works with a wide roster of freelancers, and the tool makes it easier to turn externally created articles into videos for social media distribution.

“Our aim is to increase mobile video production so that all writers can independently create videos. That’s the need I wanted to address with this tool: to help people script, edit and publish videos on their own,” Kukkonen said.

She developed the initial prototype using Google AI Studio, but its features have now been transferred into ChatGPT, bringing them into the AI environment that is used across the company.

Screenshot: Kukkonen’s first prototype of the scripting tool app was created using Google AI Studio.

A-lehdet has a fairly flat organisational structure, which means that a lot of people are involved in making content for the company’s social media channels, Kukkonen said. She estimates that now that the video script creator is widely available, about half of the editorial team are potential users of the tool.

Building ‘AI savvy’

Because A-lehdet is a Finnish publisher, the script creator was naturally built to work in Finnish. While some users of generative AI tools have found them lacking when working with smaller languages, Kukkonen said that the leading models have now improved to the point where this is no longer an issue.

Summarising her experiences in the NextGen AI Leaders programme, she credited the initiative with helping her build her “AI savvy.” Given that AI spans both IT and editorial parts of the business, she said having an “AI fluent” person in the editorial team has been helpful in navigating this reality.

The programme’s impact has also been felt more widely in the company: Kukkonen said the experiences she gained during the programme sparked many interesting conversations and have helped build internal momentum for AI use.

“Milla’s ability to combine the possibilities of AI with good journalism and established editorial practices has already made a difference to our way of working,” said Mari Paalosalo-Jussinmäki, Head of the Lifestyle Media Group at A-lehdet.

“She has played a key role in bridging the gap between our tech teams and editorial staff. She’s also great at encouraging her colleagues to try new things,” she added.

Looking back on the project, Kukkonen noted that the development of the scripting tool reaffirmed a key belief she had about AI implementation: while AI may be effective in summarising and analysing large amounts of content, human journalists have an edge that the models are unlikely to threaten.

“I believe even more strongly than before that our journalistic advantage is the ability to find and report on issues that have not been previously revealed.”

We spoke to Kukkonen to learn more about how the NextGen AI Leaders programme helped shape her views on AI leadership. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

‘AI leadership requires that you actually understand AI’: Q&A with Milla Kukkonen

WAN-IFRA: How did your perspective on AI leadership evolve during the programme?

Milla Kukkonen: One thing that stuck with me was something Anita [Zielina, one of the instructors] said: “AI is a leadership challenge, not a tech challenge.” Many issues related to AI actually come down to basic leadership questions: defining roles, responsibilities, competences, and everyday workflows. They are fundamentally management issues, and you shouldn’t think of them as “tech things.”

I also gained a better understanding of how leveraging AI requires collaboration. You need a shared understanding of what the problem is, who is responsible for what, how decisions are made, and how to measure successes.

The programme also reaffirmed the idea that AI leadership requires that you actually understand AI. You have to actively use it and try to think of ways AI can improve your own work. I don’t think you can outsource it and say, “I’m not a tech person, so I’m not going to bother.”

What level of AI resistance have you faced in your organisation? How have you dealt with it?

I wouldn’t talk about “resistance” in our company. To me, it’s not resistance if you have concerns or ask questions.

Of course, people have all kinds of opinions and concerns, and I actually understand many of them well. Even I have doubts running through my mind at times. Will AI affect the quality of journalism? Will my competence be enough going forward? Are we going to lose tasks that feel meaningful? It’s healthy to ask those questions, and I think voicing concerns and fears is actually a positive thing.

At work, we try to focus on discussing AI at the level of how it relates to our jobs. I believe that if doubts and uncertainties arise, there must be permission to voice them. And I’ve tried to make sure that we actually have those conversations when such concerns come up.

Was there a significant leadership challenge, and what did it teach you?

I’ve reflected quite a bit on how to bring together the perspectives of different experts so that the end result is genuinely helpful for people in their daily work.

We have an AI working group where I’m currently the only representative from the editorial side. So I bring our viewpoints into the discussions: how we plan training, consider guidelines, and so on. It has reinforced the idea of how important it is to genuinely understand the perspective of everyone involved.

How has participating in this programme influenced your role or career path?

Before the programme, I had a mostly informal role as the “AI person” in the newsroom. I was involved in development projects, attended workshops and learned about relevant issues.

Now my role has steered even more in that direction, as I wanted to move deeper into the AI space. The programme was a springboard, and I decided to dive in. It felt vital to ensure that the newsroom’s voice is heard inside the company.

If you could give one piece of advice to another media leader trying to implement AI, what would it be?

I can think of three things. One: invest in learning across the company. Even in a small organisation, you can get huge benefits from people realising for themselves how they can reorganise their work to be more efficient. People tend to shine when they are empowered to improve how they handle their tasks. It really pays off to ensure that learning and upskilling are coordinated in a systematic way.

Secondly, AI may end up having an important role in the creation of some content, but what AI can’t take away – and what is our competitive edge as journalists – are untold stories. There are endless untold stories in this world, and you just need the courage and capability to tackle them and dig them up.

My last point comes from the [NextGen AI Leaders] programme. It was a wonderful experience: I met amazing people, made friends, had hilarious conversations, shared experiences – and saw that everyone was wrestling with similar issues and wondering where all this is heading. That felt important on a human level.

So my advice would be: also try to do things that have nothing to do with AI. Enjoy life, pet your dog, go for walks – and spend some time with the people that you are trying to reach with your content, your audience. Don’t just obsess over AI, but remember who we’re actually making content for, and connect with those people.

AI is developing fast, but what AI will not be able to do is feel on our behalf, or be present on our behalf. You can only do that yourself. So, remember to focus on things other than AI once in a while!

The post A-lehdet speeds up AI adoption with an in-house short video script creator appeared first on WAN-IFRA.

title: Palestinian flag flies over Reichstag (VIDEO)
content:
An activist climbed a 30-meter rooftop flagpole, removed the country’s national banner, and threw it to the ground  

An anti-Israel activist has hoisted a Palestinian banner outside Germany’s parliament building, the Reichstag, in Berlin after climbing a nearly 30-meter flagpole, removing the national flag and throwing it to the ground.

The 22-year-old man scaled the pole while two accomplices, aged 20 and 32, filmed the stunt and livestreamed it on TikTok. All three were detained, although the two accomplices were subsequently released.

The activist group Peacefully Against Genocide claimed responsibility, describing the action as an expression of solidarity with Palestinians. The group has previously staged similar demonstrations at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate.

German police arrested three people in Berlin today after a man scaled the 30-metre flagpole outside the Reichstag, took down the German "Flag of Unity" and hoisted a Palestinian flag. Two accomplices filmed the climb. All three are suspected of insulting state symbols. Authorities removed the Palestinian flag using fire service equipment.

— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) November 8, 2026

The Palestinian flag flew for about an hour before firefighters removed it. The original banner, known as the Flag of Unity, could not immediately be raised again because the flagpole’s hoisting mechanism had been damaged, according to police. The authorities are investigating suspected property damage, trespassing, violations of assembly laws, and insulting state symbols.

Germany has faced mounting criticism over its military support for Israel during the Gaza conflict. Berlin imposed partial restrictions on weapons exports in August 2025 but lifted them three months later. Between November 2025 and March 2026, the government authorized another €167 million (about $193 million) in military exports to Israel, according to official figures.

A similar display took place in June 2024, when activists unfurled a large Palestinian banner on the facade of Milan’s iconic Duomo cathedral, drawing applause from people gathered in the square below.

Read more

The Reichstag incident coincided with a major pro-Palestinian demonstration in Amsterdam on Sunday, where tens of thousands of people demanded an end to violence in Gaza and urged the Dutch government to reconsider its economic and military ties with Israel.

Israel launched its Gaza offensive following a Hamas-led attack in October 2023 that killed around 1,200. Some 250 people were taken hostage. More than 75,000 Palestinians have since been killed across the Palestinian territories, including at least 21,500 children, according to a UN Commission of Inquiry.

READ MORE: Israeli president instructs Netanyahu rival to form government

In a report released on October 26, the commission concluded that Israel had continued committing “genocidal acts” in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire, with Israeli attacks killing another 1,431 Palestinians by September 30. It also accused Israel of crimes against humanity in the West Bank. Israel has rejected allegations of genocide, maintaining that its military operations target Hamas.

In October, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz reportedly said the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) were preparing for a possible war with the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, where Palestinians have faced repeated attacks by Israeli settlers.

title: Trump predicts ‘a little bit different shape’ for Ukraine
content:
Moscow has long said that any viable peace deal with Kiev must recognize new territorial realities and address the root causes of the conflict

US President Donald Trump has suggested that Ukraine will have to give up territory in order to achieve peace with Russia.

Trump made the statement ahead of the resumption of trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev, and Washington, which are scheduled to take place in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday and Wednesday.

During an interview with CBS New on Sunday, Trump said “there’s a very important meeting taking place. I believe that that war is going to end, and it’s going to end soon.”

“I think we’re going to have it done, and I think it’s going happen and they’re going to end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine,” the US president said, without elaborating.

When reminded that has been promising to end the fighting between Moscow and Kiev since his campaign for the White House in 2024, Trump reiterated his claim that the conflict would not have started if he had been president in 2022. “Zero chance. But it did start. So, I inherited that war,” he added.

Read more

Trump spoke about the need for Ukraine to make territorial concessions after his talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Anchorage in August 2025. Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky, who is backed by Western European countries, has consistently rejected any concessions despite Kiev’s continued setbacks on the front line and inability to counter Russian long-range missile and drone strikes. Zelensky’s unwillingness to make a deal prompted Trump to suggest last month that Ukraine needs a new leader.

The US president said on Sunday that he expects to hold his first in-person meeting with Putin since Anchorage at an APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next week as part of trilateral negotiations that will also include Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping. “We’ll be talking a lot of things,” he said.

There appears to be no shift in Kiev’s stance coming into the talks in UAE, with Zelensky aide Sergey Leschenko saying last week that Ukraine’s delegation would insist on “halting the fighting where it’s currently taking place, without giving up any Ukrainian territory.”

Read more

Moscow has repeatedly said it will not accept a temporary ceasefire that merely allows Kiev to regroup and rearm. According to the Russian side, the conflict requires a permanent settlement that addresses its root causes and recognizes the new territorial realities on the ground.

This includes Crimea, which reunited with Russia in 2014, and the Donetsk (DPR) and Lugansk (LPR) People’s Republics, along with Zaporozhye and Kherson Regions, which were incorporated into Russia in 2022 following referendums.

Putin said last month that he believes Moscow and Kiev “can come to an agreement. We’re open to that.”

“We do not want to fight with Ukraine. But if the current Ukrainian leadership wants to fight, well, let them fight,” the president stressed. Russia will achieve all of its goals in the conflict one way or another, he added.

title: Reuters Institute’s Nic Newman on where publishers are seeing growth
content:
Today, many traditional news publishers are “really rethinking a lot of fundamental things and less about pure reach and more about relationships – about how you build loyalty,” said Newman, Senior Research Associate at Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at Oxford University.

News publishers as a whole have seen substantial growth in their subscription businesses during the past decade, and subscription revenue remains a top priority for many. However, “now, we’re in this what you might call a ‘subscription shelf,’ and many publishers are feeling this,” he noted.

As a result, today, the focus is increasingly about delivering value, he said, and the questions are along the lines of “how do you build that value in different ways? How do you retain your subscribers by putting more value in? That’s why we’re seeing more bundling, combination of news and lifestyle content being one strategy for that.”

Likewise, if publishers are now reaching their likely peak subscriber numbers, then how can they get more out of those subscribers?

“One of the things that we see is putting in more premium layers, and trying to increase that average revenue per user (ARPU),” Newman said.

WAN-IFRA Members can replay this session and others from Digital Media Europe on our Knowledge Hub.

The rise of aggregators and fandom

When looking at the overall market of what subscribers are paying for, there are some areas that are clearly increasing, Newman noted.

“Firstly the rise of aggregators. And I think that with AI, we will probably see more aggregators as well. Things like Apple News playing an increasingly important role in countries like the UK, Canada, the United States and Germany as well,” he said.

A lot of the growth that Reuters Institute is seeing now is around products like video podcasts and newsletters “as businesses in their own right,” such as ones coming from individual Substackers.

In addition, “some of the new models are more about fandom. They’re more about shows, putting the talent at the heart and then around that core proposition, you can then build out these different out-puts.”

Take Goalhanger for example.

“Goalhanger started as a podcast company. It doesn’t call itself a podcast company any more: it does audio, it does video, it does TV. They’re investing in text. They’re investing in newsletters. And then around that, all of these different revenue models: Membership, licensing, brand partnerships. And it’s not an either-or, it’s all of those things together, including ticket sales,” Newman said.

In September, Goalhanger organised a large festival at the Southbank Centre in London. Nearly two dozen sessions featured the company’s “hosts coming together and really building those relationships. And making significant amounts of money, too.”

Originally a podcast company, Goalhanger has evolved to working in a variety of ways, including events: “They’re really building around that talent and the outputs,” Newman said.

Such diversification is also being embraced by many legacy news publishers, of course, and while reader revenue through subscriptions, memberships and events has been getting more attention, advertising remains vital. “It’s not subscription replacing advertising, it’s how you can combine these things. Advertising is really important, and brand advertising has become a bit more important over time,” Newman said.

Licensing revenue expected to rise

Another growing diversification realm is licensing: “This is the area that has increased the most,” Newman said. “Publishers believe that there will be something coming from licensing. The funding from platforms primarily was relatively small scale around innovation until a few years ago. And increasingly now, this is publishers feeling that there are opportunities in this world to build new kinds of licensing revenue.”

While pointing out that most publishers are not thinking this licensing revenue is going to be their main source of income, or even a significant one, nevertheless, 69 percent of those they talked with, “felt that there would be a source of income, a minor source of income, over the next few years.”

Asked by moderator Kevin Anderson, of WAN-IFRA, about the market for AI licensing and publishers’ expectations, Newman noted the future will likely be different than some of the headline grabbers, like News Corp’s deal with OpenAI for 250 million over five years. While the figures in some of the early deals can sound huge, Newman said the reality is that 250 million across all of the News Corp properties over five years, “it’s not really the main source of income.”

“I think it’s clearer now that a lot of the value is not necessarily in the licensing of the training data. It’s much more about the grounding data, the real-time data and that’s obviously things that the AIs and the LLMs don’t have. So, over time, what we need to build is a mechanism to allow that value to be clear and then to be paid-for and we’re starting to see some of those,” he said.

title: Bangladesh’s ousted PM seeks new passport to return – report
content:
Sheikh Hasina requested travel documents ahead of a planned December return from India even as Dhaka seeks her extradition, says Reuters

Bangladesh’s ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has formally requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return from India next month, despite facing a death sentence at home, Reuters reported on Monday.

Her lawyers at the London-based Matrix Chambers wrote to the acting high commissioner at Bangladesh’s mission in New Delhi, Preeti Rahman, seeking replacement documents after her existing passport and identity card were reportedly revoked by the previous interim government in Dhaka.

Hasina was ousted following protests in August, 2024, ending her 15-year rule and forcing her to flee to India. A United Nations report estimated that as many as 1,400 people were killed during her government’s crackdown on the protests. She was sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal last November.

Her lawyers have sought expedited processing, citing her Bangladeshi citizenship and international human rights obligations.

Her continued stay in India has strained relations between New Delhi and Dhaka. Bangladesh has insisted that Hasina should be extradited. Bangladeshi Deputy Foreign Minister Humaiun Kobir, however, dismissed the idea of providing her a passport last Thursday.

Read more

New Delhi has said the extradition request is being examined through established legal procedures and that a timeline cannot be provided.

Hasina has previously said that she and senior members of her Awami League party planned to return in December and surrender before a court. Her aides said Monday that the exact date would be announced once the necessary formalities were completed.

The former prime minister reaffirmed her intention to return in an interview last week, saying she would go back “at any cost,” despite the possibility of arrest.

title: Drought Cripples Dairy Farmers in Maharashtra in ‘Off the Charts’ Weather Year
content:
A dairy farmer holds her Kallari cow in the Solapur district of the western Indian state of Maharashtra. Credit: Rina Mukherji/IPS

By Rina Mukherji
PUNE, India & ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov 9 2026 (IPS)

Dairy farmer Sagar Pawar has to buy water and fodder at inflated rates to feed his brood of two buffaloes, three Guernsey cows and a calf. He lives in the Solapur district, which is already drought-prone, but now has to deal with the impacts of a strong El Niño as well.

Pawar was interviewed in the days leading up to the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), which opened today in Antalya, Türkiye.

The opening coincided with the release of the World Meteorological Society’s new report, which confirms that 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record.

“The year 2026 continues the protracted streak of exceptional global temperatures, melting ice and rising sea levels, with a very strong El Niño event set to unleash even more heat and extreme weather well into 2027,” the report confirms, highlighting the knock-on risks to the environment, economy, and everyday life.

“Extreme weather has made headlines throughout 2026. Behind the headlines and the statistics in this report are people who suffered the loss of loved ones, threats to their health and safety, flooded homes, failed harvests, empty shelves, lack of water and choking air,” said Celeste Saulo, WMO Secretary General.

“The past four years have been the warmest in the 177-year observational record, and the heat in the oceans is breaking records for the tenth year in a row. The ongoing El Niño is forecast to be one of the strongest on record, and the heat it releases from the ocean will continue to fuel high temperatures and extreme weather into 2027. Forecasts underpinned by sustained observations are more important than ever to monitor our rapidly changing climate and help navigate the increasing risks to societies and economies.”

UN Secretary-General António Guterres reacted to the report, noting, “We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst. Leaders must get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need.

Those among the most vulnerable live in the Solapur district in the western Indian state of Maharashtra, which has long been semi-arid. Rainfall here averages between 427 and 552 mm during the monsoon months of June to September, with few major rivers for farmers to rely on.

Impact on Most Vulnerable

Farmers here have always cultivated millets, alongside gram, lentils, horticultural crops, and fodder, which require limited amounts of water. Dairy farming and horticulture have not just supplemented rural incomes here but are the mainstay of the (rural) economy.

This rain-shadow district, as well as the Marathwada and Vidarbha regions of the state, is familiar with droughts, especially this year due to a strong El Niño.

However, groundwater depletion has hit 47% more wells than in 2015, which was a drought year. In fact, there are many more talukas facing drought this year, including some in districts like Pune, which are not drought-prone.

Solapur district and its talukas (sub-divisions) remain the worst-hit. The entire Solapur district is parched and thirsty, except for a few villages near the Seena River in and around the pilgrim town/taluka of Pandharpur, with parts like Mohol receiving as little as 193.2 mm. Sangola, renowned for its pomegranate production, is one of the 305 talukas declared drought-stricken by the state government.

As against a normal average rainfall of 468.3 mm during the monsoon months, Sangola received just 229.1 mm, amounting to a 52 per cent deficit this year.

Even millets could not be sown this year because the soil lacked the minimal moisture, as Lalit Babar, founder of the Dr Ambedkar Agricultural Development and Research Institute, a non-governmental organisation focused on agricultural research, explained to me. A few farms that planted pomegranates last year are in a poor state, with stunted plants.

Normally, dairy farmers grow their fodder here. But this year, farms were unable to yield any fodder.

In fact, the entire state is facing a fodder crisis, with some districts left with only 63-65 days of fodder. The government is helping households with drinking water. But no water is being supplied for livestock.

Dairy farmer Sagar Pawar tells me, “The Gram Panchayat (rural self-governing body) gives us one tanker of water, amounting to 2 000 litres, once every four days. It is hardly enough.”

The Pawars have a borewell on their land, which is 400 metres deep. But water runs for just two minutes, the first minute yielding only muddy water. What is pumped out is just sufficient for the household.

Hence, Pawar has to buy water and fodder at inflated rates to feed his brood of two buffaloes, three Guernsey cows and a calf.

“The fodder in the market comes from the neighbouring state and is of very low quality, but beggars cannot be choosers,” he rues.

The Waghmode brothers – Raju and Deepak – own 17 animals, including four buffaloes, seven Guernsey and 3 Killari cows, besides five calves.

Alike other dairy farmers, they are compelled to buy their own fodder and water for their animals.

“We are trying to store fodder and water to safeguard ourselves. But our storage capacity is limited,” Raju Waghmode tells me. Hanumant Kadam is the biggest dairy farmer in Dongarwadi village in Sangola, with 60 milch animals – 54 Guernsey cows, two Killari cows, and four Jaffrabadi buffaloes.

In addition, he also breeds 40 sheep and a goat. His 8-acre farm normally grows fodder for his animals, besides a little millet for family consumption. The drought has hit him hard.

“I can only buy limited amounts of the required fodder and protein feed for my animals; hence, I feed them just enough for survival.”

Kadam needs an average of 5000 litres of water daily for his animals, which, at inflated rates, amounts to a colossal sum. This means feeding a Guernsey cow just 15-20 kg of fodder, as against its normal requirement of 30 kg per day.

The same applies to his Indian killari breed, buffaloes, goats, and sheep. Consequently, milk yield has dropped. His Guernsey cows now yield only 5 litres per day, as against the normal 11 litres per day, while the milk yield from his Killari cows stands at 1 litre, as against 3 litres daily.

A dairy farmer needs fodder, protein feed and water for every animal to profit from his brood. With inflated costs, most farmers cannot afford to keep their livestock. Dairy farmer Battu Waghmode had to sell off his 30 cows and buffaloes at a throwaway price. The Atpadkars’ 3-acre farm cannot yield fodder for their buffaloes, goats and sheep.

“Our borewell can yield water for only an hour daily, which is just enough for our family,” Chandan Atpadkar tells me. Hence, they have decided to sell all their animals for now.

Rural distress can be assessed from the fact that non-banking financial institutions (NBFCs), which are major players in rural India, are curbing all lending as a cautionary move.

Government Relief for Villagers

The state government has announced an examination fee waiver for students in the 305 talukas declared drought-stricken to help the affected people. Financial relief has also been announced for the affected population, with water tankers being arranged for drinking purposes through urban local and rural self-governing bodies.

However, livelihood issues have been generally overlooked, as farmers point out, although the government has announced plans for a fodder bank to provide for future emergencies. The government has sought drought-mitigation proposals from district collectors within a fortnight while seeking immediate information on fodder and water availability at the village level.

There is also a move to grow spineless cactus as a substitute fodder for cattle across the drought-prone Marathwada region. But farmers remain sceptical. “We need immediate relief, right now.”

In Dongarwadi village in Sangola, water can be accessed only by 15 percent of the population, since water tankers cannot reach families who live on their farms, away from the asphalt roads of the main village settlement. Hence, water tankers arranged by the grassroots development organisation, Dr Ambedkar Sheti Vikas va Sanshodhan Sanstha, are the only lifeline for locals.

Role of Climate Finance

The drought in Maharashtra has come at a time when some other natural disasters have also struck South Asia. Massive floods in Northeast India and flash floods in Nepal have devastated wide swathes of land. These natural disasters have once again emphasised the necessity of climate finance for adaptation and mitigation, as well as for building resilience in the Global South, which the forthcoming COP 31 aims to address.

This issue assumes especial importance in view of the forecasts made by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) for the October-December season, given the high global sea surface temperatures. Sea-surface temperatures reflect strengthening El Niño.

Notably, the commitment by developed countries to mobilise US$100 billion annually in climate finance for developing countries, which was reinforced at the 2010 Cancun climate conference and incorporated into the 2015 Paris Agreement, was not achieved by the original 2020 deadline. Despite the establishment of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and a Climate Finance Delivery Plan, the target was only reached in 2022, when developed countries provided and mobilised US$115.9 billion.

However, developing countries maintain that this amount falls far short of their needs. The NEED’S Report, or UNFCCC’s Second Report on the Determination of the Needs of Developing Country Parties, published in 2025, estimates that between US$5 trillion and US$6.9 trillion is required to implement the climate adaptation and mitigation measures identified in developing countries’ Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) by 2030. The report notes that this figure does not capture the full extent of their climate finance needs.

As Shravan Shankar, a climate finance expert and CEO of CLIMAKE, explains, the original thinking was that prioritising emissions reduction would help limit the future costs of adapting to climate change.

“Adaptation was acknowledged, but it was still seen as a ‘future’ need,” he says. “The idea was that if we mobilise enough towards mitigation, we will be able to sufficiently reduce emissions, reduce the impact of climate change, and consequently reduce adaptation and resilience needs.”

However, the scale and urgency of the climate challenge have since changed considerably. Countries’ net-zero commitments mean that mitigation must now extend beyond renewable energy and clean mobility to more complex areas such as industrial decarbonisation and agricultural emissions reduction. These sectors are harder to commercialise and cannot necessarily follow the same investment pathways as renewable energy.

More significantly, the consequences of climate change are already being felt, making adaptation and resilience an immediate priority rather than a future consideration.

“Arguably the most significant development is that the effects of climate change are clear and present, and they are devastating,” Shankar says.

This presents a particularly difficult challenge for low-income developing economies, which often lack the financial resources and institutional capacity to protect their populations and economies against increasingly severe climate impacts. Adaptation requires investment in practical measures, from climate-resilient seeds and agricultural inputs to irrigation systems, reliable water access and improved farming practices to prevent food losses.

As Shankar points out, these countries need resources to implement measures that can protect livelihoods and strengthen resilience to drought, water stress and rising temperatures. Yet these investments often struggle to attract private capital because, unlike many renewable energy projects, they do not necessarily generate direct commercial returns.

Echoing Shankar’s views on the global emphasis on mitigation so far, Arun Krishnan, Program Director of Climate Finance at the World Resources Institute (WRI) in India, feels the need to look at adaptation and mitigation separately.

Much of the mitigation, such as utility-scale solar in favourable markets, has become commercially bankable and can attract mainstream finance without concessional support. The financing challenge lies increasingly in adaptation and in areas of mitigation that are not yet commercially viable.

“Developing countries need finance for adaptation and hard-to-finance mitigation at a much greater scale and on far better terms. Adaptation remains one of the most underfunded areas because it generates benefits largely through avoided losses rather than direct revenue,” Krishnan said.

Yet it is often vulnerable communities that experience climate impacts first and most acutely.

Emphasising the need for accessibility to climate finance for those who need it most, he calls for more grants and concessional finance. Calling for blended finance, guarantees and risk-sharing mechanisms to mobilise private capital herein, Krishnan advocates a stronger role for regulators like central banks, as well as development banks and rural and cooperative lenders, to channel finance to farmers and small businesses.

The challenge for the Global South is not merely to bridge the enormous gap between financial commitments and estimated requirements but also to distinguish the incremental costs of climate change from pre-existing developmental deficits and vulnerabilities that amplify disaster impacts, says Dr Nilanjan Ghosh, Vice President, Observer Research Foundation (ORF), and a distinguished ecological economist with expertise in climate finance.

“Adaptation finance must, therefore, be embedded within a broader framework of development resilience, encompassing water governance, ecosystem restoration, climate-resilient infrastructure, institutional preparedness and disaster-risk reduction.”

These discussions are even more urgent, as the WMO State of the Climate Update 2026 shows that the past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four. The global average surface temperature for January–September 2026 was about 1.47 °C above the pre-industrial average. This figure is likely to rise through the end of the year due to the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December.

Earth’s energy imbalance is rising, and the earth system is accumulating heat at an accelerating rate. The imbalance reached its highest level since monitoring began, as greenhouse gases trap unprecedented amounts of heat and upset the equilibrium between incoming energy from the sun and outgoing energy. The ocean absorbs 90% of this excess heat, and 2026 is on track to be the tenth successive year of record ocean warmth.

Sea level is the highest on record, and sea-surface temperatures hit monthly records during 2026. The long-term retreat of glaciers continues, with the annual mass loss of ice in 2025 filling five Olympic pools every second of the year. Freshwater storage has been dwindling since 2014.

The report commented on several natural disasters across the world caused by climate extremes including the Indian monsoon rainfall deficit from June to September, which affected about 705 000. The monsoon began with June rainfall around 40% below normal. All-India rainfall was around 12% below normal by 30 September, raising concerns for agriculture and water resources.

title: I Continue to Accuse
content:
This is the third article in a four-part series. The final article will follow.

By Saber Azam
GENEVA, Nov 9 2026 (IPS)

This piece focuses on the responsibilities of other prominent figures, leaders of intergovernmental organizations, senior diplomats, and business tycoons for the world’s current appalling state and the calamities that may await future generations. When democracy fails; when people in authority remain silent and prioritize self-interest; when regional entities become redundant; when appearance becomes more important than substance; when diplomacy is outsmarted by warmongers; when prejudice infects minds; and when business chooses unlawfulness, I continue to assert:

Saber Azam

I Accuse Other Prominent Figures

Other prominent figures—heads of political parties, senior members of legislative and judicial bodies, high-level bureaucrats and military commanders, and even some prominent artists—also bear significant responsibility for upholding their countries’ constitutions and for demanding accountability from their leaders. Many succumb to the influence of questionable lobbies or circles to strengthen their power base, secure re-election, obtain better positions, advance their careers, or defend particular interests.

Unlawful wars and mass killings occur live on camera, and major investigations and judicial processes sometimes appear to align with the political ambitions of those who rule their countries, regardless of the gravity of the crimes committed. Election rigging has become standard practice in many places around the world. White-collar and covert bribery is tolerated as long as it serves those in power or dominant circles. Underhanded tactics used to disqualify lawful competitors have become the bread and butter of many influential figures and even institutions. The rule of law often seems to apply most strictly to those with little or no means. Many high-ranking military officers appear to lack the resolve to resist unconstitutional orders.

Social and economic development, as well as political freedom, remain elusive in many “developing” countries decades after independence. Large segments of the population on earth still live in absolute poverty, while a small number of powerful figures in political, economic, and other key spheres amass vast wealth. As a result, many prominent figures worldwide have failed in their political, legislative, judicial, administrative, defense, or artistic responsibilities.

I Accuse Leaders of the Regional Intergovernmental Organizations

Contrary to the “world-loving” spirit of the United Nations (UN), regional intergovernmental organizations were established to safeguard peace and security and to promote social, political, and economic development within their respective jurisdictions. Yet they have not been immune to individual interests, superpower intervention, or the influence of economically prosperous countries and powerful industries.

To date, few regions appear politically stable. Internal crises, wars between neighbors, and regional conflicts persist across many parts of the world. Some regional entities’ resolutions remain unimplemented, fail to address underlying issues, or are framed unrealistically to “respect” the demands of actors who may not belong to the region but can influence it through military or financial power. Hidden actors exploit racial, ethnic, and religious divisions, undermining cohesion among states and peoples. Despite regional intergovernmental organizations’ obligation to address major peace, security, and development challenges collectively, many have failed to do so.

Few “poor countries” have emerged from the ocean of debt and mounting loan interest. Foreign companies often extract and exploit enormous natural wealth while paying little or nothing to its rightful owners. The regional organizations to which these countries belong either cannot rescue them or choose not to intervene. Violations of human rights and dignity follow a similar pattern. Western nations often apply these principles “à la carte,” while their defense has become rhetoric rather than a genuine concern for regional intergovernmental entities and their leaders, who, too, bear responsibility for the deplorable conditions prevailing in many parts of the world.

I Accuse Senior Diplomats

Diplomacy is defined as “an established method of influencing the decisions and behavior of foreign governments and peoples through dialogue, negotiation, and other measures short of war or violence.” It is also “the process and practice of communication and negotiation between actors in the international system to achieve their goals and resolve their conflicts and disputes.” The 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations establishes an international legal framework for diplomatic relations, privileges, and immunities. The definition and practice of diplomacy therefore imply a process characterized by negotiated outcomes and the absence of treachery and violence. This rationale is central to building trust between adversaries and to sustaining long-term peace and security.

However, like politics, multilateral and bilateral diplomacy seems increasingly to be the art of deceiving the interlocutor, whether friend or foe. The spirit of win-win scenarios seems abandoned. Military actions by powerful countries during negotiations undermine diplomatic efforts and erode trust. Likewise, providing diplomatic cover for espionage, even within multilateral institutions, and deploying career diplomats at tactical and operational levels in war zones create further contradictions. Senior diplomats from many “poor countries” aspire to secure prominent positions in international or regional entities that offer significant political and financial advantages. In contrast, most diplomats from wealthy countries rarely oppose their governments’ policies and actions, even when those policies and actions violate international norms.

Serving one’s nation in any capacity is an honor for a civil servant. The question, however, is why senior diplomats do not speak out when their governments’ policies and actions cross every imaginable red line of unlawfulness and abuse the status and principles of their profession. They therefore bear a heavy responsibility when regional or international peace and security are jeopardized.

I Accuse the Business Tycoons

Business is the lawful activity of producing, buying, and selling products or services for profit. Its foundations are legality, trust, quality, and honesty. Yet some prominent tycoons and institutions have transformed business into a platform for particular political interests. Maximizing returns at all costs, crushing competitors through unlawful acts, applying double standards, or deceiving customers also appear in supposedly “non-political” commerce. Powerful individuals have long manipulated markets in free economies, undermining lawful trade and fair risk-taking.

The weapons industry has become increasingly profitable. In addition to official transactions, the sale of light and semi-heavy weapons to non-state actors through dubious traffickers contributes to countless deaths each year and fuels proxy wars in many regions. While some countries maintain an “open-door” policy on private gun ownership, most nations restrict or prohibit their citizens from possessing and using firearms. Illicit trade, however, undermines these policies.

Beyond their devastating political dimensions, the current energy crises that threaten the peace, security, and safety of billions of people in “poor” or “developing” countries appear to benefit parts of the oil and gas industry, including actors engaged in illicit activity.

In many circumstances, bankruptcy has become an effective “legal” means of stripping ordinary people of their savings and wealth. Offshore companies can also harm national economies while benefiting only a few.

The quality of certain products on the market is increasingly questioned because some manufacturers use unsafe chemicals to make them more appealing to consumers. In many nations, particularly those with weak economies, quality control is inadequate, and child labor is practiced openly. Despite numerous international platforms that bring policymakers and financial actors together, too little is being done to curb wrongdoing. This endangers the foundations of market economies and seriously damages the social and economic progress of countless countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Oceanic Islands. Business leaders bear primary responsibility for keeping their fields of activity lawful, clean, and trustworthy.

[To be continued]

Saber Azam is a former UN official. He is the author of Soraya: The Other Princess and Hell’s Mouth: A Journey to the Heart of West African Jungles. His third book, Nowhere to Go, will be published soon.

IPS UN Bureau

title: Saudi Aramco tower damaged in Houthi strike (VIDEOS)
content:
The skyscraper housing offices of the state-owned oil giant suffered only “minor damage” with no casualties, according to Riyadh

A skyscraper housing offices of Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil giant Aramco has been damaged in a missile and drone attack by Yemen’s Houthis. The group claimed the Sunday strike came in retaliation for Saudi-led attacks over the weekend that reportedly killed more than 50 people, including women and children.

The Aramco Tower, located in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District, sustained visible damage across several floors, with windows shattered, parts of its glass facade blown out, and internal structures exposed.

Footage circulating online showed extensive damage to the exterior of the skyscraper, while witnesses reported hearing multiple explosions across the Saudi capital.

NOW: Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry reported no casualties after missile debris damaged an Aramco building in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District. https://t.co/QhBkivFJ9x

— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) November 8, 2026

Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry acknowledged that an administrative building belonging to Aramco had been targeted in an “attempted attack,” but insisted that falling shrapnel had caused only “minor damage,” with no injuries or fatalities.

New footage of the Aramco tower in the King Abdullah Financial District shows heavy damage on the upper floors. Windows are blown out. Structural impacts are visible. https://t.co/QdOAtYQmIH

— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) November 8, 2026

The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses had intercepted several missiles, including two launched toward Riyadh, as well as projectiles targeting the kingdom’s Eastern Province and southern regions.

Another Angle of the Houthi strike on Aramco Tower in Riyadh . Firefighters can be seen working , the damage seems to be not too big for a Ballistic missile though . https://t.co/1irJ3MJH5e

— Nightmare (@Nightshade00077) November 8, 2026

Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, better known as the Houthis, claimed responsibility for a series of coordinated attacks involving ballistic and cruise missiles and drones. The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the targets included Riyadh’s financial district, King Khalid International Airport, Aramco oil storage facilities, and the eastern Saudi city of Abqaiq.

Read more

The attacks followed a wave of deadly strikes in Yemen. On Saturday, airstrikes blamed on the Saudi-led coalition hit the village of al-Shariyah, east of Sanaa, killing at least 33 people, including 13 children and eight women, according to the Houthi-run Health Ministry. At least 39 others were reportedly wounded.

A day earlier, an attack on a crowded market in Taiz province killed at least 30 people. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out airstrikes, while forces aligned with Yemen’s Saudi-backed government blamed the Houthis themselves.

The latest escalation comes amid renewed fighting in Yemen, where the Houthis made major territorial gains in September, seizing strategic Red Sea ports and islands near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s busiest maritime chokepoints. The militants also encircled Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, while Yemeni troops have launched a counteroffensive supported by Saudi airstrikes.

Read more

At the same time, the Houthis have stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia’s vital oil infrastructure, targeting Aramco facilities, including the Ras Tanura refinery and the Abqaiq processing complex, as well as airports and military installations. The campaign has increased pressure on Riyadh as it struggles to protect its energy industry and maintain export routes amid the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.

Yemen has been engulfed in civil war since 2014, with Saudi Arabia launching a military intervention in its impoverished southern neighbor the following year. More than a decade of conflict has left over 22 million people in need of humanitarian assistance and millions displaced, with nearly 300,000 forced from their homes since August alone, according to the UN.

A UN-brokered truce in 2022 brought a relative lull in fighting, but hostilities erupted again in July. The Houthis have vowed to continue attacking Saudi targets until Riyadh ends its military operations and lifts its blockade of Yemen.

title: Nvidia probes ‘Chinese honeypot’ claims after CEO admits affair
content:
Beijing has dismissed US media reports of espionage as “groundless speculation”, while the the company’s shares fell sharply in early trading

American AI chipmaking giant Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into allegations that its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was targeted in a Chinese intelligence ‘honeypot’ operation, after he admitted to cheating on his wife.

Following the news, Nvidia shares fell by almost 7.5% at the start of trading in New York, wiping more than $300 billion off the company’s value.

The 63-year-old billionaire did not identify the woman involved in the affair or explicitly mention China in his Sunday message to employees. However, he acknowledged the national security concerns raised by media reports, pledged to cooperate with the investigation announced by Nvidia’s board of directors, and reaffirmed his commitment to protecting the company and US national security.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote.

The admission follows reports by the New York Times and Financial Times alleging that Huang had developed a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive formerly associated with the Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed International.

Read more

According to the reports, US intelligence officials believe the woman was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information about Nvidia and potentially influence its CEO to lobby Washington to ease restrictions on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.

Beijing has rejected the spying accusations. “The relevant report is based on groundless speculation and is purely aimed at smearing and slandering China,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on October 30.

Trump had been briefed on the intelligence allegations roughly a year ago, while Huang had not received any warning from US agencies, according to the NYT.

Trump on taking Jensen Huang on his upcoming trip to Asia. "I would certainly take him. I haven't heard he's done anything wrong." https://t.co/uAsQhEe8ws

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 8, 2026

The Nvidia CEO subsequently accompanied Trump on a state visit to China in May, even traveling aboard Air Force One. In September, Huang and his wife, Lori, also attended Trump’s state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the White House.

Read more

Trump defended Huang on Sunday, telling reporters that the Nvidia chief “hasn’t done anything wrong,” adding that he would take Huang on another upcoming trip to Asia.

The US president is scheduled to visit the Philippines before traveling to China for the APEC summit on November 18–19, where a potential trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin is being discussed.

Nvidia’s board said on Sunday that a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, would investigate reports of a “foreign intelligence effort” targeting Huang. It stressed that it had no reason to believe either US national security or the company’s secrets had been compromised, while reaffirming its confidence in Huang’s leadership.

Read more

The scandal comes amid an intensifying technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing, with advanced AI chips emerging as a major point of contention. Huang has maintained close ties with Trump and has advocated easing certain US export restrictions on Nvidia’s products.

Washington has repeatedly accused Beijing of cyberespionage, including alleged attacks on NASA, the Federal Reserve and other sensitive networks. China has consistently rejected such accusations, accusing the US of exploiting cybersecurity concerns to discredit the country.

title: Anti-Russian naval group to expand in Atlantic and Arctic – FT
content:
The UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force will focus on confronting Moscow’s submarines, Defence Staff Chief Richard Knighton has told the daily

The UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a naval grouping aimed at Russia, is about to expand its posture in the North Atlantic, Arctic, and Baltic regions, Britain’s chief of defence staff, Sir Richard Knighton, has told the Financial Times.

The newspaper reported on Sunday that parties to the initiative, which also includes the Netherlands, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia, are expected to sign a pact aimed at bolstering the grouping’s presence on Tuesday, ahead of the Atlantic Future Forum conference.

Air Chief Marshal Knighton told the FT that the countries would move “beyond memorandums of understanding and exchanges and meetings into really practical measures.”

He named confronting Russian submarines in those waters among the JEF’s key objectives.

Read more

Knighton played up claims about a military threat supposedly coming from Russia, describing the current period as the “most dangerous” in decades.

The head of the British Armed Forces argued that in the face of the US long-term pivot toward the Asia-Pacific region, European countries need to step up their rearmament drive. With this in mind, the UK government has to find ways to sell increased military spending to the British public, Knighton told the FT.

The UK, the Netherlands, Nordic nations, and the Baltic states signed a statement of intent to set up a new “multinational maritime force” outside of NATO to counter Russia in April.

Moscow has repeatedly dismissed as “nonsense” allegations that it harbors aggressive plans against NATO, with Russian officials sounding the alarm over the rapid militarization of the Arctic by Western nations. Moscow controls more than half of the coastline in the region.

Read more

In March, former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer threatened to seize Russian oil tankers, forcing Moscow to start deploying frigates to escort them.

Meanwhile, NATO ramped up its activities in the Far North earlier this year by launching the Arctic Sentry initiative and established the multinational Forward Land Forces presence in Finland in June.

Around the same time, the Western military bloc announced the creation of Task Force X-Arctic (TFX-Arctic), which is an experimental unit to test assorted unmanned systems.

Speaking last March, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow was “concerned by the fact that NATO countries as a whole are more frequently designating the far north as a bridgehead for possible conflicts.”

Read more

“I would like to emphasize that Russia has never threatened anyone in the Arctic,” he said, adding that Moscow would not tolerate any encroachments on its sovereignty and would protect its national interests in the region.

Speaking in August, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov similarly accused NATO of “driving the region towards militarization.”

“Intensive military preparations are underway in close proximity to our northern borders. NATO is conducting large-scale military exercises involving non-regional countries,” the diplomat said.

Lavrov warned that these developments could trigger an armed confrontation with “potentially disastrous consequences.”

title: MAGA influencer who whitewashed Ukrainian neo-Nazis exposed taking cash for posts – WaPo
content:
Laura Loomer allegedly charged thousands of dollars per tweet, with clients hoping to exploit her close ties to President Donald Trump

Prominent MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who traveled to Kiev earlier this year to promote Ukraine and downplay its neo-Nazi problem, has secretly received tens of thousands of dollars for political posts on social media, the Washington Post has reported, citing financial records and people familiar with the arrangements.

According to the newspaper’s investigation, bank records and transfer documents show four payments totaling more than $60,000 to Loomer and her Florida-based company, King Breaker Media, since May 2025. Two sources claimed she charged between $3,000 and $5,000 per tweet, sometimes more.

The allegations were made by Alex Bruesewitz, an adviser to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, and three others familiar with the arrangements. Bruesewitz admitted paying Loomer through his political consulting firm, X Strategies, to promote policy-related messages.

Loomer, who has 1.9 million followers on X and has met with Trump repeatedly, both privately and publicly, has been credited with influencing personnel decisions in his administration. Some clients reportedly hired her specifically because they believed her messages could reach the president.

I’ve been open about my work in this industry. My experience is what makes me uniquely qualified to say it’s gotten out of hand. I’m not against creators getting paid, I just think it’s probably time for political influencers to disclose what opinions they are being paid for. Our discourse would be healthier if those arrangements had to be disclosed. Why are you so opposed to disclosures?

— Alex Bruesewitz 🇺🇸 (@alexbruesewitz) November 8, 2026

Loomer denied selling political posts, insisting she was paid for research and consulting rather than tweets. “My business is public affairs and opposition research,” she told the newspaper. “It’s not illegal to make a living in America.”

I personally paid @LauraLoomer to post tweets earlier this year. A good amount of cash too. I will gladly share screenshots, receipts, texts, and the names of other people who paid her. It was always very intresting to hear from her who she was willing to be paid to trash and who was off limits. @alexbruesewitz @washingtonpost @thedailybeast @Jerusalem_Post

— Jacob Engels (@JacobEngels) November 8, 2026

The revelations have drawn renewed attention to Loomer’s dramatic reversal on Ukraine following her highly publicized visit to Kiev in July, during which she interviewed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and fully embraced his government’s narrative about the conflict with Russia.

Read more

Having previously denounced Ukrainian “Nazi apologists,” Loomer emerged from the trip insisting that Ukraine did not have a neo-Nazi problem – even as she personally interviewed the founder of the notorious Azov Battalion, Andrey ‘White Leader’ Biletsky. He struggled to explain his unit’s use of SS-style insignia and Nazi symbolism, yet Loomer continued to promote Kiev’s image to her American audience.

Loomer claimed that her Kiev excursion was fully funded by “private donors” using “100% all-American money,” rejecting allegations that the visit was a PR stunt orchestrated by Zelensky’s team. The Washington Post investigation found no evidence linking the trip or her statements about Kiev to any of the reported payments.

Read more

The allegations have also triggered infighting among pro-Trump influencers. Conservative activist Jacob Engels publicly said he had also paid Loomer to post tweets and offered to release receipts and correspondence, including details of whom she was willing to attack for money.

Bruesewitz, meanwhile, called for the mandatory disclosure of paid political messaging, arguing that the influencer industry had become overwhelmingly financially driven. Loomer fired back, accusing him of hypocrisy for running a firm that itself pays conservative influencers to promote political content.

title: Republicans got Trumped. So now what?
content:
The midterms exposed deep frustration with war, fuel costs and executive overreach – leaving the party’s post-election path uncertain

On the same day that he led his Republican Party into a midterm electoral slaughter, US President Donald Trump told Fox News that he would move to Israel to “become Prime Minister” if Americans “got tired” of him.

This sounds like one of those “I’m moving to Canada if I lose” things. Except that he can’t actually threaten to move to Canada. Because even some of the most populist right-wing Canadians hate him for being unable to shut up about annexing their country.

He and his apparently unquenchable thirst for colonization could head over to Israel and spend his retirement fighting with Iran from right next door. It would last about 20 minutes when Democrats cut all funding and support. Think their voters are upset about paying for Bibi’s wars? Imagine how tight-fisted they’d be with ‘Trump’s Israel.’ Iran wins, opens the Strait of Hormuz, global fuel prices stabilize, and Trump finally gets a Nobel Peace Prize for single-handedly regime changing two of the biggest global pariahs.

Barely a few hours after the midterms, Trump was already warming up to the idea of just vetoing anything that the Democrat-majority Congress tries to do. Sources close to him say that he’d also resort to executive orders. All of which would leave Congress to prioritize spending their time impeaching him and hauling his enablers and sycophants in front of congressional hearings. Great plan!

Trump doesn’t much see himself as the problem in this election, suggesting that it was the GOP candidates who weren’t up to par. Of course they weren’t – they had to be tailored to his personal satisfaction to even survive the primary process, thoroughly disqualifying them in the eyes of everyone else.

Read more

He did recognize that Americans don’t like high fuel prices, but nonetheless considers that they just need to deal with it as he suicide bombs the American economy to assuage Bibi’s perpetual fever dream of Iran getting nukes. But more probably because his family and cronies are wheeling and dealing with Israel and the checks won’t clear until the dirty work is done. 

But here’s what we know about how Americans really feel from exit polling that surveyed about the same percentage of Republicans and Democrats. Most of them (60%) considered their Congressional vote little more than a Trump performance review. Most of them (53%) strongly disapprove of the job that he’s doing. Only 37% believe that he’s been fighting for people like them – the average American – with 62% feeling that he prioritizes his own personal interests over the nation’s, and made the economy worse (65%). They don’t even particularly like the Democrats (35% “strongly unfavorably”), and admit to being hardcore capitalists (57%), but they still think that the Democrats would do a better economic job than Trump at this point.

Americans across party lines feel overwhelmingly (71%) that the Republican-majority Congress abdicated its constitutional duty to exercise checks and balances on Trump’s executive powers.

The top voting issue was the domestic economy (39%) with cost of living a major consideration for 89% of voters. Their last priority was foreign policy at just 4%. In other words, by starting an economy-crushing war with Iran for his Israeli donors, Trump was literally doing the polar opposite of what Americans wanted him to focus on.

Read more

Three quarters of voters even cited the Iran war as a major factor in their electoral choice. But Trump wouldn’t know that from watching Fox News’ neocon slop all day long. Or from consulting with the ego fluffers who surround him and obviously only tell him what they think he wants to hear. Or from obsessively scrolling in the algorithmically-controlled echo chambers rife with nutjob influencers and bots, curated by the tech broligarchy more interested in government contracts and influence than the priorities of the average American.

At least in Israel, his policy passions actually might have a shot at aligning with those of the electorate. Because in the US, where a whopping 3% of the voters are Jewish, two-thirds of them still voted Democrat.

So what’s next for right-wing populism in America? For now, it’s homeless. No one within a mile of Trump has any appeal.
