title: Flooding and Food Security: The Urgent Need for Research
content:
Flooding is a complex, sequential plant stressor, and its negative impacts on crops persist even after floodwaters recede. Credit: Shutterstock

By Esther Ngumbi
URBANA, Illinois, US, Oct 28 2026 (IPS)

Recently, countries around the world, including the United States of America, celebrated the United Nations 2026 World Food Day. This year’s theme, “Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow,” highlighted how efforts to foster innovation and forward-thinking solutions can help to ensure that everyone in our world has access to sufficient, diverse, safe, and nutritious foods while safeguarding the planet for future generations.

But realizing this vision and developing forward-thinking solutions to help nourish 9 billion people including the 645 million people who still face hunger, requires recognizing and investing in research on emerging agricultural challenges, specifically those that remain overlooked and underestimated.

Many of the currently grown agricultural crop varieties cannot withstand flooding and crop and yield losses of up to 100 percent have been reported both nationally and globally. Crops and yield losses arising because of flooding translate into economic losses and ultimately food insecurity

Arguably, flooding is one of the emerging yet underestimated and underappreciated threats to important agricultural crops, including rice and corn, and to food security, which has increased in frequency and intensity in recent years because of climate change.

Globally, between 2008 and 2018, according to a Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations report, flooding was ranked as the second driving factor resulting on crop production losses.

Flooding deprives soil and plant roots of oxygen, a necessary ingredient for all plant-sustaining life processes, including water uptake, respiration, and photosynthesis. Consequently, plants’ cellular, physiological, metabolic, and biochemical processes are disrupted, impacted, and impaired. Without oxygen, plants’ growth and development is impacted, and if flooding persists for days, they suffocate and die.

Sadly, many of the currently grown agricultural crop varieties cannot withstand flooding and crop and yield losses of up to 100 percent have been reported both nationally and globally. Crops and yield losses arising because of flooding translate into economic losses and ultimately food insecurity.

Alarmingly, flooding also negatively impacts soil biology, chemistry, functioning, quality, and microbial communities while disrupting the many beneficial relationships plants form with microbes, relationships that help plants deal with other stressors and promote growth and resilience.

Concerningly, flooding is a complex, sequential plant stressor, and its negative impacts on crops persist even after floodwaters recede. After floodwater subsides, agricultural crops enter the second phase of flooding stress, referred to as the post-flooding stress phase.

During the post-flooding stress phase, plants face additional stresses, including reoxygenation and dehydration, impaired root function, and nutritional deficiencies due to altered nutrient uptake. At the same time, plants are vulnerable to pathogens, diseases, and pests, threats that can collectively lead to agricultural crop losses.

The good news, however, is that science, research, and scientific discoveries can provide the forward-thinking solutions needed to safeguard our food systems against emerging threats.

But for research to provide these solutions, researchers working to address these questions must be funded.

Take the case of flooding. With funding and investments, researchers can pursue multiple research pathways to understand flooding while also pursuing bold and innovative ideas with the goal of developing and advancing science-based solutions to mitigate the negative and detrimental impacts flooding has on agricultural crops and soils that underpin plant and ecosystem health.

First, scientists can build a comprehensive understanding of flooding, including discovering the many strategies plants use to resist and recover from flooding and post-flooding stress.

Second, researchers can pursue both short- and long-term field-based experiments that incorporate thousands of crop varieties, including wild varieties, across different soil types to establish a more comprehensive understanding of flooding and post-flooding impacts on plant and soil health, biology, chemistry, and microbes, as well as the legacy and cascading effects of flooding.

Concurrently, this research can identify microbial taxa, communities, functions, and traits that improve flooding tolerance. Additionally, researchers can work to determine whether the current management practices that have been put in place to protect soil health and help plants resist biotic and abiotic threats, including regenerative practices, are keeping pace with intensifying flooding events.

Third and most importantly, with funding, scientists from multiple disciplines, including plant biology, entomology, engineering, agronomy, microbial ecology, predictive modelling, breeding, and soil health biology, can collaborate to design innovative solutions and accelerate the discovery of new solutions to flooding.

Ultimately, mitigating threats like flooding that could derail and undermine progress toward building climate-resilient crops and improving soil health and biology requires a comprehensive understanding of flooding and its impact on soil health, biology, and plants.

With sufficient funding and investment, scientists, in collaboration with stakeholders, can develop transformative solutions to address flooding and fulfill 2026 World Food Day theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” Time is of the essence.

Esther Ngumbi, PhD, is an Associate Professor in the Department of Entomology at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign.

title: We Cannot Afford to Manage Chemicals One at a Time
content:
By Sheila Aggarwal-Khan
GENEVA, Oct 28 2026 (IPS)

Governments today face an extraordinarily difficult set of tasks: cutting emissions, protecting nature, reducing pollution, creating jobs, strengthening economies, and improving people’s health, all while public finances remain under pressure.

Sheila Aggarwal-Khan

Chemicals sit at the centre of many of those tasks. They are essential to almost every economy and embedded in more than 95 per cent of manufactured goods. An estimated 40,000 to 60,000 industrial chemicals are in commerce globally, moving through increasingly complex supply chains and into billions of products used every day.

For much of my career, I have worked at the intersection of industry, the economy, and the environment. One lesson has become increasingly clear to me over the decades: the greatest gains come when chemical safety is built into economic and industrial decisions from the outset, rather than addressed only after harm has occurred. The global construction sector makes this particularly clear; chemicals and materials selected today can remain in buildings for decades. Safer choices at the design stage can prevent risks that otherwise become costly and difficult to manage decades later.

At the first International Conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals, taking place in Geneva this November, this lesson will come to the fore as governments, industry, workers, scientists, and civil society, including NGOs, consider how to accelerate implementation across the full life cycle of chemicals and products through sectors where change can happen at scale.

This matters because managing chemicals one substance at a time – while essential in some cases – cannot be the full strategy.

Agriculture offers a clear example. Under the Framework, stakeholders have committed to take effective measures by 2035 to phase out highly hazardous pesticides where risks remain unmanaged, and where safer and affordable alternatives are available. A new Global Alliance on Highly Hazardous Pesticides aims to turn that commitment into coordinated action, while projects supported by the Global Framework on Chemicals Fund are already helping farmers in East and West Africa move towards safer approaches.

Textiles offer another example. Argentina is testing a digital product information system that allows chemical information to move with products through the value chain. That kind of transparency can help businesses identify hazardous inputs, exposure risks, the liability that can come with that, and then choose safer alternatives and determine whether fabrics can be safely used, reused or recycled.

Exposure risks cannot be separated from the economic systems in which chemicals are used. This is also why chemicals policy cannot be driven by single ministries. Agriculture, environment, industry, health, labour, trade, and fiscal policies all influence which chemicals are used, how products are made, traded, and whether safer alternatives can compete.

The objective is not more bureaucracy. It is greater coherence in which multiple, often competing objectives across sectors, can be discussed together to find solutions that work.

Governments have a particularly important role to play in creating the conditions in which better solutions can compete and scale. Clear regulation can give businesses confidence to invest in safer alternatives. Better information can move through supply chains. Industrial and fiscal policies can support cleaner production, while chemical safety and the safety of the sectors in which chemicals are used—from agriculture, to construction, to electronics, and textiles-can be considered alongside circularity, competitiveness, jobs, and health from the outset.

The economic case for doing so is strong. The global chemicals market was valued at roughly US$5 trillion in 2017 and projected to double by 2030. A 2023 study estimated that lead exposure alone was associated with trillions of dollars in global economic losses in 2019.

Countries building industries today also have an opportunity to avoid the costly legacies inherited by economies that industrialized first as they can leapfrog to clean, prosperous economies without having to go through an era comprising pollution, health and environment impacts, and clean up. Strong institutions, modern chemicals legislation, safer technologies, and green and sustainable chemistry can help countries build competitive industries without locking in the same liabilities.

Finance, of course, is the engine of implementation. Incentivizing industries towards safer chemicals, safer products and production practices, strengthening national chemicals management systems, and scaling safer alternatives all require investment. The way in which public finances can leverage private investment, the type of fiscal policy that incentivizes these investments, and the right enabling regulatory environment, can make this journey viable. Unlocking domestic resources in this way, coupled with funding from financing mechanisms such as the Global Environment Facility and the Global Framework on Chemicals Fund and private investment all have a role.

The challenge is therefore bigger than only managing a longer and longer list of harmful chemicals. It is to make chemical and product safety part of how whole sectors grow, innovate, and compete.

If we can get that right, safer chemistry can become part of how stronger economies are built, with safety built in from the start for people and planet.

Sheila Aggarwal-Khan is Director of the UNEP Industry & Economy Division

title: The World Is Watching Norway. Will the Country Protect Antarctica?
content:
Credit: Liv Arnesen

By Liv Arnesen
OSLO, Norway, Oct 28 2026 (IPS)

A global boycott of Antarctic krill products is gathering support. As a Norwegian, I want my country – the world’s largest krill-fishing nation – to change course when it comes to protecting Antarctica.

Scientists, explorers and ocean advocates are urging consumers to stop buying supplements and pet food containing Antarctic krill and to avoid farmed fish raised on feed containing it. This follows earlier moves by retailers – from Holland & Barrett in Britain to dm-drogerie markt in Germany and supermarket giants Woolworths and Coles in Australia – to remove krill supplements from their shelves.

I hope my government is listening. This boycott is highlighting a little-known industry and putting pressure on governments that support it. From 19 October, the 27 members of CCAMLR – the international commission responsible for conserving Antarctic marine life – will gather in Hobart, Australia, to negotiate fishing rules and marine protection for the last pristine place on our planet. Norway’s choices will matter far beyond our borders.

Liv Arnesen

In 1994, I skied alone to the South Pole, as the first woman to do so solo and unsupported. Six years later, Ann Bancroft and I crossed Antarctica, skiing from Queen Maud Land through the South Pole to the Ross Sea. Those journeys made headlines worldwide, highlighting women’s achievements. For me, they began a lifelong connection with Antarctica.

Antarctica taught me what it means to live on nature’s terms. Its vastness felt almost timeless. But as I have returned as a guide and lecturer, and paddled through its waters, my sense of its permanence has given way to concern. Human activity is changing this remote place. What once seemed beyond our reach is increasingly exposed to our appetite for resources.

Among those is krill: small, shrimp-like animals that sustain whales, penguins, seals and seabirds. Yet we harvest krill for supplements, pet food and aquaculture feed while climate change alters the conditions on which the ecosystem depends.

This month, scientists reported that the chinstrap penguin population on Zavodovski Island has declined by almost two-thirds since 2011, as warming waters are changing the availability of krill, their main food source. This raises an urgent question: how can we justify expanding industrial fishing when the ecosystem it depends on is changing so profoundly?

As the largest Antarctic krill-fishing nation, Norway cannot continue to claim leadership in ocean protection while treating the needs of Antarctic wildlife as secondary to commercial expansion.

For two consecutive seasons, the krill fleet has reached the 620,000-tonne catch threshold months before the season’s end, forcing an early closure. This is not evidence that governance is working. That total catch figure masks how heavily the fishing became concentrated in feeding grounds for whales, penguins and seals after regional limitations expired in 2024.

Krill may be abundant across a vast ocean, but wildlife needs its food where it can reach it. A penguin feeding chicks must return repeatedly to its colony. Krill hundreds of kilometres away cannot replace food removed from nearby waters. Fisheries management must account for those local needs.

CCAMLR decisions require consensus among all 27 members. Norway cannot secure an agreement alone, but the Norwegian government must use its influence to push for stronger protection. It must support a moratorium on Antarctic krill fishing until binding, science-based rules protect vital wildlife feeding grounds. Fishing should resume only when up-to-date evidence shows it will not harm the ecosystem.

Protected areas need effective restrictions that safeguard habitats and wildlife in the long term. Norway must support all the proposed marine protected areas – around the Antarctic Peninsula, East Antarctica and the Weddell Sea – and work to secure their adoption. These areas must provide meaningful, lasting protection, without making it conditional on permission to catch even more krill elsewhere. China and Russia must stop blocking their adoption.

The Norwegian krill industry says it supports marine protection and better fisheries management. That commitment should include accepting a moratorium. But we should also ask: why do Norwegian companies continue taking this food source from Antarctica at all? Algae-based sources of the omega-3s used in supplements already exist. A moratorium is the immediate priority. In the longer term, governments and businesses should invest in alternatives, and plan a phase-out of commercial krill fishing.

Norway’s krill industry is closely tied to one of the country’s wealthiest billionaires. Our government must explain whose interests it is defending: private businesses or one of Earth’s last great wildernesses?

I have carried Norway’s flag across Antarctica. I want our delegation to carry a clear commitment to its protection into Hobart: support a moratorium on commercial krill fishing, secure meaningful protected areas and reject higher catches.

The world is watching. Norway should give it a reason to believe that protection can still prevail over profit.

Liv Arnesen is Norwegian polar explorer, educator and ambassador for Our Antarctica

title: Trump’s Canada squeeze backfires as US 'desperately' needs crucial import
content:
President Trump's effort to squeeze Canada is coming back to bite American businesses as a new report reveals just how hard it is for the US to find an alternative to something it has long purchased from its northern neighbor.

"This country desperately needs aluminum," Trump admitted during an August telephone rally for Oklahoma Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei. He later added: "We don't have it. We get it all from Canada, for the most part, and we need it badly."

That admission now looks very odd as Trump has imposed a 50 percent tariff on Canadian aluminum imports, yet American companies still need the metal to make cars, build houses, manufacture aircraft, construct data centers and all sorts of other things.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the tariffs have driven the premium paid for aluminum in the US to record levels, adding costs for businesses that have very few real alternatives.

Higher material costs could eventually make their way to car buyers and families trying to build homes.

The issue is decades old, as there were 24 operating aluminum smelters in America 26 years ago. Today, there are just four, with Canada providing about 70 percent of US aluminum imports.

It's not simply that Canadian companies can produce the metal cheaper. Aluminum production requires enormous amounts of electricity, so the advantage of having access to cheap power is crucial. Quebec's huge hydropower resources give its smelters an advantage that their American counterparts simply can't match.

There's an irony in the very fact that America helped Canada build its aluminum factories. During World War II, the US helped turn the remote Saguenay region of Quebec into an aluminum powerhouse to supply aircraft and munitions. Thousands of Canadians built smelters and a hydropower plant in freezing conditions in just 18 months, and the region has supplied American manufacturers ever since.

Rio Tinto is investing $1.5 billion in modernizing its operations in the region, while a proposed $4 billion smelter in Oklahoma is meeting resistance over pollution, foreign ownership, and the public money required to get it built.

That leaves US manufacturers paying more today, while Trump's domestic replacement remains very much in doubt.

Canada, in the meantime, has found other partners, with its aluminum shipments to Europe up 77 percent year on year through August, according to the Journal, indicating that producers are finding other markets as Washington makes their principal market increasingly difficult to access.

For American businesses, that creates another problem. Even if Trump eventually wants more Canadian aluminum, suppliers may have other places to sell it.

title: Trump’s rally words obliterates his own case for Iran escalation
content:
President Donald Trump has spent the past week campaigning across the U.S., delivering remarks that a poke holes in his case for war against Iran.

The Bulwark's Will Saletan cited 13 rallies or press gaggles in which Trump detailed his expectations for the war and reasons for it. Saletan noted the president's claims just don't add up.

Saletan's video is aimed directly at Trump voters, and he's using the president's own words against him.

At a Trump rally in South Carolina on Oct. 21, Trump claimed, "Half of the things I am telling you I did I never discussed in the campaign ... I never said we're gonna take over Venezuela beautifully. I never said we're gonna stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon. You know, we have to do it."

Saletan noted that the president is spot on he not only never told Americans he'd end up in a war with Iran, he told voter the opposite. Trump told voters he believed in "America First," and that meant "no new endless wars."

Another point came from Trump's claim that "we obliterated Iran's nuclear program" after the 2025 bombing. But in February 2026, he had to do it again.

He made the point with an NBC Montana reporter on Oct. 14 while visiting the state. Trump said, "And they will never have a nuclear weapon. It was all about the nuclear weapon and we've already done that with our B2 bombers. They will never have a nuclear weapon."

Despite his claim that the U.S. took out all of Iran's nuclear weapons a second time in February 2026, eight months later the U.S. remains.

Then, on Oct. 23, Trump told his audience in Florida, "We obliterated Iran's nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer. You remember that? Late at night, 1 in the morning."

Trump also said he knew then it would drive up gas prices, telling his Arizona rally on Oct. 14 that he expected the numbers to be much higher.

"This is a very small price, people," Trump told the audience. "But we have to meet tomorrow because the Islamic Republic of Iran is two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon."

Saletan questioned why Iran was two weeks away when Trump said he "obliterated" the nuclear program the previous year.

"So he decided to start a war at your expense to stop a nuclear program that he had already destroyed," Saletan said.

During an Oct. 2 rally in Alabama, Trump told the audience he promised the war would be over in a few weeks. At a rally in Oklahoma the day before, he similarly recalled promising that the war would be over in four to six weeks.

"And I said it numerous times that it would take four to six weeks to get rid of the Iran nuclear threat, and I did it in one night. That was when the B-2 bombers went in there," said Trump.

Saletan said that he appeared confused as the B-2 bombers went out last June, not in February.

So, why are we still there, asked Saletan. Trump told an audience in Kansas on Oct. 19 that the U.S. could leave at any time because he'd already achieved the objective.

"By the way, somebody said you could leave right now. It's true. We could leave right now. They're not going to have a nuclear weapon. Those B-2 bombers," said Trump

He repeated the same claim at the Alabama rally, noting, "It would take them years to rebuild."

So he believes that the U.S. defeated Iran's nuclear program and he believes that they're not interested in starting it again.

"It raises the question," said Saletan, "why don't we leave? And the answer from Trump is that he won't leave until Iran signs a permanent agreement."

Speaking to Newsmax on Oct. 15, Trump made it clear that the U.S. could pull out, but they may be back in a year. Trump said he's worried that he "may not be here" in a year. He didn't elaborate. Instead, Trump doubled down a few days later to reporters, saying he wanted a written guarantee from Iran. Former President Barack Obama secured a 25-year pause of the nuclear program in Iran, but Trump ripped that up.

title: Choosing the Next UN Secretary-General: The Threat of Veto or Veto Itself Must Not Silence the World
content:
By Anwarul K. Chowdhury
NEW YORK, Oct 27 2026 (IPS)

The selection of the next Secretary-General of the United Nations has reached a critical juncture. It raises fundamental questions about fairness, transparency, regional balance, and the democratic legitimacy of the world’s most universal organization.

Ambassador Anwarul K. Chowdhury

The announcement on 21 October by the United Arab Emirates nominating its Minister of State, Ambassador Lana Nusseibeh, has introduced another dimension to an already prolonged selection process.

Ambassador Nusseibeh is an experienced diplomat with an established record of service to the United Nations. However, the timing of this candidature raises legitimate questions about the integrity and credibility of the selection process.

Two Women Lead a Historic Selection Process

Six rounds of Security Council straw polls have already taken place. Two distinguished and competent women from the Latin American and the Caribbean regional group of the United Nations, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana, have emerged as the two topmost leading candidates, with the former receiving at the last straw poll the Charter-required minimum nine votes of the 15-member Council.

It is a not only a historic first but a pioneering opening in the selection of the first woman as the Secretary-General of the United Nations, thereby fulfilling a Charter obligation (Article 8) and at least a decade-long global aspiration to set right the aberration of a lineup of men only at the leadership of the UN.

The two topmost candidates have campaigned diligently, presented their visions, engaged with Member States as well as civil society and endured the rigours and uncertainties of successive straw polls. Their perseverance deserves our sincere respect and recognition.

Yet their candidatures face opposition from two permanent members of the Security Council.

The Veto Must Not Override the Will of 191 Member States

This brings us to a fundamental question: Why should the preferences of two veto-wielding countries outweigh the collective interests of the remaining 191 UN Member States?

The United Nations belongs to all its members. Its leadership should reflect that universal ownership.

The veto, inherited from the geopolitical circumstances of 1945, continues to cast a long shadow over the Organization. When the preferences of a few determine the choices available to the many, the principle of sovereign equality becomes increasingly difficult to reconcile with institutional practice.

The overwhelming majority of Member States should not be held hostage to the veto preferences of two powerful permanent members. Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett have even received three positive encouragement, thereby majority of the five veto-wielding members.

The General Assembly Must Assert Its Charter Authority

There is also a constitutional dimension which deserves renewed attention.

Article 97 of the UN Charter clearly stipulates that the Secretary-General shall be appointed by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.

The General Assembly’s authority to appoint is explicit. It should never be reduced to a ceremonial rubber-stamping of the Council’s decisions negotiated behind closed doors.

If the Assembly finds a recommendation unacceptable, it has the authority to reject it. That constitutional responsibility should be exercised with independence, conviction, and without fear or favour.

The General Assembly represents the universal membership. Its voice, its authority must count.

Regional Balance and the Case for Latin America and the Caribbean

Regional representational balance is another essential consideration.

An established, though informal, understanding has guided the geographical rotation of the Secretary-Generalship. Asia was represented immediately before the current Secretary-General, António Guterres, who is the fourth head of the UN from West Europe, by Ban Ki-moon of the Republic of Korea.

Latin America and the Caribbean have produced only one Secretary-General, Javier Pérez de Cuéllar of Peru, who served from 1982 to 1991, 35 years ago from now.

The region’s expectation that its turn has arrived therefore rests on a compelling historical foundation.

Its candidates have invested considerable effort in the selection process. They have faced scrutiny, uncertainty, and political resistance. They weathered the storm with dignity.

To bypass them now, primarily because two permanent members remain dissatisfied, would raise troubling questions about the value of the entire process.

Late Candidatures and the Credibility of the Process

Late candidatures are permissible under existing practices. Nevertheless, entering the contest after six straw polls, including the decisive color-coded exercise identifying permanent-member opposition, inevitably raises concerns about procedural fairness.

It resembles arriving at harvest time to enjoy the fruit without having planted or nurtured the tree.

Various political calculations, sometimes rather arbitrary, surrounding the Secretary-General’s appointment have surfaced and featured often. They should not become a substitute for a transparent and credible selection process.

The next Secretary-General must possess integrity, independence, and courage. Gender equality and regional balance in representation should strengthen, rather than diminish, the search for these qualities.

The selection now before Member States is an opportunity to demonstrate that the United Nations remains faithful to its founding principles.

Eighty-One Years, Nine Men, Not One Woman

Above all, let me reiterate that one historic injustice and unacceptable reality demand correction.

In its eighty-one years of existence, the United Nations has not yet elected a woman Secretary-General — eight decades plus, nine men, and not one woman.

What an embarrassment – what a shame!

How can an institution that speaks of equality at every podium continues to model inequality at its pinnacle?

The credibility of the UN’s advocacy depends on its own reflection in the mirror.

This is an extraordinary contradiction for an Organization committed to gender equality and women’s empowerment.

The appointment of a woman as the tenth Secretary-General is long overdue.

The current two leading women candidates should not withdraw because of the threat of veto and pressurized by these two P5 members.

Their candidatures remain alive and valid before the General Assembly till it takes the final decision.

The veto must not become the voice of the United Nations.

The General Assembly must assert its rightful authority, as empowered by Article 97.

Ambassador Anwarul K. Chowdhury, former Under-Secretary-General and High Representative of the United Nations, Initiator of the UNSCR 1325 on Women and Peace and Security as the President of the UN Security Council in March 2000 underscoring women’s equality of participation; President/Chairman of the UNICEF Executive Board on two occasions; Founder of the Global Movement for The Cultural of Peace (GMCoP) and a well-known analyst of the UN system’s work.

IPS UN Bureau

title: 'Clunkers': Kushner’s dad flagged among 'flagrantly unqualified' Trump picks
content:
A new profile in The New Yorker examines the role of Charles Kushner, father of President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, who's served as U.S. ambassador to France since 2025.

Discussing Trump's ambassador appointees, Eric Rubin, a former U.S. Ambassador to Bulgaria, told The New Yorker's Lauren Collins, “Every Administration has what we call ‘clunkers,’ but we’ve never had quite this number of flagrantly unqualified people.”

From the beginning, it was clear —even by Kushner’s own admission — that he didn’t have the experience required for the coveted role. But being the father of President Trump’s son-in-law seemingly trumped all prerequisites. Kushner has no previous diplomatic experience. The New Jersey real-estate developer never served as a diplomat or lived abroad before taking office in 2025. Because he does not speak the native language, there is a communication barrier that could hinder his ability to engage with his host country. Kushner said publicly that he knew “a limited amount about France” when he arrived in the country.

Since taking on the role, Kushner has not been received well by French government officials, primarily because he is viewed as disrespectful to French protocols, which has caused friction. In one example, author Lauren Collins notes that Kushner failed to meet with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot when serious issues arose between the two countries. Kushner’s disregard for the meetings further complicated diplomatic relations rather than assisting in managing tensions between the United States and France. Kushner, instead, saw the meeting request as a form of reprimand rather than a chance to create reconciliation and understanding between the two. Explaining why he ignored the first summons, Kushner said, “I'm seventy-two years old. I'm not getting called to the principal at this stage in my life.”

Kushner has been publicly critical of France’s domestic policies, intervening when many believe he should not have. The author gives the example of Kushner visiting former President Nicolas Sarkozy in prison before criticizing Sarkozy's imprisonment, saying it was a “terrible slap in the face to France,” despite Sarkozy's conviction. Kushner himself has also been asked to answer questions about a controversial past, which includes tax fraud and intimidation schemes.

Kushner hasn’t seemed interested in the relationship-building crucial for his role, nor does he seem to have a presence at important events, such as official receptions and ribbon-cutting ceremonies. Instead, he prefers events that are deemed more entertaining to him, such as his efforts to bring an NFL regular-season game to Paris.

Kushner’s behavior has made many in the general public and internationally question whether he is an effective representative of the United States. Furthermore, it calls into question the long-term effects and how U.S. politics are viewed globally.

title: Trump fumes at Don Jr. behind closed doors over Russian wedding gift
content:
President Donald Trump isn't happy with his son, and reports say they've been battling over several issues in recent weeks.

The Wall Street Journal reported Friday night that corruption allegations are growing and are now on Trump's radar.

"The president has also privately complained to aides that his son Donald Trump Jr. exhibited bad judgment for allowing Russian businessman Umar Kremlev to pay for his post-wedding party in the Bahamas," the report said.

Trump Jr. recently married Bettina Anderson on a private island where friends and family were treated to lush food, beautiful weather and even a fireworks show. The island rental and events cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and the fact that it came from a Russian oligarch was yet another connection between the Trump and Russian nationals.

It makes it difficult for the president to claim that the probe into his campaign's ties to Russia was illegitimate when Russian oligarchs are handing out money and jobs to those who work with him.

Trump has said his son paid back Kremlev, though there's no indication of when or how.

The reporting came after it was revealed that Trump and Don. Jr. are also fighting over the Iran war.

“Remember when they said Trump would get us into a full-blown war with Iran?” Don Jr. wrote on X in April 2024, as Iran sent missiles and drones toward Israel. “Times like these should make us all realize how lucky we were to have Trump, his strength and his resolve.”

Behind closed doors, Don Jr. is ranting and raving about his father's war, The Atlantic reported earlier this week.

“Don has kept his views on the subject private, as he would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this, but I can’t imagine anyone who knows Don would be surprised by his personal views on the subject,” said a person close to the president’s son. Trump Jr. wouldn't comment.

The White House, meanwhile, said in an official statement, “Iran has been decimated, and one way or the other, the conflict in Iran will be over very soon.”

Trump has said the same thing since April.

Meanwhile, the week wasn't a good one for Trump Jr., who has taken public blow after blow.

One example is his ex, Kimberly Guilfoyle, who was ousted last week after she allegedly shook down a GOP donor for cash to pay her American Express bill. Guilfoyle is now threatening a tell-all book about the Trumps from her close six-year relationship with Don Jr.

On Friday, Don Jr. was linked to a recent revelation that Russian energy giant Novatek was pulling the strings behind the curtain for a project, known as Polar Train, which would help with Alaska's infrastructure problem on the North Slope.

The Financial Times on October 24 that the venture was initially associated with Gentry Beach, a longtime friend of Donald Trump Jr. who also served as a finance vice chairman for President Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration.

"The venture was initially associated with Gentry Beach, a longtime friend of Donald Trump Jr. who also served as a finance vice chairman for President Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration," said a report.

The Russian funds were going through the UAE-based company Tech Wave.

It's just another connection between Russia, the president and his family.

title: Fox News veteran demolishes Trump envoy’s 'absurd' Putin praise
content:
Fox News chief political analyst Brit Hume put President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff on blast after he praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" during peace talks in St. Petersburg.

When asked about how he felt about the interaction, Hume did not hold back, calling Witkoff’s comment extravagant before adding: "The guy's a war criminal, for God's sake, and he's rained down bombs on civilians without regard to human life."

Hume, speaking with host John Roberts on Wednesday's edition of America Reports, called the Putin praise "absurd," pointing to Russia's war with Ukraine and the high civilian casualty count, with millions more displaced.

Witkoff gave the compliment after Putin announced the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American who had spent more than four years in Russian custody.

"You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again," Witkoff told Putin during their meeting.

Hubbard, a retired teacher from Michigan, was detained by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022. Russian authorities accused the then-70-year-old of being a mercenary for Ukraine. He denied the allegations, and the United States determined that he was illegally detained.

Roberts excused Witkoff’s comments as diplomatic flattery, and Hume acknowledged that possibility, while seemingly taking a dig at Trump’s diesel deal with Russia

Hume then discussed Donald Trump’s reason for putting a pause on the Russia sanctions in Sen. Lindsey Graham’s bill.

The Fox News star said the president told reporters on the South Lawn that you don’t punish people you’re trying to strike a deal with.

“When you’re trying to get a guy out of what has been locked up for four years illegally, you don’t insult the guy,” Hume said. “Maybe you flatter him.”

North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis called the praise "embarrassing and outrageous," mentioning how the comment is insulting to the families of Ukrainian children killed or made homeless by the war.

Texas Sen. John Cornyn offered a rebuke, calling Putin a "stone-cold killer."

The criticism comes as Trump faces criticism for what many believe is capitulating to Putin’s demands and turning his back on Ukraine.

During the Fox News discussion, Hume also addressed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's willingness to freeze current battle lines as a potential starting point for peace talks.

Hume said the proposal now requires a response from Putin, who has rejected previous proposals to put the brakes on the fighting. He also noted that it challenges Trump, who has repeatedly blamed Zelensky for the lack of progress toward ending the war that Russia started.

title: Insiders reveal the singular theory guiding Trump’s historic world blunder
content:
Three sources close to President Donald Trump said that he has convinced himself that there is an evil actor meddling in the 2026 election to ensure Republicans lose.

The Atlantic's Jonathan Lemire and Simon Shuster reported late Tuesday that the president is operating under his own delusion that Ukraine is responsible for the effort to overthrow the midterms.

Ukraine understands that there are three major world events that could determine its future. One is the U.S. election. Another is the upcoming mid-November meeting in southern China, "where Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to meet with Trump and Chinese President Xi," the report said.

Finally, the G20 summit at Trump's country club in Miami, Florida is scheduled for mid-December. The authors noted that Trump had been dreaming about a peace agreement between Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russia's Vladimir Putin, advisors told them. It isn't likely to happen.

The report cited one Ukrainian official, who said, “It looks like this is all happening without us."

While talks are ongoing, Trump's recent decision to announce a ceasefire without it being approved by either Russia and Ukraine prompted anger from the latter as they paused and Russia continued to bomb the country's civilians. At that point, Zelenskyy said, "We're done," according to NBC News. The report implied that Ukraine has been holding back on bombing Russia's oil infrastructure. Trump has desperately hoped to protect the refineries in Russia to keep the costs of fuel low ahead of the 2026 elections. It appears Ukraine believes continuing is in its own best military interest.

"Some in Trump’s orbit have suggested that the United States go further and stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine" the report said. "Trump’s deference to Putin has been a theme for a decade, yet this new round of kowtowing has handed Republicans another obstacle ahead of the elections."

The reference is to Trump's decision to deliver $4 billion to Russia for a small sliver of diesel in what is expected to be a failed effort to reduce fuel costs in the U.S. The price of oil is determined on a global scale. The main issue is supply disruptions from the Iran war and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump "blames those strikes for the rise in energy prices while ignoring the real culprit, Iran’s ability to defy the United States and close the Strait of Hormuz. He’s convinced himself, three people close to him have told us, that Ukraine’s attacks on the refineries are, in part, meant to undermine Republicans’ chances next month — and, by extension, Trump," the report said.

Trump hasn't responded to the attacks on Ukraine's civilian population and their electrical grid. In fact, Trump commented that Russia hasn't "been doing much." Zelenskyy responded with photos of dead children in a park.

The Atlantic reporters recalled the 2024 campaign when Trump promised he could end the war within his first 24 hours in office. He later added that he could probably solve it before he was sworn in.

Putin appears to have convinced Trump to hold a private meeting with Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in China to discuss, among other things, Ukraine. Trump told reporters on Monday that he was open to it.

"It is no surprise that Trump is drawn to the idea," the report said. "His deference toward Putin is rivaled only by his regard for Xi, whom he hosted in lavish fashion at the White House last month. He has previously been intrigued by the idea of the three powers — China, Russia, the United States — dividing the globe into spheres of influence, although Moscow these days hardly wields the international clout of Washington or Beijing."

In the background, activists have been sharing memes claiming that after Russian data centers were bombed, pro-conservative, pro-Republican and far-right promotion significantly dropped. They've noted that since then, Republicans allege that Ukraine is meddling in the election, which activists think is an admission that they knew Russia was helping them.

title: WSJ warns of Trump threat to 'blow up US global credibility'
content:
The Wall Street Journal Editorial Board panned President Donald Trump’s emerging alliances with hostile nations China and Russia against U.S. allies.

“It’s hard to know what President Trump is up to at any one moment because he operates so much on tactical impulse. But he has long coveted grand bargains with Russia and China, and that may be his motivation now as he hardens his hostility to Ukraine and Europe and courts a Yalta 2 summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping,” the board opined.

The WSJ was quick to point out that the Yalta analogy doesn’t even apply because the original team of the first Yalta summit, Stalin and Churchill were U.S. allies in 1945. But the trio do resemble Trump’s plan in the way they seek to “carve up the globe,” according to the WSJ, and that is “the danger with what Mr. Trump says he’s open to now.”

“As we wrote before the 2024 election, this was one of our main fears for his second term,” said the board, pointing out that Putin has floated a meeting with China and Trump to divvy up Ukraine — which would pose a clear threat to U.N. allies.

“A new triumvirate that divided the world into spheres of influence would blow up America’s global credibility as a reliable ally. U.S. allies may be punching bags these days, but the U.S. network from NATO to Japan, South Korea and Australia allows America to deter aggression and maintain peace before threats are dire,” said the board.

And all that damage is pointless, said the board, because Trump can’t “force Ukraine into capitulation.” Plus, Trump “would own the ugly scenes of carnage that followed if he pulled intelligence and targeting help.”

“Curb your enthusiasm about a China alliance as well,” warned the board. “Mr. Trump might want China’s promise not to help Iran, but … Mr. Xi wants Taiwan in his strategic soul, and he aspires to subdue the island without having to take the risk of a blockade or military assault.”

Xi, predicts the WSJ, will no doubt exploit any opening Trump provides to push the U.S. out of the Pacific, even if that means abandoning 23 million free people “across the Taiwan Strait.”

“Trump’s advisers may tell him that voters don’t care about the post-1945 ‘global order.’ But the public understands that China and Russia aren’t American friends, and they know looming trouble abroad when they see it,” said the board. “GOP lawmakers are already unhappy with the President’s appeasement of Mr. Putin, especially given that Mr. Trump has so far failed to rebuild the U.S. military.”

Handing over Europe to Russia, and the Pacific to China, would open a “major party division” at a time when Trump is rapidly cascading into his “lame duck” period.

“It’s true that Congress and the courts can’t stop a determined President on foreign policy, but they can make him pay a political price,” said the WSJ. “A second Yalta is arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term, and the President would be betting far more than his own legacy.”

title: Trump’s Greenland threats spark arctic power grab as Russia looms
content:
The European Union announced plans to strengthen its presence in the Arctic as rising temperatures, geopolitical tensions and competition for energy resources and critical minerals reshape the region, the LA Times reports. The move comes amid President Donald Trump’s threats to take control of Greenland, a self-governing territory of Denmark, and growing unease in Iceland after Trump posted a map depicting both islands in the colors of the American flag.

As the Arctic warms much faster than the rest of the planet, new challenges are emerging, including the opening of new shipping routes, increased Chinese trade through the region, and a Russian military buildup that is heightening security concerns. “When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned stability in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

As a result, the EU wants to help set up a cable center which would assist in undersea communication efforts in the North Atlantic and Arctic. Russian submarines are suspected of preparing to sabotage critical underwater infrastructure in the region. The EU plans to use the funding to deploy cameras, sensors, and satellites to monitor the region and detect potential threats.

At the same time, the European Commission plans to support the development of a “sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable” that would directly connect Greenland to the EU, per a new strategy document. The cable monitoring system would be part of a larger security hub.

In September, the United States and Denmark reached a security agreement concerning Greenland in an effort to ease tensions sparked by President Donald Trump’s threats to seize the territory. Trump announced the agreement on Truth Social, claiming Denmark would grant the U.S. “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland, including the establishment of a “large military presence” on the Arctic island.

Danish and Greenlandic leaders also voiced support for strengthening security in the region, while emphasizing the importance of respecting Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination. The agreement was formalized by U.S. President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, which some believe is a pivotal moment in negotiations over Arctic security and Greenland’s strategic future.

Trump has repeatedly dismissed the science behind global warming, despite the Arctic’s rapidly changing temperatures. He has called climate change “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world,” arguing that predictions by the United Nations and other organizations have been inaccurate. He has also criticized climate initiatives as a “green scam,” warning that countries embracing them risk economic failure, PBS reports.

title: Ex-Canadian leader maps out the historic trap Trump’s sleepwalking into
content:
Former Canadian Deputy Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland has a warning for Americans: Trump’s attempts to push Canada around are hurting the United States, and driving a longtime ally to look elsewhere.

Speaking with The New York Times’ Ezra Klein in a podcast published Tuesday, Freeland described a relationship transformed by tariffs and threats to Canadian sovereignty. A country Canadians once regarded as a trusted ally is increasingly seen as a threat.

Trump wanted Canada to become the 51st state. Instead, his pressure campaign is encouraging Canadians to strengthen ties with Europe and China and reduce their dependence on the United States.

Drawing on her experience negotiating with Trump during his first term, Freeland offered a straightforward rule for dealing with him: “We do not escalate, and we do not back down.”

What doesn’t work, she argued, is excessive flattery from leaders who believe they can manipulate Trump by appealing to his ego.

“Well, I’ll just sort of butter him up. I will outrageously flatter him, and maybe I’ll agree to some things he wants, but it will just be on paper. It won’t be real, and it will all be fine,” she said, describing the thinking behind an approach she rejects.

Freeland favors something less theatrical: stay calm, refuse to be intimidated and make clear that threats will not produce submission.

“I’m not going to suck up to you, I’m not going to be bullied by you, but also I’m not going to raise the emotional register with you,” she explained.

That matters because Canadians see the confrontation as more than a dispute over trade. Trump’s threats have made it a question of national independence — and Freeland said Canadians understand that defending it could come at a steep economic cost.

“This is an asymmetric confrontation. And it means it will be more painful for Canada. Canadians recognize that,” she said. But she remains confident they will “hold the line.”

Trump’s tariffs, meanwhile, are also hurting the Americans he claims to be protecting.

Canada supplies U.S. companies with materials they need to make other products: aluminum for manufacturing, lumber for construction and potash for fertilizer. Taxing those imports increases costs for American businesses, which can pass those costs along to consumers.

“So tariffs on Canadian goods make stuff in the United States more expensive, and then Canada’s retaliation actually has an impact,” Freeland said.paste.txt

She called the idea that America benefits from tariffs on Canadian aluminum “perverse.” Her argument is simple: making essential materials more expensive undermines the American companies that rely on them.

Freeland recalled that Canada responded to Trump’s first-term tariffs by targeting politically sensitive American products while trying to limit the damage to its own economy.

“The last time the United States imposed tariffs on Canada, we retaliated dollar for dollar. I was the minister responsible for that, and, ultimately, America dropped its tariffs,” she said.

The goal was to create pressure inside the United States. When American businesses and workers felt the consequences, they would have a reason to demand that Washington change course.

Freeland wants more of that pressure now: international allies coordinating their responses, businesses speaking out and Republican lawmakers challenging policies that hurt their constituents.

She also suggested the midterms could change the calculations of business leaders who have accommodated Trump. If Democrats take back the House and Senate in November, for example, it's possible they could try to change course with Canada and return to the way things were by reasserting their authority.

“If they see that President Trump and MAGA no longer deliver at the ballot box, you may start seeing some very different behavior,” she said.

Her larger warning is that America’s strength depends partly on other countries wanting to work with it. Treating allies as adversaries gives them a reason to find other partners — and, she argued, China is benefiting.

“The part about all of this that I find not just depressing but horrifying is that the biggest winner is China," she said.

title: Trump has 'nothing left to lose' — and Putin has everything to win: Krugman
content:
Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman argued on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s increasingly open support for Russian President Vladimir Putin is really more about refusing to hide his longstanding support for the foreign leader.

In the column, Krugman warned that Trump’s weakening political position is making him more willing to indulge his authoritarian instincts, like Putin.

David Sanger's recent reporting for the New York Times walked through the president's efforts to rehabilitate Russia after years of war against Ukraine.

“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump claimed while speaking to reporters before leaving for a campaign rally.

“We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us. Remember that," Trump complained.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky replied to Trump's comment with a photo of a baby girl who was dead in a stroller after another Russian bombing of civilians in a park near a cafe.

Krugman agreed with Sanger's assessment that Trump's support for a dictator like Putin is unusual from an American president.

"What makes Trump’s support for Putin even more remarkable is that Russia has, by many accounts, been actively aiding Iran against America in the war Trump started. Who says so? Well, among others, Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. And the aid goes beyond intelligence sharing that has helped Iran target U.S. forces. Russia has also reportedly been sending Iran explosives and weapons components," said Krugman.

He wondered what Republicans would be saying if a Democratic president made the same move: "Even as that dictator was helping another nation kill American troops? They would be crying 'treason.' But this is all apparently 'fine' with Trump."

The reality is that Trump hasn't made a "pivot," the way the right appears to be claiming, said Krugman. When Trump claims "we" gave Ukraine "a lot," Krugman wondered what he means by "we," since Trump "cut off all economic and military aid to Ukraine as soon as he took office."

Krugman described it as a kind of "political bankruptcy" and the freedom to be the worst version of himself, which supports "corrupt, murderous dictators."

He also thinks that Trump resents Zelensky’s demonstrated courage.

The economist predicts much more is coming, largely because Trump has nothing left to lose if he flops in the midterms. Electoral pressures will no longer restrain the president and what he wants to get out of Putin.

"Trump can’t and won’t make America great again. But he can betray everything America stands for, and he’s doing it as we speak," Krugman closed.

title: Trump faces investigation threat in stunning GOP revolt over huge betrayal
content:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, U.S. Representative for Pennsylvania’s 1st congressional district, gave a fierce warning on Monday, October 19, when speaking of the recent alleged U.S. betrayal of Ukraine. He says he intends to hold any U.S. officials “fully accountable” if discovered that they were involved in limiting Starshield in Ukraine during a Russian missile attack last week. Fitzpatrick shared his lengthy response on X.

“I will be speaking with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his team this week to discuss Starshield, sanctions, and other matters pertaining to the defense of our strong ally, Ukraine,” he wrote in part. He added: “I will be assuring President Zelenskyy that anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable, to include public congressional oversight hearings, and immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head.”

His statement continued, adding, “Congress will unequivocally reaffirm that Ukraine is an indispensable ally to the United States, that Russia is a self-declared enemy of the United States, and that the United States will 100 percent support and defend the people of Ukraine in their fight for their own freedom against this brutal, illegal, and unprovoked Russian invasion.”

He says the country has a duty. “The United States must provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself. The United States must not import a single drop of Russian oil,” he wrote, adding in part. “Sanctions against the Russian regime must be harsher and stronger than they’ve ever been before. Each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor—and each and every one of these items will pass on the House Floor by an overwhelming margin.” He also referenced former President Ronald Reagan, saying it’s the way Reagan would handle things, and that the U.S. should follow suit.

Zelenskyy has accused Trump of betrayal over the ordeal, saying he was blindsided by it. "It's a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner," Zelenskyy said, as reported by Yahoo.

Starlink is a satellite internet network operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX that provides internet access across the United States and other countries. Ukraine has relied on the network to support its defense against Russia throughout nearly five years of escalating war.

Because of the limitations last week, Zelenskyy said things were made difficult on their end. Trump has denied any involvement in interfering with Starshield. "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon. And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been," he said on October 16 while speaking with the media.

title: 'Fair to say' Kushner-Ivanka Trump resort in Albania is 'dead': reporter
content:
Extremism reporter Will Sommer of The Bulwark believes Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner's efforts to build a luxury resort in Albania are likely dead.

Albanians haven't stopped protesting the plan since the announcement, and over the weekend protesters burned their Supreme Court building to the ground. Meanwhile, the parliament and the education department have been vandalized, and the prime minister is in hiding.

The plan was for Trump and Kushner to spend $1.4 billion to $4 billion to build a luxury resort on Sazan Island and parts of the nearby Zvërnec peninsula along Albania's southern coast. The problem is that citizens don't want to lose access to their beaches, which are part of a protected ecosystem.

Allegations suggest the president and other government officials are being influenced by investors. Meanwhile, there are residents on the Zvërnec peninsula who claim that their homes and land were sold out from under them to Kushner and Trump. The dispute centers on government actions, not on Kushner directly stealing the land.

At the same time, the environmentally protected land is a habitat for flamingos. As Sommer explained, the community's love for the birds and other wildlife on one of the islands has prompted the activists to name their uprising the Flamingo Revolution.

A New York Times exposé revealed that the project has already cleared large amounts of land and built roads and bridges. This happened even while the government claimed that everything was on pause for an environmental assessment.

While it began as an issue over the resort project and ties to the Trump family, it has become part of a larger issue of fighting corruption.

"I don't understand why this land project is not just dead," said The Bulwark's Sam Stein. "Clearly, no one wants it."

"I think it's fair to say it's pretty dead," Sommer explained. "I mean, you know, some of the payments have been frozen because of various corruption questions. Now they're calling for the president to resign. And, so, I think at that point maybe he can hang on to his job. If he does that, I don't think he's going to say, 'Now back to building the resort.'"

Stein thinks that the resort was cursed from the start.

They went on to mock Ivanka Trump for her comments about the "beautiful hectares of land" after she mispronounced "hectares." The pronunciation and seriousness of Trump prompted the men to burst into hysterics.

"And she just walked on it. It was pristine," said Stein with a laugh.

"It was like a Cold War submarine base," Sommer said.

"With a bunch of flamingos that had ended up there," Stein continued. "We had to have it. It's going to be this big eco-friendly resort. And now we have a Supreme Court building burning down because of this dumb, dumb idea. Let it rest. They should come out and say 'We're not doing this. Don't burn anymore buildings.' It's one of those situations where they started the fire. They should put it out."

title: George Conway delivers brutal Trump swipe after he loses Nobel Peace Prize
content:
President Donald Trump did not win the Nobel Peace Prize again this year, and ex-Republican George Conway is laughing about it.

The award is given annually to those whose work was essential in making the world more peaceful and just the previous year.

Conway mocked the latest loss and teased a different kind of peace the president with bring about in the "not-too-distant-future."

"With deep sorrow and regret I must report that President Donald J. Trump did not win this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. I know how devastated all of you must be. But inevitably someday in the not-too-distant-future he will give the world something much greater to celebrate," he wrote on X on Friday.

Those in the replies couldn't help but note that having a woman of color win the prize instead made it much better.

"A woman of color, on the International Court of Justice for her work vs genocide, war crimes etc. That was a direct shot from the committee at Trump, Bibi [and] Putin. So Trump is gonna be p——," biomedical engineering student Ben Johnson replied.

South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was named on Friday as the award winner “for her efforts to promote peace and international law," ABC News reports.

In 1967, Pillay became the first woman to open a law practice in South Africa’s Natal province, defending anti-apartheid activists. She became the first Black woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court in 1995, the details on the Nobel website said.

She also served as a United Nations high commissioner for human rights, so the committee highlighted her decades of legal experience in pursuing justice and accountability on the international stage.

The committee’s choice of Pillay focused on her lifetime of defending human rights and strengthening international justice.

Previous U.S. winners include former President Jimmy Carter, Vice President Al Gore and former President Barack Obama.

Trump has lobbied for the award but has never secured it.

Norwegian politicians fear that Trump could retaliate against their country if he doesn't win the prize, the Washington Post reported Thursday.

As the Post noted, vice rector for research at Oslo New University College Kjetil Tronvoll argued the committee should "suspend the prize for three years until he steps down, in order for him not to be unnecessarily provoked by it."

“Peace-promoting activities are more needed than any time before,” Tronvoll said. “But the prize committee has earlier shown very much a lack of contextual, deeper global knowledge to understand how sensitive this prize is, and they don’t do enough due diligence and risk-awareness analysis.”

title: Rubio hired tech firm after Kremlin-link warnings surfaced: report
content:
The State Department Secretary Marco Rubio awarded a $50,000 contract to Oxygen Forensics months after allegations about the firm’s Russian ownership and links to Kremlin agencies circulated within the federal government, according to a report.

PunchUp reported that the State Department granted the contract on August 28 via the U.S. Embassy in Zagreb, Croatia. The records indicate that the purchase order amounting to $49,999.76 was for "ICITAP - OXYGEN SOFTWARE", which is supporting a Justice Department initiative that collaborates with foreign law enforcement agencies. The award has a possible end date of September 1, 2027.

The contract was reached several months after Max Weissberg, a former employee of Oxygen, made a public claim that the Virginia-based company had been secretly controlled by Russian interests and that its software had been developed in Russia. According to PunchUp, Oxygen admitted in a lawsuit filed in August that government customers had asked the company about Weissberg's allegations as early as February 23 and that a document relating to the claims had been circulated among the Department of Homeland Security and other federal agencies.

Oxygen brought its lawsuit against Weissberg on August 28, the same day the contract with the State Department was awarded. The company rejected his claims, charged him with defamation and demanded damages in excess of $1.85 million.

On September 23, the Justice Department announced that Lee Reiber, the CEO of Oxygen, and the Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov had been arrested and accused of conspiring to commit wire fraud. The prosecutors claim that Reiber had hidden from American agencies the fact that Oxygen had been owned and controlled by five Russian nationals via a holding company based in Cyprus and that the company's software had been developed in Russia.

Federal prosecutors state that those same five Russians were also the owners of a Russian company which supplied versions of the software to customers allegedly comprising the Federal Security Service, the Investigative Committee of Russia, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It is alleged that the Russian owners of Oxygen kept on making major decisions of the company after their names had been taken off the public corporate records as a result of the broadened U.S. sanctions against Russia in 2022.

The Justice Department stated that its complaint does not claim that Oxygen's software included malicious code or had been used to gain unauthorized access to customers' systems or data; Reiber and Davydov are considered innocent until they have been proven guilty.

PunchUp also stated that in May 2025 the State Department gave Oxygen a contract which could be worth about $180,664.

When asked if the officials had known about the ownership allegations at the time the August agreement was approved, the State Department told PunchUp that it was “aware” of the claims and said it “takes seriously the security of its systems and the integrity of its procurement processes.”

title: Trump opens door to Russia deal that could enrage even his own GOP allies
content:
President Donald Trump has supported a plan that involves giving Russia some sanctions relief in return for the release of political prisoners, a move that could cause his administration to be at odds with Ukraine, the European governments and certain Republicans in Congress.

According to a report by The Atlantic, the initiative was put forward by John Coale, Trump's envoy to Eastern Europe, and it’s still in its early phases. Coale said to the magazine that he mentioned the idea to Trump following their talks about the release of prisoners, including Russian journalist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov, and that the president had then agreed for him to go ahead with it.

According to the proposal, Moscow would set free dissidents, journalists and other prisoners, while Washington could reply by relaxing a number of its economic restrictions. In Belarus, Coale has previously employed a similar strategy, whereby U.S. negotiations led to the release of hundreds of prisoners as Washington waived some of its sanctions and looked into trade agreements.

As Coale told The Atlantic, “All this stuff works toward the possibility of peace. The more interaction, the more trade-offs — either economic, prisoners, or whatever — leads step by step toward, hopefully, peace.”

The proposal follows by only a few weeks on the back of Trump signing legislation that authorizes tougher sanctions against Russia and countries that are carrying on major economic transactions with Moscow. According to Reuters, the law permits tariffs of up to 100 per cent to be applied to imports from countries that maintain significant trade with Russia or Iran.

Some lawmakers have urged Trump to impose greater costs on Moscow over the war in Ukraine, and therefore a shift towards sanctions relief could lead to tension within Trump's own party, especially if Russia has not agreed to a cease-fire.

Republicans, such as Sen. Mitch McConnell, have argued for tougher actions against Russia, while all but seven House GOP members backed the sanctions Trump signed last month.

Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine's president, has also stated that sanctions should not be relaxed before the fighting is over. Speaking to The Atlantic, he said that he would attempt to “block” such a decision and cautioned the United Nations that greater trade with Russia could provide Moscow with more resources to keep the war going.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time,” Zelensky said.

The White House stated that Trump was still focused on arriving at a settlement. According to an official speaking to The Atlantic, the President and his team are firmly committed to carrying on a constructive role in bringing about an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Coale's suggestion could also open the way for renewed business relations between the United States and Russia in the areas of energy, minerals and other commodities. The basis of his approach is the belief that economic engagement can reduce tensions and provide incentives for peace.

Ukraine, together with a number of European officials, has adopted the contrary view, stating that the sanctions should stay in place as long as Russia carries on its military campaign.

title: New White House claim exposes Trump’s 'incoherence and incompetence'
content:
New claims out of the White House are "mind-boggling," according to a new analysis from MS NOW, and further expose President Donald Trump's "remarkable combination of incoherence and incompetence."

Trump recently hosted a controversial state visit from Chinese President Xi Jinping last week, after which David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, made the "mind-boggling" claim that the president had asked his counterpart if he wanted to purchase American military hardware. Trump himself later denied hearing about such an offer, but also added, "they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea."

Perdue's explanation came as he broke down Trump's conversation with Xi about U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, a longstanding point of contention with China. Trump supposedly tried to downplay the relationship, as Perdue explained it, arguing, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,' before he then “actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point?' Official statements from the White House and State Department did not dispute that Trump brought up the idea to Xi, but stressed that no official offer is in place.

"This scenario, if true, is mind-boggling," MS NOW reporter Zeeshan Aleem wrote. "And if Perdue’s claims are not true and he was saying something false, that’s a significant and confounding problem, too, because it would not just be a major lie, but a foolish one... China is the only country in the world that threatens the U.S.’ status as the world’s preeminent military power, and the U.S. takes great pains to guard its technological edge against its rivals... Selling highly coveted U.S. arms to China would undermine the U.S.’ military advantage. It is common sense to not empower a country that lands on the opposite side of a lot of global geopolitical jockeying. Given that, for example, Trump asked Xi to curb assistance to Iran, it would not make sense to boost Beijing’s arsenal."

He added further: "If Trump made the offer, it would demonstrate total incoherence on China policy in the administration. Under the One China policy that has governed U.S. policy since 1979, the U.S. officially acknowledges China’s position on Taiwan but maintains informal diplomatic ties with the island nation, and crucially, routinely supplies it with billions of dollars worth of defensive arms... If the U.S. were to sell arms to China, it would undermine that entire calculation and would be akin to scoring an own goal."

Aleem also noted that, despite the alarming nature of the alleged offer, it was on some level "not surprising at all" coming from Trump, given that "he lacks even a rudimentary knowledge of how things like trade and diplomacy work, and has an even poorer grasp of — or commitment to — U.S. traditions in those spheres." It would have also fit with his well-established tendency to flout long-standing ties with democratic allies in order to better align himself with authoritarian states, whose leaders he openly admires.

"The capitals of the world are always watching Washington closely," Aleem concluded. "This episode shows a president who seems to have fewer and fewer wits about him — and a staff that lacks the competence or willpower to make up for it."
